The Unification of Matter, Forces, and Spacetime from the Bost–Connes System

Shao-Wu Hu
Shanghai, China · forest@xindong.com
ORCID: 0009-0009-8300-4691

Abstract

Starting from a finite p-adic reduction of the Bost–Connes system, we investigate the common dynamical origin of matter, mass, and forces. Matter is characterized as stable excitations whose patterns are preserved under propagation and exchange: the relative phases of their persistent evolution yield mass frequencies, exchange between stable states produces resonance responses, and the influence of the background energy distribution on motion produces a metric response.

We construct the complete process from the formation of a stable pattern to its persistent evolution. Directions and historical correlations retained in formation enter common subsequent exchanges, making path spectral responses, node overlaps, and generational distributions matrix elements of one mass generator. The same mass parameter then governs both the rest-frame energy gap and the inertial response at low momentum, while a common background response provides a unified energy scale.

On the basis of these dynamical relations, we use an odd prime pp as a structural parameter to establish evaluation relations for mass spectra and coupling constants. With p=7 and the common energy calibration E0=1GeVE_0=1\ \mathrm{GeV}, we obtain an electroweak scale of 246.19 GeV and an inverse electromagnetic coupling of αEM−1=137.03636\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}^{-1}=137.03636. The absolute relative deviations of the nine charged-fermion masses from the reference central values are all below 1.5%, and those of the three charged leptons are below 0.003%. The neutrino spectrum predicts absolute masses of 5.07, 9.96, and 50.63 meV for the three mass eigenstates, with a mass-squared difference ratio of Δm312/Δm212=34.52\Delta m_{31}^2/\Delta m_{21}^2=34.52.

Chapter 1. Introduction

The Bost–Connes system connects the multiplicative structure of number theory with time evolution in quantum statistical mechanics 1. Within its finite p-adic reduced state space, Dynamics of the Bost–Connes State Space (Hu, 2026) 2 establishes a joint cycle centered on exchange between an excitation and the background. The background provides a reference for identifying excitation patterns, whose form is determined by the relative amplitudes and phases at different positions. When a specified propagation action multiplies all components by the same nonzero complex factor, the pattern is preserved. The corresponding mode is called a stable state and takes the form of a stable standing-wave pattern. In actual exchange, the returning component continues the original excitation; its pattern and the share that persists are determined by the return action and the exit process, respectively.

Free evolution, formation exchange, and pattern reconstruction constitute a complete cycle. Free evolution accumulates phase. Formation exchange allows the original excitation to return or exit into the background, and also allows the background to form new excitations. The returning component, newly formed component, and restored background together constitute the joint final state. Pattern reconstruction gives its position distribution and coherences, and the resulting state continues into the next cycle. Changes in the position distribution provide a reading of motion, while repeated exchange determines formation, survival, and thermalization. The decay products of specific particles are identified in the corresponding physical processes.

These changes become comparable events through references and records internal to the whole system. A readable record exists when distinctions between processes remain stored in the environment or auxiliaries after a complete cycle and can be distinguished by mutually orthogonal pointer subspaces. Observational spacetime is a readout of the same state-space process: actual elapsed durations calibrate time, and position pointers calibrate space. Its geometric structure is used in Chapter 4. Cycles continue to advance, whereas a selected event may occur only after several cycles; cycle counts and record counts are therefore kept separate.

The pattern established during the formation of a stable state participates in subsequent exchange and determines the maintenance action available to each direction. The rate at which the maintenance phase accumulates relative to the same background gives the mass reading. A stable state exchanges with other excitations through directions that can be matched, producing a resonance response. The change it induces in the available states of the common background propagates to other positions, modifies the maintenance phases of local stable states, and produces a metric response. Mass and the two types of force are thus linked within the same process of formation, maintenance, and exchange. The records retained in the complete output determine how histories compose, while actual elapsed durations convert per-cycle actions into comparable frequencies and event rates.

Different stable states have different directions and distributions and participate in exchange in different ways. How do these internal differences become observable differences between specific forms of matter? Evaluating masses and forces therefore involves three questions:

  1. Why do stable states have mass? Which reading of persistent evolution can characterize mass, and why do different patterns produce different frequencies?

  2. How do stable states interact? Through which endpoints do the complete carriers exchange, and what determines the form, strength, and range of the interaction?

  3. How can these masses and forces be calculated? How do paths, participation shares, and a common calibration enter the evaluation of masses and couplings and establish their correspondence with specific forms of matter?

The structure of stable states, parameterized by an odd prime pp, together with their formation and exchange conditions, provides the basis for evaluating masses and couplings. Specific numerical values also depend on the structural parameter, the identification with matter, and calibration of the common energy scale. Calculations of mass spectra and coupling constants are thereby connected to the internal structure of stable states and to actual processes.

Chapter 2. Stable States

Matter retains a recognizable structure while participating in interactions. In the finitely reduced state space, this structure takes the form of an excitation pattern of amplitudes and phases. Exchange with the background forms the pattern, and subsequent outflow and return sustain its existence; the same process can also leave a phase relative to the background. To obtain mass from this picture, pattern formation, persistent action, and phase readout must be connected within a single joint evolution. The central question is how the spectral structure of an excitation enters actual exchange and becomes the frequency at which its original pattern is maintained.

2.1 Definition and Classification

Fix an odd prime p and a finite reduction depth K≥1. The address ring is the standard finite quotient of the p-adic integers 3. Each residue class modulo pᴷ corresponds to a lattice site, and the complex amplitudes at all sites together constitute a pattern in state space:

Xp,K = ℤ/pKℤ, ℋ = L²(Xp,K, ℂ)
dimℂ ℋ = pK
(2.1)

The background and excitations belong to the same space. With the normalized counting measure assigning weight 1/pᴷ to each site, the constant function b(x)=1 is a normalized pattern with equal amplitudes and phases; we use it as the background reference. Excitations are distinguished relative to this reference by the amplitude and phase relations between sites. This first specifies the reference for comparing patterns; the background preparation actually used in a cycle is supplied by the particular exchange process.

Nonzero sites are grouped into shells according to their powers of p, with zero forming a separate terminal shell. The equal-amplitude, equal-phase patterns on the shells span the shell-average subspace 𝒞; their orthogonal complement is the direction space ℳ. A general directional excitation may contain several components. Different propagation responses change their relative amplitudes and phases. If the entire excitation always acquires only a common nonzero complex factor, these relative relations remain unchanged, producing a stable standing-wave pattern.

Pattern preservation is illustrated in Figure 1-1.

Pattern preservation of a directional excitation is assessed through the shell-preserving response TelT_{\mathrm{el}}. Fix a regular spectral point s*s_{*} where it is well defined. A nonzero vector ψ∈ℳ satisfying

Tel(s*)ψ = λψ, λ ≠ 0, (2.2)

is called a stable state under this response. The common factor preserves both the shape of the position distribution and the coherence between positions. Representing the complete pattern by its pure-state projector gives

P[ψ] = |ψ⟩⟨ψ|‖ψ‖²
P[Tel(s*)ψ] = P[ψ]
(2.3)

Conversely, a nonzero vector after one response with the same pure-state projector lies in the same one-dimensional subspace as the original vector, and therefore differs from it by a nonzero complex factor. The condition above is thus equivalent to pattern preservation. Repeating the same response merely accumulates this common factor. A stable state here is a pattern-preserving excitation; a stationary state in the discussion of thermalization is a fixed point of the complete reduced cycle.

This criterion establishes stability under the specified response. In an actual cycle, thermal exchange, retrieval, and control must also be included to determine whether the returned component preserves the original pattern. The fraction of the original excitation surviving from cycle to cycle may decrease, while the background may form new excitations. Pattern preservation, survival of the original excitation, and total occupation are therefore described separately.

Elementary States

An elementary state is a directional excitation with a definite phase arrangement on the unit group. It extends over the entire unit shell: all unit sites have equal amplitude moduli, their relative phases are determined by the chosen direction, and amplitudes outside the unit group vanish. Different elementary states can consequently have the same position probability distribution but different coherent patterns.

To construct this pattern, denote the unit group at depth K by Gp,KG_{p,K}=(ℤ/pᴷℤ)×, containing N=pᴷ⁻¹(p−1) sites. The natural reduction π:Gp,KG_{p,K}→Gₚ,₁ maps each unit site to its residue class modulo p. Choose a nontrivial multiplicative character χ of the species-layer unit group Gₚ,₁. In the normalized site basis, the corresponding direction vector is

|ψχ⟩ = 1√N ∑u∈Gp,K χ(π(u))|u⟩.(2.4)

A character satisfies χ(ab)=χ(a)χ(b) and has values of unit modulus, so this vector is normalized. The sum of a nontrivial character over the group is zero. Pullback along π repeats every residue class equally many times, so the sum remains zero. The vector is therefore orthogonal to the unit-shell average state. It vanishes on all other shells and is orthogonal to their average states as well, hence belongs to ℳ.

The phases follow the order of successive powers of a generator of the species-layer unit group. Deeper addresses in the same residue class modulo p share the same phase. Section 2.2.2 develops the coordinates and repetition structure.

This distinction resides in the coherence between positions. The ratio of amplitudes at two unit sites u and v is χ(π(uv⁻¹)), so the full character determines their relative phase. Position probabilities retain only squared amplitude moduli and omit these relations. Identifying an elementary state therefore also requires the coherence information in its pattern.

The multiplicativity of the character makes the pattern invariant up to a common factor under unit-multiplication pullbacks. Applying f(x)↦f(ax) multiplies every nonzero component by the same χ(π(a)). The shell-preserving response acts diagonally along these directions, with normalized eigenvalue given by the resonance ratio:

Tel(s*)|ψχ⟩ = Rχ(s*)|ψχ⟩,
Rχ(s*) = L(s*, χ)ζ(s*).
(2.5)

At the chosen regular spectral point, this direction satisfies the stable-state criterion whenever Rχ(s*)≠0R_\chi(s_*)\ne0 and is called an elementary state. Repeated application of the same shell-preserving response accumulates only the common factor Rχ(s*)mR_\chi(s_*)^m, leaving the normalized pattern unchanged.

The species-layer unit group is cyclic of order p−1 and has exactly p−1 characters. Removing the trivial character χ₀, which gives the equal-amplitude, equal-phase pattern on the unit shell, leaves p−2 nontrivial species labels. Their directions are mutually orthogonal. If all these responses are nonzero at the chosen spectral point, there are p−2 elementary-state directions. A zero-response direction still belongs to ℳ but does not satisfy nonzero pattern preservation at that point.

This count concerns only directions on the unit shell pulled back from the species layer. The complete finite state space also contains directions of higher conductor and on other valuation shells. If several directions have the same nonzero complex response, their coherent superpositions preserve the pattern as well. Spectral degeneracy enlarges the corresponding stable subspace; pattern preservation of an individual elementary direction does not require a simple spectrum.

The character fixes the spectral direction of a species. Section 2.3 prepares shell-average components and conjugate directions as a coherent source, then combines them with the target and auxiliaries into a persistent carrier whose relative phase provides the physical mass reading.

Emergent States

Elementary states distinguish species through nontrivial phase arrangements on the unit shell. The collective picture used for emergent states involves the whole space: units, nonzero nonunits, and zero all participate with equal amplitudes and phases. This coherent pattern over the entire space describes the structure of collective condensation and provides the starting point for emergent states.

Write d=pᴷ. In the normalized site basis, the collective pattern is

|b⟩ = 1√d ∑x∈Xp,K |x⟩, d = pK.(2.6)

Every position has probability 1/d, and the relative phase between any two positions is zero. This coherent pattern extends over the entire ring. Under the normalized counting measure used here, its function is precisely b(x)=1; the site-basis coefficients 1/√d agree with the normalization convention for function values.

Participation over the whole space can be expanded shell by shell. Let eⱼ be the normalized equal-amplitude, equal-phase vector on shell j and hⱼ=|Sⱼ|/d its share of all sites. Then

b = ∑j=0K √hj ej,
hj = |Sj|/d, ∑j=0K hj = 1.
(2.7)

Thus b belongs to the shell-average subspace 𝒞 and is orthogonal to ℳ. The trivial character χ₀ on the unit group gives only e₀; b also includes coherent components on all remaining shells and at zero. The unit-shell share is h₀=1−1/p, and the zero-element share is hKh_K=p⁻ᴷ. These shares describe how the components form one pattern; the trivial direction on the unit shell cannot itself be identified with the whole-space pattern.

Scaling invariance fixes the relative amplitudes of the shells. Let D be the scaling pullback of amplitudes, (Df)(x)=f(px). After K successive applications, every address maps to zero modulo pᴷ, so Dᴷf=f(0)b. A scaling-invariant pattern therefore satisfies f=Dᴷf=f(0)b. Conversely, the constant function plainly satisfies Db=b. Hence

Db = b, ker(D−I) = ℂb.(2.8)

Unit-group invariance requires equal amplitudes and phases within each shell but allows different amplitudes on different shells. Requiring scaling invariance as well selects the unique constant-function direction over the whole space. This uniqueness concerns the direction of the fixed pattern; overall normalization and common phase still describe the same pure state.

This pattern also has a definite role in the full spectral response. For every positive integer n, the multiplicative pullback Tₙf(x)=f(nx) satisfies Tₙb=b. In the convergence region Re s>1, the unnormalized spectral transfer and its normalized form therefore obey

ℬ̃(s)b = (∑n≥1 n−s)b = ζ(s)b,
ℬ(s) = ℬ̃(s)/ζ(s), ℬ(s)b = b.
(2.9)

The normalized identity continues to hold at regular continuation points where it is well defined. Every multiplicative term gives the same pattern for b, so the spectral sum accumulates only a common factor. Nontrivial elementary directions instead carry the phase weights of their characters. The two types of pattern thus have different spectral responses.

This collective response exhibits the pole structure of ζ near s=1, arising from the infinite spectral sum over all positive integers. The pole disappears if the sum is truncated to finitely many terms.

The actual dynamics also includes phase evolution between shells. With shell energies HKH_Keⱼ=j log p·eⱼ, free evolution of the constant-function pattern is

b(t) = e−itHKb = ∑j=0K √hj e−itj log p ej.(2.10)

Shell occupations remain unchanged, while relative phases generally vary with time. Fixedness under the spectral response and maintenance in the complete cycle therefore have distinct criteria. The latter requires examining the actual exchange, returned components, and their coherence to establish whether the same pattern is recovered at the end of a cycle.

The background reference and a collective excitation may have the same system pattern. Their roles in the joint process and their readings relative to the reference determine their respective physical identities.

A stable pattern also determines how it can participate in exchange. Directions, accompanying resources, and correlations retained after formation enter subsequent action together, so a persistent carrier can be a joint structure. We first establish its structure and dynamics for general pp; channel selection and evaluation follow in later chapters.

2.2 Structure of Stable States

The structure of a stable state determines which components can participate in subsequent exchange. Shells specify the extent of participation, characters arrange phases within each shell, and position pairing organizes local occupation and coherence. A collective pattern additionally requires coherence between shells. These structures are developed below as the common basis for formation, matching, and mass readings.

2.2.1 Shells and Directions

Shells group sites of equal valuation, allowing participation in a pattern to be described layer by layer. We use the standard structure of discrete valuation and unit decomposition 4. A nonzero residue class is uniquely written x=pʲu with u a unit modulo pᴷ⁻ʲ and 0≤j<K. Fixing j gives the valuation shell SjS_{j}; zero forms the terminal shell SK={0}S_{K}=\{0\}. Each position belongs to exactly one shell, whose size is

|Sj| = (p−1)pK−j−1（0≤j<K）,
|SK| = 1.
(2.11)

Different phase patterns are possible within a nonzero shell. The equal-amplitude, equal-phase pattern gives the shell-average state eje_{j}, while nontrivial characters arrange phases according to the multiplicative structure of the unit group. Both are uniformly distributed in amplitude on the shell; their distinction lies in relative phases between sites. In the normalized site basis, the corresponding direction is

|fj,χ⟩ = 1√|Sj| ∑u∈Gp,K−j χ(u)|pju⟩.(2.12)

The trivial character gives eje_{j}. Nontrivial characters are orthogonal to it and form an orthonormal basis for the remaining directions on the shell. The component of any pattern on this shell can be expanded in these directions 5. Different shells have disjoint supports and are mutually orthogonal. All shell-average states span a (K+1)-dimensional subspace, whose orthogonal complement is the direction space:

ℋ = 𝒞 ⊕ ℳ,
dim 𝒞 = K+1, dim ℳ = pK−K−1.
(2.13)

A direction fj,χf_{j,χ} thus has both a shell label and a character label. The former determines its support and shell energy, and the latter its phase arrangement within the shell. Superposition coefficients then give the amplitude distribution of a general pattern. Which directions satisfy the stable-state criterion still depends on the nonzero-response condition of Section 2.1; pᴷ−K−1 counts the entire direction space.

A phase rule at a shallower level can be repeated on deeper unit groups by natural reduction. The smallest modulus pᶜ on which the rule can be defined is the conductor of the character. If θ denotes its primitive character, fj,θf_{j,θ} can be formed on shells j=0,…,K−c. Species labels, shells, and address resolution therefore have distinct meanings. For elementary states, we first take species-layer directions on the unit shell j=0 with conductor p, retaining the full space for formation and exchange.

Species directions, vacuum-counting addresses, and propagation wave numbers play different roles in the exchanges below. Characters label internal species directions; counting addresses distinguish participating, occupied, and available background modes. Position is a logical degree of freedom of matter and its local background, and propagation wave number is its Fourier description under translations. Although all three may be constructed from a common group structure, their actual maps and tensor factors must be specified separately. A formation pattern in a propagation zero mode does not mean that matter has no position; species shares at formation do not directly give occupation probabilities at distant positions. Chapter 4 controls contact and transport by actual position, while the configuration encoding in Section 6.2 is read through its own actual matching.

2.2.2 Phase Structure of Elementary States

Elementary directions have the same position occupations on the unit shell, so occupation alone cannot distinguish them. Their difference is how phase changes as one traverses the successive powers of a generator of the unit group. Fix a generator g of the species-layer unit group and label characters by ℓ. At site gᵗ, the phase factor is

χℓ(gt) = exp(2πiℓt/(p−1)),
ℓ ∈ ℤ/(p−1)ℤ.
(2.14)

Here t is the integer index ordering positions along the generator. Once the generator is fixed, ℓ determines the complete phase rule. Changing the generator changes the coordinates, while the group homomorphism represented by the character remains the same. The label ℓ=0 gives the trivial direction on the unit shell; the others give the elementary directions defined in Section 2.1.

Factoring p−1 into pairwise coprime prime powers expands a species label into several coordinates. Write p−1=∏i=1rqibip-1=\prod_{i=1}^{r}q_i^{b_i}, where qᵢ are distinct primes, i=1,…,r. The Chinese remainder theorem 6 gives

ℤ/(p−1)ℤ ≃ ∏i=1r ℤ/qibiℤ,
ℓ ↔ (ℓ1, …, ℓr),
ℓi = ℓ mod qibi.
(2.15)

These coordinates form the mode vector. Specifying them uniquely determines the species label; changing one coordinate can leave all others fixed. This is independence of the labeling structure. Whether an actual exchange couples different components depends on its operator. The product space of mode vectors is a space of species labels, not a direct specification of positions in observational spacetime.

The order of the character determines the repetition length of the phase arrangement. Write this order as oχ. The first return of the phase to 1 along the generator requires p−1 to divide ℓoχ, so

oχ = p−1gcd(ℓ,p−1),
oi = qibigcd(ℓi,qibi),
oχ = lcm(o1, …, or).
(2.16)

The image of the character is the group of oχ-th roots of unity, so there are oχ distinct phase values. Positions of equal phase form cosets of ker χ. Each phase occurs (p−1)/oχ times at the species layer and pᴷ⁻¹(p−1)/oχ times after pullback to the unit shell at depth K. The kernel describes phase repetition, not nodes of zero amplitude; a single character has constant amplitude modulus throughout its supporting shell.

The order and kernel size do not replace the complete character. Different labels can have the same order and phase multiplicities while assigning phases to different positions. The repetition length here counts generator steps. A temporal oscillation frequency must instead be read from phase accumulation and duration in the actual cycle.

2.2.3 Pairing and Observation Units

A complete pattern usually extends over many sites. Pairing by negation forms two-dimensional observation units describing occupation and coherence within each pair of positions. This local description retains relations within a pair; the complete pattern also contains relations between units.

Position negation pairs a with −a. Complex conjugation of amplitudes leaves position labels fixed and changes the phase rule χℓ to χ−ℓ. The two operations act on positions and amplitudes, respectively. For a species-layer character,

χℓ(−a) = χℓ(−1)χℓ(a),
χℓ(−1) = (−1)ℓ, χ̄ℓ = χ−ℓ.
(2.17)

Negation parity is given by χ(−1)=±1. Self-conjugacy requires 2ℓ=0 mod p−1: apart from the trivial label, only the order-two character ℓ=(p−1)/2 is real. The remaining nontrivial labels form (p−3)/2 conjugate pairs, an empty set when p=3. Conjugate phase patterns have the same order. At a real regular spectral point, their responses are complex conjugates but are generally unequal. A label counts as an elementary-state direction at that point only if its response is nonzero.

Identifying these two operations with spin or time reversal in observational space requires a separate construction.

Since p is odd, 2 is invertible modulo pᴷ, and a=−a has only the zero solution. All nonzero positions therefore split into (pᴷ−1)/2 distinct orbits Da={a,−a}D_{a}=\{a,-a\}. Each pair is a doublet, and its two-dimensional span is an observation unit. Zero forms a separate one-dimensional space:

ℋDa = span{|a⟩, |−a⟩},
QDa = |a⟩⟨a| + |−a⟩⟨−a|.
(2.18)

The two positions of a pair lie in the same valuation shell. The unit shell contains pᴷ⁻¹(p−1)/2 observation units, whereas the species-layer unit group modulo p contains only (p−1)/2 pairs; the latter cannot replace the full-depth observation-unit count. Dₐ and D₋ₐ are the same orbit. Fixing the multiplicative identity 1 as the observation reference point gives the reference unit {1,−1}\{1,-1\}. Its role differs from that of the background reference b, which specifies an equal-amplitude, equal-phase pattern.

Let ρ be the density operator obtained by reducing the actual joint state to the system. Its compression to unit D, occupation share, and normalized state are respectively

ωD = QDρQD, qD = Tr ωD,
ρD = ωD/qD（qD>0）.
(2.19)

Here qDq_{D} is the occupation share of the unit, and ρDρ_{D} is its normalized local state conditional on occupation, including position occupations and coherence. No normalized state is defined when qD=0q_{D}=0. Once compression gives the local state, the actual observation action must still determine which distinctions can be read by a pointer and retained as records.

For an elementary state of Section 2.1, let N=|S₀|=pᴷ⁻¹(p−1). Its component in the unit associated with unit position a is

QDa|ψχ⟩ = χ(π(a))√N(|a⟩+εχ|−a⟩),
εχ = χ(−1) = ±1.
(2.20)

Every unit-shell observation unit has occupation 2/N and normalized local pure state (|a⟩+εχ|−a⟩)/√2. The common factor χ(π(a)) cancels in its density matrix, so only negation parity remains within the unit. Different elementary states of the same parity give identical occupations and local density matrices in every unit-shell observation unit.

Their global distinctions remain in coherence between different units. Such relations become observable distinctions only when actual joint actions and internal references can read them. Complete species identification therefore requires examining how the whole pattern participates in observation. The connection of position units to physical generations and masses must likewise be established through actual readout and evaluation.

2.2.4 Collective Structure of Emergent States

The collective structure of b consists in participation by all sites with definite relative phases in a single pure state. Knowing that every position has occupation 1/d is insufficient to identify this pattern. The shell expansion displays both shell shares and intershell coherence. Its pure-state density operator is

Pb = ∑j,ℓ=0K √(hjhℓ) |ej⟩⟨eℓ|.(2.21)

The diagonal terms give shell shares, and the off-diagonal terms retain intershell coherence. Removing this coherence gives a shell-dephased background while preserving coherence within each shell. Removing all coherence between distinct positions then gives the maximally mixed state I/d. All three have position probability 1/d. Off-diagonal matrix elements directly distinguish the whole-space pure state from the maximally mixed state:

⟨x|Pb|y⟩ = 1/d,
⟨x|I/d|y⟩ = δxy/d.
(2.22)

In any nonzero observation unit, b has occupation share 2/d and normalized local state (|a⟩+|−a⟩)/√2; zero contributes another 1/d. Because both positions of a unit always belong to the same shell, the shell-dephased background gives the same local state in each unit. Identifying the full b pattern also requires examining coherence between shells. If an actual cycle uses another background preparation, its unit shares and coherence must be recalculated accordingly.

These structures specify what formation must establish. Shells determine the participation range, characters determine species phases, and observation units give local occupation and coherence; off-diagonal terms across units and shells preserve the complete pattern. Formation must establish these relations, and maintenance must preserve them after exchange and return. We now construct the actual process accordingly.

2.3 Formation and Maintenance

Exchange between excitation and background produces both formation and exit: the background can supply amplitude to a direction, while an existing direction can flow back to the background. Whether a returned component retains its pattern depends on the complete exchange and its records. We first distinguish these destinations in the original thermal cycle, then use the non-self-conjugate even elementary family to construct coherent pattern preparation and persistent action. The formed source, tracked target, and auxiliary degrees of freedom still involved in return jointly constitute the carrier; mass will be read from this joint object’s evolution.

2.3.1 The Thermal Exchange Cycle

A cycle begins with the system state and environment preparation, followed by free evolution, joint exchange, directional retrieval, and background restoration. The final system state enters the next cycle. The background and directions belong to the same finite state space; the environment comprises other degrees of freedom responsible for exchange, retrieval, and records. Each cycle contacts a fresh preparation ηℰ\eta_{\mathcal E} independent of the system and old environment. The old environment retains existing correlations but no longer interacts; this condition is called environment refreshing. The shell-average part is restored to a fixed preparation. The complete order appears in Figure 1-2.

Let 𝕌\mathbb U denote the complete joint unitary, VV the shell-preserving input control, and gg the specified restoration shares. Then

Ωnout=𝕌(ρn⊗ηℰ)𝕌†,ρn+1=Tr⁡ℰΩnout=ℱV,g(ρn). \Omega_n^{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb U(\rho_n\otimes\eta_{\mathcal E})\mathbb U^\dagger,\qquad \rho_{n+1}=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal E}\Omega_n^{\mathrm{out}} =\mathcal F_{V,g}(\rho_n). (2.23)

The joint final state retains all outputs and records. The partial trace gives system position shares and coherence for the next cycle; pattern reconstruction introduces no additional action. The total elapsed duration includes preparation, exchange, retrieval, and restoration. Environment preparation and controls are process data.

The same exchange directly connects formation and exit. Let |ν⟩|\nu\rangle be a directional mode and eae_a a shell-average endpoint, with shell energies Eν,EaE_\nu,E_a. Pair Faν=|ea⟩⟨ν|F_{a\nu}=|e_a\rangle\langle\nu| with an environment matrix element. On two joint states balanced in total energy and total unit-group charge, take

Waν|ν,u⟩=cos⁡αaν|ν,u⟩+sin⁡αaν|ea,v⟩,Waν|ea,v⟩=cos⁡αaν|ea,v⟩−sin⁡αaν|ν,u⟩. W_{a\nu}|\nu,u\rangle=\cos\alpha_{a\nu}|\nu,u\rangle+\sin\alpha_{a\nu}|e_a,v\rangle,\qquad W_{a\nu}|e_a,v\rangle=\cos\alpha_{a\nu}|e_a,v\rangle-\sin\alpha_{a\nu}|\nu,u\rangle. (2.24)

A directional input transferred to a shell-average component represents exit of the original excitation; a background input transferred to a direction represents formation of a new excitation. The environment carries the opposite energy and group-charge changes. The actual records determine how events are distinguished.

Write the exit share as ϵaν\epsilon_{a\nu}, formation share as fνaf_{\nu a}, and inverse thermal environment temperature as β\beta. The occupation probabilities of the two preparations multiply the same squared transfer modulus sin⁡2αaν\sin^2\alpha_{a\nu}. On a nonzero channel at finite β\beta,

ϵaνfνa=e−β(Ea−Eν). \frac{\epsilon_{a\nu}}{f_{\nu a}} =e^{-\beta(E_a-E_\nu)}. (2.25)

Thermal preparation constrains the forward-to-reverse ratio. The transfer magnitude also depends on channel occupation and exchange angle, and the angle depends on the actual generator and interaction time. Channel coefficients are given in Supplementary Proof S1.3.

Components remaining in the direction space after exchange are coherently retrieved through zero. Let z=|0⟩z=|0\rangle, with retrieval auxiliary input gg and temporary label aνa_\nu. The round trip executes |ν,g⟩→wν|z,aν⟩→wν|ν,g⟩|\nu,g\rangle\to w_\nu|z,a_\nu\rangle\to w_\nu|\nu,g\rangle, where |wν|=1|w_\nu|=1. The auxiliary temporarily stores directional information and returns to the common input at the end, permitting coherence between directions to survive. The net phase must also include free evolution.

The shell-average part is restored to σgsh=∑agaPea\sigma_g^{\mathrm{sh}}=\sum_a g_aP_{e_a}, where ga>0g_a>0 and ∑aga=1\sum_ag_a=1. The actual isometry maps eae_a to Ya=∑jgjej⊗rjaY_a=\sum_j\sqrt{g_j}\,e_j\otimes r_{ja}. Restoration labels are mutually orthogonal and orthogonal to the directional-return input. Thus Tr⁡R|Ya⟩⟨Yb|=δabσgsh\operatorname{Tr}_R|Y_a\rangle\langle Y_b|=\delta_{ab}\sigma_g^{\mathrm{sh}}, and cross terms between directional and restored outputs vanish as well. The system loses the corresponding coherence while correlations remain in the joint output. The auxiliary state gg and restoration share gag_a are used separately here.

Let ϵν=∑aϵaν\epsilon_\nu=\sum_a\epsilon_{a\nu} and Pν=|ν⟩⟨ν|P_\nu=|\nu\rangle\langle\nu|, and denote the original excitation’s return subchannel by 𝒬I\mathcal Q_I. Without input control, V=IV=I,

ℱI,g(Pν)=(1−ϵν)Pν+ϵνσgsh,ℱI,g(Pea)=∑νfνaPν+(1−∑νfνa)σgsh,𝒬In(Pν)=(1−ϵν)nPν. \begin{aligned} \mathcal F_{I,g}(P_\nu)&=(1-\epsilon_\nu)P_\nu+\epsilon_\nu\sigma_g^{\mathrm{sh}},\\ \mathcal F_{I,g}(P_{e_a})&=\sum_\nu f_{\nu a}P_\nu +\left(1-\sum_\nu f_{\nu a}\right)\sigma_g^{\mathrm{sh}},\\ \mathcal Q_I^n(P_\nu)&=(1-\epsilon_\nu)^nP_\nu. \end{aligned} (2.26)

The first two equations retain every destination of directional and background inputs, respectively, each with total trace one. The third tracks the original excitation continuously before its exit. Its normalized pattern after every return remains PνP_\nu, while its survival share can decrease each cycle. New excitations formed later from the background are counted separately. Stationary total occupation and permanent survival of the original excitation are therefore different statements. A lifetime additionally requires the complete cycle period and exit channels.

The original cycle provides directional formation, pattern-preserving return, background restoration, and the thermal ratio of formation to exit shares. The next subsection constructs a common source comprising background and conjugate directions through label alignment and feedback, then generates phase through actual return. Coherence recurrences and conserved-energy conditions for the fixed thermal cycle are in Supplementary Proof S1; thermalization follows Section 4.4 of Ref. 2.

2.3.2 Formation of a Coherent Pattern

Subsequent exchange requires a coherent pattern containing background and conjugate-direction components, allowing constructive or destructive interference within position groups. Fix a non-self-conjugate even direction θ,θ‾\theta,\bar\theta and write σ0=(ψθ+ψθ‾)/2\sigma_0=(\psi_\theta+\psi_{\bar\theta})/\sqrt2. At the background input e0⊗bse_0\otimes b_s accepted by the common thermal preparation, use conjugate equal-angle exchange, label alignment, and positive-branch feedback.

The bare exchange on the bright plane ℬ=span⁡{e0,σ0}\mathcal B=\operatorname{span}\{e_0,\sigma_0\}, the two-dimensional subspace coupled to the common input, is XA=|e0⟩⟨σ0|+h.c.X_A=|e_0\rangle\langle\sigma_0|+\mathrm{h.c.}. Its eigenpatterns Φ±=(e0±σ0)/2\Phi_\pm=(e_0\pm\sigma_0)/\sqrt2 have background and directional components of equal amplitude. Feedback sends both input branches to the same Φ+\Phi_+, transferring their distinction to records.

Specifically, use a zero-energy pointer and apply a Hadamard, controlled eiαPAe−iαXAe^{i\alpha P_A}e^{-i\alpha X_A}, and another Hadamard. For outcome 1, apply background–direction sign feedback. Finally, apply e−iαXAe^{-i\alpha X_A}, where PA=XA2P_A=X_A^2. Multiplying the two pointer outputs (I±eiαPAe−iαXA)/2(I\pm e^{i\alpha P_A}e^{-i\alpha X_A})/2 by the feedback gives, on the bright plane,

A0|ℬ=e−iαP++cos⁡αe2iαP−,A1|ℬ=−isin⁡α|Φ+⟩⟨Φ−|,P±=|Φ±⟩⟨Φ±|. \begin{aligned} A_0|_{\mathcal B}&=e^{-i\alpha}P_+ +\cos\alpha\,e^{2i\alpha}P_-,\\ A_1|_{\mathcal B}&=-i\sin\alpha\,|\Phi_+\rangle\langle\Phi_-|, \qquad P_\pm=|\Phi_\pm\rangle\langle\Phi_\pm|. \end{aligned} (2.27)

At the first full-exchange angle α=π/2\alpha=\pi/2, retaining every pointer and thermal label, any bright-plane input satisfies

xΦ++yΦ−↦−iΦ+⊗(x|0⟩+y|1⟩)D⊗bs. \boxed{x\Phi_++y\Phi_- \longmapsto-i\Phi_+\otimes(x|0\rangle+y|1\rangle)_D\otimes b_s.} (2.28)

Source and records factorize, with all joint information retained. Starting from e0e_0, the two outcomes each have share one half; failures of the initial thermal preparation are retained separately. One-cycle delivery is not guaranteed for components of the three-dimensional source outside the bright plane; their formation is treated in Section 2.3.7.

Take a well-defined real spectral point s*∈ℝs_*\in\mathbb R. For a nonzero spectral response L(s*,θ)≠0L(s_*,\theta)\ne0, next apply its polar-decomposition unitary on the selected conjugate-direction block and the identity on the background. Writing the bare spectral phase as δθ=arg⁡L(s*,θ)\delta_\theta=\arg L(s_*,\theta) gives

σδθ=eiδθψθ+e−iδθψθ‾2,Φδθ=e0+σδθ2. \sigma_{\delta_\theta}=\frac{e^{i\delta_\theta}\psi_\theta+e^{-i\delta_\theta}\psi_{\bar\theta}}{\sqrt2},\qquad \Phi_{\delta_\theta}=\frac{e_0+\sigma_{\delta_\theta}}{\sqrt2}. (2.29)

When adopting Rθ=L(s*,θ)/ζ(s*)R_\theta=L(s_*,\theta)/\zeta(s_*), compensate the denominator phase with the same spectral reference so that the relative background–direction phase follows the convention of LL. The control realizes the common exchange angle; its strength, total elapsed duration, and feedback energy supply for an always-on exchange term are included in the process.

Group shares of this pattern follow directly from interference. Take the species-layer reference point x0=1x_0=1. Let 𝒟j\mathcal D_j be all deeper lifts of the point pair modulo pp, PjP_j the group projection, and d‾j\bar d_j the normalized equal-phase vector within the group. For an even character faithful and non-self-conjugate on the quotient, m=(p−1)/2≥3m=(p-1)/2\ge3. Fixing the phase order, uniform lifting gives

⟨d‾j|e0⟩=1m,⟨d‾j|ψθ⟩=e2πij/mm,⟨d‾j|Φδ⟩=1+2cos⁡(δ+2πj/m)2m. \begin{aligned} \langle\bar d_j|e_0\rangle&=\frac1{\sqrt m},\qquad \langle\bar d_j|\psi_\theta\rangle=\frac{e^{2\pi ij/m}}{\sqrt m},\\ \langle\bar d_j|\Phi_\delta\rangle &=\frac{1+\sqrt2\cos(\delta+2\pi j/m)}{\sqrt{2m}}. \end{aligned} (2.30)

The complete group projection selects the equal-phase direction within the group from this pattern, hence

pj(δ)=⟨Φδ|Pj|Φδ⟩=|⟨d‾j|Φδ⟩|2=[1+2cos⁡(δ+2πj/m)]22m,∑jpj=1. p_j(\delta)=\langle\Phi_\delta|P_j|\Phi_\delta\rangle =|\langle\bar d_j|\Phi_\delta\rangle|^2 =\frac{[1+\sqrt2\cos(\delta+2\pi j/m)]^2}{2m},\qquad\sum_jp_j=1. (2.31)

Uniform lifting of the species layer makes the result valid for every KK. Lower-order characters, nonuniform deeper preparations, and self-conjugate directions require calculations with their own patterns. Formation has now supplied pjp_j; Section 2.4.4 calculates how it becomes a coefficient of persistent action.

2.3.3 Formation-Phase Corrections

A formation pattern can acquire a further phase modification during a complete spectral excursion and return. Two quantities must be calculated together: the action produced by spectral auxiliaries and the phase left after they return. Let UθU_\theta be the spectral unitary completed with failure outputs, rr its input, and xx the specified single-address output. Its effect is

Qθ=Uθ†PxUθ,wsp=⟨r|Qθ|r⟩. Q_\theta=U_\theta^\dagger P_xU_\theta,\qquad w_{\mathrm{sp}}=\langle r|Q_\theta|r\rangle. (2.32)

The squared term comes from two independent auxiliaries; reusing correlated auxiliaries requires recalculating their joint moment. To convert this mean into phase, the auxiliaries must participate in the outward evolution and return to a common input while preserving the action within the formation space.

On the formation space ℋF=span⁡{e0,ψθ,ψθ‾}\mathcal H_F=\operatorname{span}\{e_0,\psi_\theta,\psi_{\bar\theta}\}, let ZF=Pθ−Pθ‾Z_F=P_\theta-P_{\bar\theta} and embed the common auxiliary input as 𝒥Fψ=ψ⊗rM\mathcal J_F\psi=\psi\otimes r_M. The two outward stages are generated by G0=ZF⊗A0G_0=Z_F\otimes A_0 and G1=−ZF⊗A1G_1=-Z_F\otimes A_1. The return retraces the actual subspace path, using simultaneous arms with a relative minus sign to cancel action leaving that subspace while retaining its internal phase. The first stage leaves swspZFsw_{\mathrm{sp}}Z_F and the second −swsp2ZF/m-sw_{\mathrm{sp}}^2Z_F/\sqrt m. They commute within the input space, giving

ℛs(ψ⊗rM)=eisaZFψ⊗rM,ZF=Pθ−Pθ‾. \mathcal R_s(\psi\otimes r_M) =e^{isaZ_F}\psi\otimes r_M,\qquad Z_F=P_\theta-P_{\bar\theta}. (2.34)

The background component e0e_0 is unchanged, while the two directions acquire opposite phases. The formed source becomes Φs:=Φδθ+sa\Phi_s:=\Phi_{\delta_\theta+sa}, with group shares pj(s):=pj(δθ+sa)p_j(s):=p_j(\delta_\theta+sa). Reflections along the path are determined by the input preparation and act on the entire space to be formed and its controllable auxiliaries. The return generator, ordered composition, and actual round-trip duration are derived in Supplementary Proof S2.

Here ss is the actual net action, determined jointly by spectral coupling and action duration in the complete return and accounted for separately from the completed-event count. The formation angle retains this variable; its correspondence with the chosen spectral kernel and its evaluation are given in Section 8.1.

2.3.4 Formation Records and Coherence

Formation can leave different records while producing the same source. What matters is whether those distinctions remain correlated with subsequent logical states. For an accepted bright background input, both full-feedback outcomes produce the positive source and execute the spectral modification only once. Completion records no longer participate in later action, and unaccepted resources no longer couple to the source.

Let hh label accepted fine preparation histories, bhb_h their amplitudes, and d=0,1d=0,1 the full-feedback outcome. Let 𝒥in\mathcal J_{\mathrm{in}} be the isometry combining the fixed background input and retained logic, and 𝒥F,s\mathcal J_{F,s} the common delivery. Finitely many independent preparation attempts satisfy

Kh,d𝒥in=−ibh2𝒥F,s,QM=∑hwithin the first M attempts, accepted|bh|2≤1.K_{h,d}\mathcal J_{\mathrm{in}}=-\frac{i b_h}{\sqrt2}\mathcal J_{F,s},\qquad Q_M=\sum_{h\,\text{within the first }M\text{ attempts, accepted}}|b_h|^2\le1.(2.35)

The two feedback outcomes together assign weight |bh|2|b_h|^2 to each accepted history; unaccepted outcomes and the waiting tail have total share 1−QM1-Q_M. For single-attempt acceptance probability qFq_F, Q1=qFQ_1=q_F. Only a separately labeled input branch requires multiplication by its additional weight. Waiting changes the delivery probability and time without repeatedly accumulating the formation angle on a completed source. Under incomplete feedback, negative-branch occupation is multiplied each round by cos⁡2α\cos^2\alpha and must still be treated as input undergoing formation.

Common return has a general criterion. Let 𝒥,𝒥out\mathcal J,\mathcal J_{\mathrm{out}} be fixed input and output isometries and VV a fixed logical unitary. The return subchannel equals qAd⁡Vq\operatorname{Ad}_V on this space if and only if every actual fine history satisfies

Kh𝒥=ch𝒥outV,∑h|ch|2=q. K_h\mathcal J=c_h\mathcal J_{\mathrm{out}}V,\qquad \sum_h|c_h|^2=q. (2.36)

Sufficiency follows by summation. For q>0q>0, necessity follows from the rank-one Choi matrix of the channel: all Kraus vectors must be collinear. When q=0q=0, every Kh𝒥K_h\mathcal J is zero. With nonzero return, arbitrary input superpositions and coherence with spectator systems return under the same VV, a stronger statement than restoration of one pure state.

The common-return criterion retains reversible working auxiliaries, permanent records, and incomplete flags. Reversible auxiliaries participate in later retrieval; permanent records that never recouple preserve path distinctions. Section 2.4.2 explains how environment overlaps enter output shares. Specific return examples appear in Supplementary Proofs S6.1, S4.4, and S14.

Formation may also deliver a joint structure that remains correlated with subsequent action. Write its complete output as

Γψ=∑h|h⟩AKhψ,∑hKh†Kh=I.\Gamma\psi=\sum_h |h\rangle_A K_h\psi, \qquad \sum_hK_h^\dagger K_h=I.(2.37)

Here AA retains the complete formation record and used resources, and KhK_h includes both successful and failed outputs. When subsequent action still accesses a direction or record, evolution continues on this joint state. The inverse retrieves the current work, whereas earlier records remain with matter; these have different roles in a complete return. The factorized delivery above is a special case of this description.

2.3.5 Maintenance of a Stable State

To provide a source of mass, the formation pattern must continue to participate in actual exchange. Target branches match different position groups of the source and thereby acquire different interaction strengths. Source, target, and auxiliaries still participating in return form the persistent carrier. The isometry 𝒥s\mathcal J_s embeds the target together with the formed source Φs\Phi_s, spectral auxiliaries, nodes, and necessary records into the joint space.

The image of this isometric embedding is called the code subspace; inside and outside the code refer to this image and its orthogonal complement. The given preparation determines the projection needed to preserve the carrier. Let 𝒰s\mathcal U_s be a reference unitary preparing the fixed source and auxiliaries from a simple input 𝒥in\mathcal J_{\mathrm{in}}. Define

𝒥s=𝒰s𝒥in,Ps=𝒥s𝒥s†,Ss=2Ps−I=𝒰s(2Pin−I)𝒰s†. \mathcal J_s=\mathcal U_s\mathcal J_{\mathrm{in}},\qquad P_s=\mathcal J_s\mathcal J_s^\dagger,\qquad S_s=2P_s-I=\mathcal U_s(2P_{\mathrm{in}}-I)\mathcal U_s^\dagger. (2.38)

The operators Ps,SsP_s,S_s are fixed during the persistent stage. Let the actual self-adjoint exchange X=X†X=X^\dagger include spectral access, nodes, original address matching, and all auxiliaries and failure outputs. Use two simultaneous arms, each of strength g/2g/2:

ĤX=g2(X+SsXSs),hX=g𝒥s†X𝒥s. \widehat H_X=\frac g2(X+S_sXS_s),\qquad h_X=g\mathcal J_s^\dagger X\mathcal J_s. (2.39)

Since Ss𝒥s=𝒥sS_s\mathcal J_s=\mathcal J_s, we have (X+SsXSs)𝒥s=2PsX𝒥s(X+S_sXS_s)\mathcal J_s=2P_sX\mathcal J_s, and hence

ĤX𝒥s=𝒥shX,e−itĤX𝒥s=𝒥se−ithX. \boxed{\widehat H_X\mathcal J_s=\mathcal J_sh_X,\qquad e^{-it\widehat H_X}\mathcal J_s=\mathcal J_se^{-ith_X}.} (2.40)

The joint pattern produced by formation and its preparation determine the persistent carrier. The two simultaneous arms cancel amplitudes leaking out of the carrier, while exchange within it accumulates phase; Eq. (2.40) gives the intertwining for all times. For inputs that remain correlated after formation, 𝒥s\mathcal J_s retains the unknown logical components and adds only the work prepared for the current cycle, with the preparation reflection acting on the corresponding joint space. One maintenance action can thus support several persistent modes: formation determines their occupations and correlations, while the matrix elements of the actual XX in the complete preparation determine their phase rates.

The reference unitary can be synthesized from existing operations. Starting at the known background input, perform e−iπXA/4e^{-i\pi X_A/4} and multiply the direction by ii to obtain Φ+\Phi_+, followed by the spectral polar-decomposition unitary and complete round trip. Inverse preparation, input marking, and preparation then implement SsS_s. This path prepares the reference state from a fixed input; actual formation proceeds through the feedback process above. Formation auxiliaries and the common reference must be accessible, while permanent records remain factors on which the action is the identity, or block labels.

This balance has a direct structural constraint. For the complete carrier PP and reflection S=2P−IS=2P-I, (I−P)(aX+bSXS)P=(a−b)(I−P)XP(I-P)(aX+bSXS)P=(a-b)(I-P)XP. If the original exchange transfers between blocks, preservation at all times requires equal-strength coherent arms; common calibration still determines their overall strength. Both arms must reach the same complete output. Independent records or finite serial pulses generally alter the cancellation. Changing the formation angle changes the pattern, preparation reflection, and background readout. With original address matching fixed, formation shares consequently alter maintenance frequencies through actual matrix elements.

When several actions share this preparation, their sum retains the intertwining. This connects matter maintenance and the background gradient to one carrier: after writing into the background, transporting both actions and their reflections by the same writing unitary preserves their common intertwining. Passing both actions through balanced exchange with the available output column then makes background occupation constrain the matter phase and gradient response by the same availability factor. Chapter 4 derives the force from this structure. The operator proof is in Supplementary Proof S7. Section 2.3.7 connects the same maintenance action to unready inputs to calculate convergence after formation.

2.3.6 Survival and Re-formation

Persistent evolution must also undergo thermal processing. The original fixed restoration removes system coherence between background and directions. Here reversible auxiliaries and thermal outcomes are retained, and the actual deformation is compensated separately for each outcome, allowing successful returns to continue along the same carrier. This compensation introduces no new mass phase.

Let MηM_\eta be the thermal outcome map including preparation weights, defined on the logical space to be returned. 0<rη≤λmin(Gη),Fη=rη𝒥TGη−1/2Wη†,FηMη=rη𝒥T,Fη†Fη≤I. \begin{gathered} 0<r_\eta\le\lambda_{\min}(G_\eta),\qquad F_\eta=\sqrt{r_\eta}\,\mathcal J_TG_\eta^{-1/2}W_\eta^\dagger,\\ \boxed{F_\eta M_\eta=\sqrt{r_\eta}\,\mathcal J_T,\qquad F_\eta^\dagger F_\eta\le I.} \end{gathered} (2.41)

Conversely, exact return of all unknown inputs requires rηI≤Gηr_\eta I\le G_\eta. An outcome with a zero eigenvalue cannot return the whole space with positive weight. Every outcome must retain thermal labels usable for control, and failures count as exits.

The logical operator associated with each fine survival record is therefore rηI\sqrt{r_\eta}I, with total qT=∑ηrηq_T=\sum_\eta r_\eta; all remaining outputs have total effect (1−qT)I(1-q_T)I. The common per-cycle survival probability comes from this actual instrument, not temperature alone. Transport, filtering, restoration, and recording all contribute to the cycle period.

Let ℒf\mathcal L_f be the actual trace-nonincreasing family-loading map, with output in the target logical space and ℓf(ρ)=Tr⁡ℒf(ρ)\ell_f(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal L_f(\rho). After loading, embed by 𝒥s\mathcal J_s. Each round evolves under U=e−itHhU=e^{-it_Hh} for an active window tHt_H, followed by thermal processing and the remaining waiting time. ρlive(n)=QMqTn𝒥sUnℒf(ρ)U†n𝒥s†. \rho_{\mathrm{live}}^{(n)}=Q_Mq_T^n\mathcal J_sU^n\mathcal L_f(\rho)U^{\dagger n}\mathcal J_s^\dagger. (2.42)

(1−QM)+QM(1−ℓf)+QM(1−qTn)ℓf+QMqTnℓf=1. (1-Q_M)+Q_M(1-\ell_f)+Q_M(1-q_T^n)\ell_f+Q_Mq_T^n\ell_f=1. (2.43)

The four terms are source-delivery failure, family-loading failure, cumulative first exits, and continued survival. The complete output retains every record. The background after an exit may form new excitations; these are counted separately from uninterrupted survival of the original excitation. Actual decay products, generation lifetimes, and stability of the lowest generation still require their respective exit channels.

Different histories have preparation durations ThT_h; combining them at one absolute time requires summing according to their actual completed cycles. 2.3.7 Convergence of Formation

The preceding delivery specifies an exact carrier. For unready inputs, we must also show that the same operating process gradually establishes it. We insert source and auxiliary repair between active intervals while tracking thermal exit. Restrict the source domain to 𝒮=span⁡{e0,ψθ,ψθ‾}\mathcal S=\operatorname{span}\{e_0,\psi_\theta,\psi_{\bar\theta}\} and use the product-form isometric embedding 𝒥sψ=Φs⊗r⊗ψ\mathcal J_s\psi=\Phi_s\otimes r\otimes\psi. Here rr contains only auxiliaries that can be independently re-prepared. Target, position, orientation, background gradient, and permanent records remain in ψ\psi. Write Ps=𝒥s𝒥s†P_s=\mathcal J_s\mathcal J_s^\dagger and Qs=I−PsQ_s=I-P_s. This construction does not replace degrees of freedom carrying permanent information in a nonproduct family encoding.

Each round first applies the complete generator, then pauses activity for repair. Once a fresh auxiliary is independently prepared, an actual exchange replaces the old one, transferring it and its correlations to outgoing records. The source undergoes 𝒯s=Ad⁡Ds𝒯Ad⁡Ds†\mathcal T_s=\operatorname{Ad}_{D_s}\mathcal T\operatorname{Ad}_{D_s^\dagger}. Thermal return must also cover transient inputs. The parameter qRq_R controls formation convergence, qTq_T the survival envelope, and hh phase evolution. A finite lifetime reduces the samples that complete formation; frequencies within the carrier remain unchanged at the scalar thermal-return interface used here.

The selected serial cycle period is τ=tH+TR+TX\tau=t_H+T_R+T_X, where TRT_R is the repair duration and TXT_X the thermal-processing duration. Auxiliary replacement, reuse, and complete timing are described in Supplementary Proof S3.3.

Matter, motion, and background are active and paused together within this serial cycle, sharing the active fraction of Section 2.4.6. The product-form isometric embedding and scalar thermal return connect formation, persistence, and exit in one cycle. We now calculate its accumulated phase.

2.4 Elementary-State Mass

A pattern can preserve its form while its phase relative to a common reference changes with time. Rest mass is read from the rate of this relative phase against actual elapsed duration. When a symmetric pair of frequency branches is used, the half-gap is read after identifying their symmetry center. Propagation, node exchange, and return together form this persistent process, through which the excitation’s spectral structure enters actual phase evolution. We first derive the mass generator during activity, then include return, thermal processing, and waiting in the total duration to obtain the actual mass reading.

2.4.1 Spectral Response and Exchange Strength

The zero element z=|0⟩z=|0\rangle connects shell-average components and directions, but is neither the unit-shell average state e0e_0 nor the whole-space reference bb. Take N=|S0|N=|S_0| and Pz=|z⟩⟨z|P_z=|z\rangle\langle z|, with additive translation (τaf)(x)=f(x+a)(\tau_af)(x)=f(x+a). From [Pz,τa]=|z⟩⟨a|−|−a⟩⟨z|[P_z,\tau_a]=|z\rangle\langle a|-|-a\rangle\langle z| we obtain the directional vertex

Jχ=1N∑a∈S0χ(π(a))[Pz,τa]=|z⟩⟨ψχ‾|−χ(−1)|ψχ⟩⟨z|. J_\chi=\frac1{\sqrt N}\sum_{a\in S_0}\chi(\pi(a))[P_z,\tau_a] =|z\rangle\langle\psi_{\bar\chi}|-\chi(-1)|\psi_\chi\rangle\langle z|. (2.47)

Each component can be balanced by the environment as in Section 2.3.1. The operator JχJ_\chi organizes the order of access; in the non-self-conjugate case it cannot directly serve as a self-adjoint Hamiltonian. The actual exchange pairs each joint matrix element with its adjoint.

Denote the spectral variable by ssps_{\mathrm{sp}}. In its convergence domain, the unnormalized spectral transfer ℬ̃(ssp)=∑n≥1n−sspTn\widetilde{\mathcal B}(s_{\mathrm{sp}})=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s_{\mathrm{sp}}}T_n gives L(ssp,χ)L(s_{\mathrm{sp}},\chi) along a direction, then continues to the same real regular spectral point s0:=s*s_0:=s_*. This variable is distinct from the formation round-trip action s. Write Lχ=L(s0,χ)L_\chi=L(s_0,\chi) and Rχ=Lχ/ζ(s0)R_\chi=L_\chi/\zeta(s_0). Every multiplicative pullback preserves the whole-space pattern bb, whose unnormalized response is ζ(s0)\zeta(s_0), supplying the denominator of the spectral comparison. The unit-shell average state e0e_0 instead removes multiples of pp and has response (1−p−s0)ζ(s0)(1-p^{-s_0})\zeta(s_0). Spectral reference, zero endpoint, and actual environment preparation thus have distinct roles. An actual instrument must also provide its capacity and complete outputs. If the selected spectral unitary UχU_\chi has matrix element rχ=Lχ/cLr_\chi=L_\chi/c_L at the specified success port, then

Kχ=⟨suc|Uχ|r⟩,Kχ†Kχ+∑bFχb†Fχb=I. K_\chi=\langle{\mathrm{suc}}|U_\chi|r\rangle,\qquad K_\chi^\dagger K_\chi+\sum_bF_{\chi b}^\dagger F_{\chi b}=I. (2.48)

On the accessed eigendirection, the success column produces rχr_\chi. Capacity must at least make every accessed success column contractive; an instrument handling several directions must normalize all of them simultaneously. The quantity |Lχ|>1|L_\chi|>1 can be a response coefficient but cannot be a passive one-shot success amplitude. We retain cLc_L and the failure columns until their conditional cancellation in the background calibration using a common source.

2.4.2 Composition of Propagation Paths

Character multiplication specifies label changes by modular addition of CRT coordinates. Actual paths additionally specify how zero, directions, and auxiliaries connect in sequence. For example, Jχ2Jχ1|z⟩J_{\chi_2}J_{\chi_1}|z\rangle returns to zero only when χ2=χ‾1\chi_2=\bar\chi_1. To obtain χ1→χ1χ2\chi_1\to\chi_1\chi_2 requires the corresponding absorption–formation matrix elements and environment balance; multiplying labels cannot replace exchange.

For the selected conjugate double excursion, the spectral response acts only on directions and zero serves only as a relay. Applying the vertices of Section 2.4.1 successively to the input gives

Jθ|z⟩=−θ(−1)|ψθ⟩,Jθ‾ℬ̃Jθ|z⟩=−θ(−1)Lθ|z⟩,LθLθ‾=|Lθ|2. \begin{aligned} J_\theta|z\rangle&=-\theta(-1)|\psi_\theta\rangle,\\ J_{\bar\theta}\widetilde{\mathcal B}J_\theta|z\rangle &=-\theta(-1)L_\theta|z\rangle,\qquad L_\theta L_{\bar\theta}=|L_\theta|^2. \end{aligned} (2.49)

After the first return, conjugate access is repeated. The two orientation signs multiply to one, and conjugate responses at a real spectral point give the final squared modulus. This first evaluates the algebraic product of spectral accesses; the complete instrument then supplies its actual normalization.

Using two explicit success accesses while retaining every failure output gives the actual joint success amplitude and effect:

rθrθ‾=|Lθ|2cL2,⟨Qpath⟩=|Lθ|4cL4,Qpath=Upath†PsucUpath. r_\theta r_{\bar\theta}=\frac{|L_\theta|^2}{c_L^2},\qquad \langle Q_{\mathrm{path}}\rangle=\frac{|L_\theta|^4}{c_L^4},\qquad Q_{\mathrm{path}}=U_{\mathrm{path}}^\dagger P_{\mathrm{suc}}U_{\mathrm{path}}. (2.50)

This is the specific origin of the fourth spectral power in the effect. A single excursion, coherent composition of an entire path, and independent acceptance at successive stages can give different results; closure alone does not fix the power. Noncommuting paths are composed by full matrix multiplication, and inserting intermediate bases gives their history amplitudes.

For paths from the same pure preparation reaching the same system final state, write their amplitudes as a𝒫a_\mathcal P and complete environment final states as e𝒫e_\mathcal P. Then

wf=∑𝒫,𝒫′a𝒫a𝒫′¯⟨e𝒫′|e𝒫⟩. w_f=\sum_{\mathcal P,\mathcal P'}a_\mathcal P\overline{a_{\mathcal P'}} \langle e_{\mathcal P'}|e_\mathcal P\rangle. (2.51)

Identical final states require amplitude addition, orthogonal final states require addition of squared moduli, and partial overlaps retain cross terms; see 9 for the two-path visibility–distinguishability relation. When stages produce actual records, each subsequent stage starts from the preceding actual output. Using outcome maps of quantum instruments 10, let ℐrk(k)\mathcal I_{r_k}^{(k)} be the completely positive, trace-nonincreasing map for outcome rkr_k at stage kk, including every degree of freedom participating later. The joint share of a recorded history is

p(r₁,…,rm)
= Tr[𝓘rm(m)∘⋯∘𝓘r₁(1)(ρ₀)].
(2.52)

For two stages this is p(r1)p(r2∣r1)p(r_1)p(r_2\mid r_1). It factors further into independent shares only when actual re-preparation or other conditions remove the dependence. Components of mixed preparations are combined with their weights. These rules apply to both open and closed paths.

The resulting path quantity then enters a self-adjoint action. For example, a specified effect QpathQ_{\mathrm{path}} can act on the carrier through conditional exchange between two orientations. The complete spectral auxiliaries must remain involved in maintenance, so evaluating 𝒥†X𝒥\mathcal J^\dagger X\mathcal J yields the stated weight. If success has already been measured and only the normalized successful state is delivered, the preceding success probability generally affects yield alone; that is a different process.

2.4.3 Node Normalization Factors

Node factors come from overlaps among input, actual connection, and complete output. On a symmetric orbit of dd points, the normalized equal-phase vector |η⟩=d−1/2∑x|x⟩|\eta\rangle=d^{-1/2}\sum_x|x\rangle has overlap 1/d1/\sqrt d with one specified endpoint and event share 1/d1/d. If both entrance and exit each involve an overlap, both factors must be retained.

A binary coherent node connects its preparation orientation to the spectral response. BN=FN⊗U+FN†⊗U†,⟨nβ,r|BN|nβ,r⟩=ηNRe⁡⟨r|U|r⟩.B_N=F_N\otimes U+F_N^\dagger\otimes U^\dagger,\qquad \langle n_\beta,r|B_N|n_\beta,r\rangle=\eta_N\operatorname{Re}\langle r|U|r\rangle.(2.53)

Once the node preparation and coherent port are fixed, the coefficient follows from the matrix element. The common internal reference determines phase orientation; a real part cannot arbitrarily be replaced by a modulus. If subsequent action uses an endpoint effect, compress that effect rather than applying an amplitude node factor again.

Distinguishable outputs are likewise counted through the complete operator. For dd colors, let each color retain the same transfer KK, E=K†KE=K^\dagger K, and dE≤IdE\le I, and set Ωd=∑c=1d|c,c‾⟩\Omega_d=\sum_{c=1}^d|c,\bar c\rangle. Two orthogonal failure-output subspaces give the isometry

Vinψ=(Ωd⊗Kψ⊗r)⊕I−dEψ⊕0,Voutψ=(Ωd⊗Kψ⊗U†r)⊕0⊕I−dEψ,Vout†Vin=d⟨r|U|r⟩E. \begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{in}}\psi&=(\Omega_d\otimes K\psi\otimes r)\oplus\sqrt{I-dE}\,\psi\oplus0,\\ V_{\mathrm{out}}\psi&=(\Omega_d\otimes K\psi\otimes U^\dagger r)\oplus0\oplus\sqrt{I-dE}\,\psi, \end{aligned}\qquad V_{\mathrm{out}}^\dagger V_{\mathrm{in}}=d\langle r|U|r\rangle E. (2.54)

The color count and spectral response thus jointly enter actual return. Replacing each color’s transfer by K/dK/\sqrt d, or allowing coherent overlap at failure outputs, changes the result. Having dd colors therefore fixes a multiplier only together with per-color strength and failure outputs.

The geometric factor for a relay to a complete species-layer group is

|d‾j⟩=12pK−1∑π(u)∈{aj,−aj}|u⟩,⟨d‾j|e0⟩=1m. |\bar d_j\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt{2p^{K-1}}}\sum_{\pi(u)\in\{a_j,-a_j\}}|u\rangle, \qquad \langle\bar d_j|e_0\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt m}. (2.55)

It holds at any depth because the port reads all deeper lifts. A single deeper point pair instead gives 2/|S0|\sqrt{2/|S_0|}. Repeated application of the same projection satisfies P2=PP^2=P and does not automatically add a normalization factor each time. Every new multiplicative factor must correspond to a new access, relay, or preparation.

2.4.4 Generational Factors

Fix the formation source Φs\Phi_s and use the original same-group matching between source and target:

QTS=∑jPjT⊗PjS,⟨Φs|QTS|Φs⟩S=∑jpj(s)PjT. Q_{TS}=\sum_jP_j^T\otimes P_j^S,\qquad \langle\Phi_s|Q_{TS}|\Phi_s\rangle_S=\sum_jp_j(s)P_j^T. (2.56)

When they carry motion, their matching to source groups is connected through auxiliary labels and actual routing; retained labels cannot be replaced by position projections altered by translation.

Place group matching, path effects, and node exchange in the same complete preparation. Write the common instrument capacity as Λ\Lambda and unnormalized path weight as 𝒫f\mathcal P_f; conjugate double access uses 𝒫f=|Lθ|4\mathcal P_f=|L_\theta|^4. Path, node, and source respectively give 𝒫f/Λ\mathcal P_f/\Lambda, ηN\eta_N, and group shares pj(s)p_j(s). Renaming does not remove this factor: it must be retained together with the same background readout. Auxiliary units added by new nodes must enter the new 𝒥s\mathcal J_s and reflection. Protection omitting those auxiliary units cannot be reused.

The reference group is fixed by x0x_0. Choose group zero with p0>0p_0>0. The background branch also traverses the same source and actually matches this group, so its matrix element contains p0p_0. The reference group need not be maximal or fully transmitted. Section 2.5 calibrates both actual branch frequencies together, leaving the relative generational factor pj/p0p_j/p_0; its denominator was not inserted into the target action in advance.

For a family with a nondiagonal chain-matrix output, retain the full matrix and permanent records before taking eigenvalues. Several nonzero formation shares do not by themselves establish independent persistent spectral lines. The common carrier of Section 2.3 and the actual mass matrix jointly determine whether those lines occur.

2.4.5 Phase Corrections and Frequency Shifts

Formation modification changes the source angle, while a spectral insertion during maintenance can also change the rest-frame generator. Retain the actual self-adjoint action AA of Section 2.3, with preparation mean aa. In the specified connection commuting with maintenance exchange XX, insertion of I−AI-A gives

h0=g𝒥s†X𝒥s,hcorr=g𝒥s†X(I−A)𝒥s,CX,A=𝒥s†XA𝒥s−a𝒥s†X𝒥s. h_0=g\mathcal J_s^\dagger X\mathcal J_s,\qquad h_{\mathrm{corr}}=g\mathcal J_s^\dagger X(I-A)\mathcal J_s, \qquad C_{X,A}=\mathcal J_s^\dagger XA\mathcal J_s-a\mathcal J_s^\dagger X\mathcal J_s. (2.58)

Direct expansion yields

hcorr=(1−a)h0−gCX,A. \boxed{h_{\mathrm{corr}}=(1-a)h_0-gC_{X,A}.} (2.59)

Equation (2.59) gives the necessary and sufficient criterion for an exact proportional correction: CX,A=0C_{X,A}=0. This construction uses independent complete modification auxiliaries, so Mf=(1−a)Mf(0)M_f=(1-a)M_f^{(0)}, while the motion term retains its original action. For correlated preparations, the additional contribution is −gCX,A-gC_{X,A} in the same equation.

Within-cycle correlations, accumulated formation action, and cycle-period corrections affect this result separately. Fixing marginal means or refreshing auxiliaries each round does not fix the within-cycle CX,AC_{X,A}. A different dwell protocol that lengthens the cycle yields a corresponding frequency factor such as 1/(1+a)1/(1+a). The actual accumulated action in the formation angle follows Section 2.3.3; its evaluation is given in Section 8.1.

2.4.6 Mass and Motion

Phase is read against a common reference internal to state space. The overall phase of a single eigenstate cancels in the projector |ψ⟩⟨ψ||\psi\rangle\langle\psi|, so position occupation does not display this rotation. Determining relative phase requires actual nonzero coherence between two components and separate readings of its two quadratures in repeated trials.

Let the eigenvalues of the actual persistent generator be EaE_a and the active window tHt_H. Combine repeated preparation repair, thermal processing, return, filtering, and waiting that equalizes branch durations into TprocT_{\mathrm{proc}}. Then

τ=tH+Tproc,νcyc=τ−1,fact=tH/τ. \tau=t_H+T_{\mathrm{proc}},\qquad \nu_{\mathrm{cyc}}=\tau^{-1},\qquad f_{\mathrm{act}}=t_H/\tau. (2.60)

Here factf_{\mathrm{act}} is the fraction of a cycle during which phase accumulates. Formation and initial-loading time are counted only as often as they actually occur; every recurring process enters τ\tau. At the survival interface of Section 2.3.6, the coherence mode and its readable frequency are

λab=qTe−i(Ea−Eb)tH,ωabobs=fact(Ea−Eb),γexit=−log⁡qTτ(0<qT≤1). \lambda_{ab}=q_Te^{-i(E_a-E_b)t_H},\qquad \omega_{ab}^{\mathrm{obs}}=f_{\mathrm{act}}(E_a-E_b),\qquad \gamma_{\mathrm{exit}}=-\frac{\log q_T}{\tau}\quad(0<q_T\le1). (2.61)

The argument and modulus of the same survival root determine phase and exit rates, respectively. Maintenance accumulates phase among survivors, while thermal excursions determine how much of the branch remains; both are divided by the complete cycle period. Initial coherence c0≠0c_0\ne0 becomes cn=λabnc0=qTne−in(Ea−Eb)tHc0c_n=\lambda_{ab}^n c_0=q_T^ne^{-in(E_a-E_b)t_H}c_0 after nn successive rounds. Reading real and imaginary parts, fix the phase branch by continuously varying the active duration or by sampling with adjacent phase increments smaller than π. Continuously unwrapping the phase change relative to the initial state, negating it, and dividing by nτn\tau yields fact(Ea−Eb)f_{\mathrm{act}}(E_a-E_b). Reading logarithmic decay of its modulus yields γexit\gamma_{\mathrm{exit}}. With fixed per-cycle phase and survival probability, adding compensated common waiting rescales both rates by the same period factor. Neither the endpoint principal argument alone nor division by only the phase-active window gives the complete-cycle reading.

For formation during operation in Section 2.3.7, Supplementary Proof S3 also bounds the remaining transient spectral radius by qTκq_T\sqrt\kappa, below the modulus qTq_T of the roots within the code. Formation transients therefore decay further relative to the survival envelope, and long-time visible frequencies still come from the same hh. A particular line requires nonzero overlaps with preparation and observation. Separation of survival envelope and phase slope depends on the specified thermal interface and need not hold for a general thermal channel. Two-branch interference directly reads a frequency difference: branches ±μj\pm\mu_j give beat frequency 2factμj2f_{\mathrm{act}}\mu_j. Assigning the single-branch mass factμjf_{\mathrm{act}}\mu_j requires an established symmetry center or zero-mass reference.

As the carrier propagates between positions, internal maintenance continues to act on the same object. We use a joint preparation in which two opposite exchanges share a coherent port and both endpoints undergo the same simultaneous maintenance. On this carrier, the family mass matrix MfM_f and position propagation give

hf(k)=Mf⊗Y+gI⊗Zmovsin⁡(kℓx),Y2=Zmov2=I,{Y,Zmov}=0. h_f(k)=M_f\otimes Y+gI\otimes Z_{\mathrm{mov}}\sin(k\ell_x),\qquad Y^2=Z_{\mathrm{mov}}^2=I,\quad\{Y,Z_{\mathrm{mov}}\}=0. (2.62)

The operators Y,ZmovY,Z_{\mathrm{mov}} act on the two-state space of motion orientations and are defined separately from ZFZ_F, which acts on formation directions. Let μj>0\mu_j>0 be a positive eigenvalue of MfM_f. Squaring cancels cross terms, so

Ej,±obs(k)=±factμj2+g2sin⁡2(kℓx),cobs=factgℓx,Min,jobscobs2=factμj. E_{j,\pm}^{\mathrm{obs}}(k)=\pm f_{\mathrm{act}}\sqrt{\mu_j^2+g^2\sin^2(k\ell_x)},\qquad c_{\mathrm{obs}}=f_{\mathrm{act}} g\ell_x, \qquad M_{{\mathrm{in}},j}^{\mathrm{obs}}c_{\mathrm{obs}}^2=f_{\mathrm{act}}\mu_j. (2.63)

The last expression follows from the curvature of the positive branch at the origin, using ℏ=1\hbar=1. On a finite ring, this uses the continuous symbol or a long-wave-packet curvature reading. One parameter controls both the rest-frame half-gap and inertia at the origin. This does not identify the full lattice dispersion with a Lorentz relation at all momenta or exclude other low-energy valleys in the complete position spectrum.

This driven generator must also be distinguished from the shell energy HKH_K of the original thermal exchange. Energy conservation at a bare joint endpoint does not imply work-free new control or hf=HKh_f=H_K. Supplementary Proof S1.5 retains the constraint on conserved quantities under the same complete unitary, environment energy, and strict contraction; its premises do not extend to the modified joint process here.

Propagation of a joint carrier also preserves the relative structure that determines contact. For matter position XX and an accompanying contact resource at RR, an actual position loading ℒ\mathcal L can transport the original shift as ℒSXℒ†=SXSR\mathcal L S_X\mathcal L^\dagger=S_XS_R. The joint shift preserves relative position; reversible auxiliaries retain the original position information and restore it on return. When the complete preparation is compatible with this shift, the shared-port derivation acts on the entire joint carrier, and the same internal mass matrix continues to determine the rest-frame half-gap and inertia at the origin.
