2.5 Common Energy Scale

Exchange strengths and persistent frequencies of different stable states must be compared against a common background. Processes can involve different mode ranges and weights, but participating and background responses must use the same scale. This section uses a common source and schedule to compare their squared responses, retaining actual participation ranges and weights.

2.5.1 Participation Weights

Common calibration first requires identifying participating modes and their weights. The total participating mode quantity differs from a normalized pattern. For whole-space participation, for example, b is one coherent direction with nonzero amplitude at all d=pᴷ positions. Position modes provide an orthogonal expansion basis, while the pattern specifies relations among their components. The projection counting participating positions and that selecting the collective pattern are therefore respectively

Pall = ∑x∈Xp,K |x⟩⟨x| = Iℋ, 　Pb = |b⟩⟨b|,
rank Pall = d, 　rank Pb = 1.
(2.67)

A normalized pattern can be composed of d positions. The rank of the pattern and dimension of its participation range are counted separately.

First define the common participation quantity in the specified mode space. Let the participating subspace be spanned by normalized orthogonal vectors uαu_{α} indexed by 𝒮, with orthogonal projection P𝒮P_{𝒮}. Represent the unnormalized evaluation weights by a dimensionless positive operator Γ, and set

P𝒮 = ∑α∈𝒮 |uα⟩⟨uα|, 　Γ ≥ 0,
wα = ⟨uα|Γ|uα⟩ ≥ 0,
W𝒮 = Tr(P𝒮ΓP𝒮) = ∑α∈𝒮 wα.
(2.68)

Here W𝒮W_{𝒮} is the total spectral weight of selected participating modes. In a general participation basis, wαw_{α} are diagonal weights; in an eigenbasis of the compressed operator P𝒮ΓP𝒮P_{𝒮}ΓP_{𝒮}, they are its nonnegative eigenvalues. With P𝒮P_{𝒮} and Γ fixed, a change of orthonormal basis preserves the trace. An orthogonal decomposition of the participating subspace gives additive weights. For Γ=I, every orthogonal mode has unit weight and W𝒮=rank⁡P𝒮W_{𝒮}=\operatorname{rank} P_{𝒮}. Whole-ring position participation therefore gives d=pᴷ and unit-shell position participation gives pᴷ⁻¹(p−1), the counts for these respective ranges under unit weighting.

Each process must specify its participating modes and justify the weights used. A projection only marks the summation range; formation and exchange operators must also establish that the process actually involves it. Repeated paths leading to the same indistinguishable final state combine amplitudes first, as in Section 2.4.2. Path names alone cannot increase the number of orthogonal modes.

For W𝒮>0W_{𝒮}>0, the corresponding normalized evaluation weight is

σ𝒮 = P𝒮ΓP𝒮/W𝒮, 　Tr σ𝒮 = 1,
⟨uα|σ𝒮|uα⟩ = wα/W𝒮.
(2.69)

This separates total quantity from relative shares. Mathematically, σ𝒮σ_{𝒮} is a density operator; identifying its shares as actual observation probabilities additionally requires a specific preparation and readout. Overall scaling of Γ cancels under normalization: for c>0, replacing Γ by cΓ preserves σ𝒮σ_{𝒮} but changes W𝒮W_{𝒮} to cW𝒮cW_{𝒮}. If the subsequent energy scale uses W𝒮W_{𝒮}, its specified absolute weights must be retained rather than changed by arbitrary renormalization.

Weights also do not replace coherent preparation. Both Γ₁=I and Γ2=dPbΓ_{2}=dP_{b} have unit diagonal entries in the site basis and trace d, yet normalization gives I/d and PbP_{b}, respectively. Section 2.2.4 described their coherence difference; collective formation must still satisfy Section 2.5.4.

Thermal weighting further requires specifying the spectrum and energy origin. The weight sum on the BC logarithmic energy spectrum indexed by positive integers generally differs from Gibbs weighting of the finite shell generator. This chapter uses the former for spectral evaluation and the latter for actual thermal exchange. Supplementary Proof S5 compares them and treats finite cutoffs. Once the participation projection and absolute weights are fixed, write their total as W and calculate the common response.

2.5.2 Background Response

Participation weights specify mode contributions; background calibration must also specify each mode’s response. Take W>1 and a common energy calibration E₀>0. We first calculate squared responses on the process and background sides, then connect them to actual exchange strength.

The logarithmic spectrum indexed by positive integers supplies the spectral reference. For the complete initial spectral segment 1,…,N, the level count and highest energy obey the exact relation

𝒩(ε) = #{n ≥ 1 : log n ≤ ε} = ⌊eε⌋,
max1≤n≤N log n = log N.
(2.70)

Here N is the integer number of modes in the initial segment. For general positive participation weights, we adopt the common response scale Ω(W)=log⁡W\Omega(W)=\log W and sum squared mode responses with positive weights. This collective-response prescription extends the initial-segment relation; a general weighted participation quantity WW does not itself determine the highest energy. Actual frequency is read from phase and elapsed duration after connecting the response to exchange.

A participation projection and positive weight operator express the common response. Set Acoll=Ω(W)P𝒮A_{\mathrm{coll}}=Ω(W)P_{𝒮}, assigning the same response coefficient throughout the chosen participating subspace. Summing squared responses with positive weights gives, on the process side,

𝒬proc = Tr(Γ Acoll†Acoll)
= Ω(W)² Tr(ΓP𝒮) = W log²W.
(2.71)

The last step uses P𝒮2=P𝒮P_{𝒮}^{2}=P_{𝒮} and cyclicity of the trace, also for Γ\Gamma not commuting with P𝒮P_{𝒮}. The quantity 𝒬proc\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{proc}} is this response’s unnormalized square. For different response coefficients on orthogonal modes, the general expression is ∑αwα|aα|2\sum_\alpha w_\alpha|a_\alpha|^2; the common-coefficient formula is a special case.

The background side uses adjacent gaps of the same logarithmic spectrum indexed by positive integers. Let Δn=log⁡(n+1)−log⁡nΔ_{n}=\log (n+1)-\log n. Each link has two orientations, each assigned an orthogonal response coordinate. Define gbg(n,+)=Δng_{\mathrm{bg}}(n,+)=Δ_{n} and gbg(n,−)=−Δng_{\mathrm{bg}}(n,-)=-Δ_{n} on these coordinates. Their squared norm defines the intrinsic metric constant C*, the background squared-response constant of the complete logarithmic spectrum:

Δₙ = log(1 + 1/n), 　gbg ∈ ℓ²(ℕ* × {+, −}),
C* := ‖gbg‖² = 2 ∑n=1∞ Δₙ².
(2.72)

Since 0<Δn<1/n0<Δ_{n}<1/n, the square sum is finite and positive. The factor 2 counts both orientations of each link: each is squared before summation. The vector gbgg_{\mathrm{bg}} describes the gradient response of the spectral reference and is distinct from the constant-function pattern b in the finite state space; its norm cannot be conflated with normalization of b.

The background reference uses the complete logarithmic spectrum. A different choice of finite open chain 1,…,J, J≥2, has J−1 links. Its normalization and truncation error satisfy

CJ* = 2 ∑n=1J−1 Δₙ²,
0 < C* − CJ* < 2 ∑n=J∞ n−2 < 2/(J − 1).
(2.73)

The final bound follows from a tail integral. For the open chain of nonzero address representatives 1,…,pᴷ−1, take J=pᴷ−1 and denominator CJ*C_{J}^{*}, without adding the zero residue class or a closing link. Background cutoff J and participation-weight cutoff L are specified separately.

Using E/E₀ as the common amplitude with which an excitation drives the background gives response (E/E0)gbg(E/E_{0})g_{\mathrm{bg}} and squared quantity (E/E₀)²C*. Matching the squared quantities on the process and background sides for the same response yields

(E(W)/E₀)² C* = W log²W,
E(W) = E₀ √(W/C*) log W, 　W > 1.
(2.74)

Taking the positive root for E≥0E\ge0 determines this energy scale; E0E_0 is supplied by physical calibration. A finite background follows the same derivation, replacing only C*C^* by CJ*C_J^*: EJ(W)=E0W/CJ*log⁡WE_J(W)=E_0\sqrt{W/C_J^*}\log W. At fixed W,E0W,E_0, EJ(W)/E(W)=C*/CJ*E_J(W)/E(W)=\sqrt{C^*/C_J^*} quantifies the effect of background truncation on the reading.

The shells of a collective state participate with shares hjh_j in one pattern bb with definite relative phases. The common E0E_0 and background square constant cancel in the ratio, while each period is still timed from its own operations. Background exchange produces a coherent pattern, and actual matching turns group shares into coefficients of the persistent generator. Return preserves the carrier, exit determines its survival envelope, and relative phase gives the rest frequency. The same generator controls inertia at the origin, while squared matching to the same-source background fixes the common mass scale. Collective states use this scale as well, with intershell coherence and complete return realized in Chapter 9. The next chapter treats joint exchange between maintained carriers.

Chapter 3. Resonance Forces

Stable states persist through exchange with the background and can also send excitations to other stable states through a common environment. When the emitting and absorbing endpoints have compatible spectral channels, a component released by one can enter the formation or return process of the other, allowing the two carriers to affect each other through actual exchange. This exchange interaction, carried by common spectral channels, is called a resonance force.

An exchange changes the carrier states and may also leave a record in the environment. Its strength must be determined by comparing the input and output of the same joint process: endpoint overlap determines whether the excitation can enter, propagation and return determine how amplitudes combine, and the actual records and elapsed duration determine the event share and rate of change that are read out. With a calibrated momentum reading, the rate of momentum change caused by exchange is the corresponding mechanical force. The participation of elementary and emergent states follows Chapter 2; the responses of both are calculated using these physical relations.

3.1 Resonant Exchange

3.1.1 Transfer of a Directional Excitation

First consider the case in which the emitting and absorbing endpoints can access the same nontrivial direction χ. This direction is represented by the phase pattern ψχψ_{χ} on the unit shell, with projection Pχ=|ψχ⟩⟨ψχ|P_{χ}=\vert ψ_{χ}\rangle \langle ψ_{χ}\vert. Using the shell-preserving response defined at a regular spectral point s*s_{*} in Chapter 2, write Rχ=Rχ(s*)R_{χ}=R_{χ}(s_{*}). Then

Pχ′Tel(s*)Pχ=δχ′χRχPχ. P_{\chi'}T_{\mathrm{el}}(s_*)P_\chi=\delta_{\chi'\chi}R_\chi P_\chi. (3.1)

This selection rule follows from character orthogonality: after traversing this response segment, a component entering direction χ remains in that direction, multiplied by the corresponding complex coefficient. We say that the emitting and absorbing endpoints have a common spectral channel when both have a nonzero component in this direction. This means that their patterns can connect; how much amplitude actually leaves the emitting endpoint, and whether it can reach the absorbing endpoint, must still be determined by the exchanges at both endpoints and the intervening process.

The squared spectral response also has a definite but limited meaning. For a normalized prepared state ρ, selecting this direction with PχP_{χ} gives

Tr⁡(ρPχTel†TelPχ)=|Rχ|2Tr⁡(ρPχ). \operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\rho P_\chi T_{\mathrm{el}}^{\dagger}T_{\mathrm{el}}P_\chi\right)=|R_\chi|^2\operatorname{Tr}(\rho P_\chi). (3.2)

Here Tr⁡(ρPχ)\operatorname{Tr}(ρP_{χ}) is the input share in the selected direction. The squared response of the normalized conditional input is |Rχ|2\vert R_{χ}\vert ^{2}, while the unnormalized spectral response gives |L(s*,χ)|2\vert L(s_{*},χ)\vert ^{2}; the actual probability and frequency shift are further determined by the joint exchange and its elapsed duration.

Specify subsystems A and B, an environment C, and their actual interactions within the whole. Use the direction–shell-average exchange of 2.3.1 as the vertex at each endpoint: C receives the component released by A and exchanges with B after propagation. This tensor decomposition is a condition of the joint construction. We first calculate transfer between the selected endpoints, then incorporate the complete carriers comprising formation source, target, and auxiliaries in 3.1.2. In the actual temporal order, the joint unitary action during transfer is

𝕌ex=UBC(IAB⊗UC)UAC,𝒜fi=⟨f|𝕌ex|i⟩. \begin{gathered}\mathbb U_{\mathrm{ex}}=U_{BC}\,(I_{AB}\otimes U_C)\,U_{AC},\\[3pt]\mathcal A_{fi}=\langle f|\mathbb U_{\mathrm{ex}}|i\rangle.\end{gathered} (3.3)

The local operators of A and B act on different factors, but the two complete exchanges share C, so UACU_{AC} and UBCU_{BC} generally cannot be interchanged. The amplitudes, phases, and records retained by C at the intermediate stage determine what the second vertex actually receives. To discuss return, append the specified release and retrieval actions after absorption; the transfer stage itself occupies only part of the complete cycle.

Let A initially carry the directional excitation, let B absorb from its shell-average endpoint, and let environment C receive and convey the excitation between them. This process can be restricted to a minimal closed transfer subspace. Choose shell-average endpoints eae_{a} and ebe_{b} for A and B, and orthogonal states u and vχv_{χ} for C, and define three normalized joint vectors:

|i⟩=|ψχ⟩A|eb⟩B|u⟩C,|m⟩=|ea⟩A|eb⟩B|vχ⟩C,|f⟩=|ea⟩A|ψχ⟩B|u⟩C. \begin{gathered}|i\rangle=|\psi_\chi\rangle_A|e_b\rangle_B|u\rangle_C,\\[3pt]|m\rangle=|e_a\rangle_A|e_b\rangle_B|v_\chi\rangle_C,\\[3pt]|f\rangle=|e_a\rangle_A|\psi_\chi\rangle_B|u\rangle_C.\end{gathered} (3.4)

These states are balanced at both vertices in total energy and total unit-group charge. Denote the energies of the directional states at the two endpoints by EAχE_{Aχ} and EBχE_{Bχ}, and the environment energies by εuε_{u} and εvε_{v}. The required energy condition is EAχ−Ea=εv−εu=EBχ−EbE_{Aχ}-E_{a}=ε_{v}-ε_{u}=E_{Bχ}-E_{b}. The energies used here are those specified by the actual joint generator; with the shell generator HKH_{K} of the original exchange in 2.3.1, these are the corresponding shell energy differences. If the mass frequencies of Chapter 2 are further used as these exchange energies, Eq. (S13) in Supplementary Proof S1.5 and the subsequent compatibility conditions between phase and conserved energy must also hold, and the balance must be checked with the corresponding environment energies. A shared character label gives only directional matching.

In this closed three-state subspace, the first vertex performs a unitary rotation between i and m through angle α; the second rotates between m and f through angle γ; and intermediate propagation gives m a relative phase ϑ. The remaining endpoint is unchanged during each rotation, and the two forward-transfer coefficients are chosen as sin α and sin γ. Applying the actions in order gives

𝕌ex|i⟩=cos⁡α|i⟩+eiϑsin⁡αcos⁡γ|m⟩+eiϑsin⁡αsin⁡γ|f⟩,𝒜fi=eiϑsin⁡αsin⁡γ,Pi→f=sin⁡2αsin⁡2γ. \begin{gathered}\mathbb U_{\mathrm{ex}}|i\rangle=\cos\alpha|i\rangle+e^{i\vartheta}\sin\alpha\cos\gamma|m\rangle+e^{i\vartheta}\sin\alpha\sin\gamma|f\rangle,\\[3pt]\mathcal A_{fi}=e^{i\vartheta}\sin\alpha\sin\gamma,\\[3pt]P_{i\to f}=\sin^2\alpha\sin^2\gamma.\end{gathered} (3.5)

The squared moduli of the three orthogonal outcomes sum to 1, and the completed-transfer amplitude is the product of the two vertex amplitudes and the propagation phase. When several paths lead to the same complete final state, propagation phases enter the interference. Actual exchange angles are determined by the vertex actions, while energy balance and the relative phases at successive contacts ensure resonance. The source, auxiliaries, and retrieval of the persistent carriers are incorporated in the next subsection.

Group-charge conservation can be checked within the same joint process. Let DA(u)D_{A}(u), DB(u)D_{B}(u), and DC(u)D_{C}(u) be the unit-group actions on the respective subsystems, and let q denote the character eigenvalue function of each state under these actions. If every exchange and the intermediate propagation commute with the total group action, then every nonzero matrix element between input and output components of definite group charge satisfies

[𝕌ex,DA(u)⊗DB(u)⊗DC(u)]=0(∀u),𝒜fi≠0⇒∏S=A,B,CqSout=∏S=A,B,CqSin. \begin{gathered}[\mathbb U_{\mathrm{ex}},D_A(u)\otimes D_B(u)\otimes D_C(u)]=0\ \ (\forall u),\\[3pt]\mathcal A_{fi}\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ \prod_{S=A,B,C}q_S^{\mathrm{out}}=\prod_{S=A,B,C}q_S^{\mathrm{in}}.\end{gathered} (3.6)

To prove this, simply move the total group action through the joint unitary operator: the same matrix element is multiplied by the total character of the input and that of the output, so it must vanish when these differ. The notation χ and its conjugate is interchanged when multiplicative pullback is replaced by its inverse action; the eigenvalue function q used here preserves the convention actually adopted. If the input and output states of C belong to the same definite-charge sector, the charge changes at the two endpoints cancel; if C remains in another sector, it carries the remaining charge. Even if a reference containing coherence across charges returns to the same state, one cannot directly cancel a definite charge for it in this component formula. Total energy is balanced in the same way when it is conserved by the joint generator. Direction preservation along the propagation segment and joint conservation in the complete exchange thus have distinct, well-defined scopes.

3.1.2 Exchange between Stable States

Two persistent carriers interact through their target logical states, while their formation sources, auxiliaries, and old records remain part of the complete objects. Using the product-form isometric embedding of 2.3.5, first prepare the two endpoints separately: 𝒥αψ=ωα⊗ψ\mathcal J_\alpha\psi=\omega_\alpha\otimes\psi and α=A,B\alpha=A,B, where ωα\omega_\alpha contains the source and auxiliaries already prepared at that endpoint, and old records no longer participate in this interaction. For each target choose actually accessible orthogonal modes |0⟩α,|1⟩α|0\rangle_\alpha,|1\rangle_\alpha and write ℒα=span⁡{|0⟩α,|1⟩α}\mathcal L_\alpha=\operatorname{span}\{|0\rangle_\alpha,|1\rangle_\alpha\}. Logical inputs are restricted to ℒA⊗ℒB\mathcal L_A\otimes\mathcal L_B and may be entangled with spectator records; 0 does not denote exit into the background.

Relay C has endpoints u,vu,v and is prepared in u at entry. The endpoint projections Pα=𝒥α𝒥α†P_\alpha=\mathcal J_\alpha\mathcal J_\alpha^\dagger act as the identity on C, allowing it to store the logical state temporarily.

First specify endpoints capable of contacting the target, rather than only the fixed source. Let 𝖡α\mathsf B_\alpha be an actual self-adjoint action on the local source and auxiliaries, with βα=⟨ωα|𝖡α|ωα⟩>0\beta_\alpha=\langle\omega_\alpha|\mathsf B_\alpha|\omega_\alpha\rangle>0. Set the following target transitions to zero outside the selected two levels, and define

LA=|0⟩A⟨1|⊗|v⟩C⟨u|,LB=|1⟩B⟨0|⊗|u⟩C⟨v|,Xα=i𝖡α⊗(Lα−Lα†),𝒥=𝒥A⊗𝒥B⊗IC. \begin{aligned} L_A&=|0\rangle_A\langle1|\otimes|v\rangle_C\langle u|,& L_B&=|1\rangle_B\langle0|\otimes|u\rangle_C\langle v|,\\ X_\alpha&=i\mathsf B_\alpha\otimes(L_\alpha-L_\alpha^\dagger),& \mathcal J&=\mathcal J_A\otimes\mathcal J_B\otimes I_C. \end{aligned} (3.7)

The other carrier and its auxiliaries, omitted from these expressions, carry the identity. This explicitly selects ports between the carriers: the minimal example takes 𝖡α=I\mathsf B_\alpha=I, and a spectral auxiliary can also enter as one actual action. If an endpoint acts only on the fixed source and as the identity on the target, its compression has no off-diagonal matrix element LαL_\alpha and cannot implement the transfer below. The two selected modes must also remain closed during exchange; an abstract change of basis alone cannot establish that an actual port is available.

Reuse the reflections Sα=2Pα−IS_\alpha=2P_\alpha-I synthesized from the respective preparations in 2.3.5, with both arms acting simultaneously at each endpoint. Termwise compression gives

Ĥα=gα2(Xα+SαXαSα),Ĥα𝒥=𝒥hα,hα=iΩα(Lα−Lα†),Ωα=gαβα. \begin{aligned} \widehat H_\alpha&=\frac{g_\alpha}{2}(X_\alpha+S_\alpha X_\alpha S_\alpha),\\ \widehat H_\alpha\mathcal J&=\mathcal Jh_\alpha, \qquad h_\alpha=i\Omega_\alpha(L_\alpha-L_\alpha^\dagger), \qquad\Omega_\alpha=g_\alpha\beta_\alpha. \end{aligned} (3.8)

As before, the two arms cancel components outside the local preparation space, while 𝒥α†𝖡α𝒥α\mathcal J_\alpha^\dagger\mathsf B_\alpha\mathcal J_\alpha gives βα\beta_\alpha on the source and auxiliary factors. The preparation at the other endpoint is unaffected, so both terms preserve the common carrier. Sharing C does not make the two terms commute; they are composed below in the actual order.

Write Rα(x)=exp⁡[x(Lα−Lα†)]R_\alpha(x)=\exp[x(L_\alpha-L_\alpha^\dagger)], so that x=Ωαtx=\Omega_\alpha t. First perform the full transfer T=RA(π/2)T=R_A(\pi/2) at endpoint A, temporarily storing A’s logical state in C; then perform a partial exchange between C and B through angle γ\gamma; finally perform the actual inverse retrieval at the same A endpoint. For C entering in u, the three stages act as

W=T†RB(γ)T,W(ψAB⊗u)=(VγψAB)⊗u,Vγ|00⟩=|00⟩,Vγ|11⟩=|11⟩,Vγ|10⟩=cos⁡γ|10⟩+sin⁡γ|01⟩,Vγ|01⟩=cos⁡γ|01⟩−sin⁡γ|10⟩. \begin{aligned} W&=T^\dagger R_B(\gamma)T,\\ W(\psi_{AB}\otimes u)&=(V_\gamma\psi_{AB})\otimes u,\\ V_\gamma|00\rangle&=|00\rangle,\qquad V_\gamma|11\rangle=|11\rangle,\\ V_\gamma|10\rangle&=\cos\gamma|10\rangle+\sin\gamma|01\rangle,\\ V_\gamma|01\rangle&=\cos\gamma|01\rangle-\sin\gamma|10\rangle. \end{aligned} (3.9)

Check each of the four logical inputs: the first stage sends |a⟩AuC|a\rangle_Au_C to |0⟩A|a⟩C|0\rangle_A|a\rangle_C, the middle stage acts only on B and C, and the final stage completely retrieves both components of C, so C returns to u for every input. T retains the signs of a real rotation at other inputs. If only emission and absorption are retained, return of the mediator for |10⟩|10\rangle does not guarantee its return for |01⟩|01\rangle; the third stage completes retrieval over the entire logical space.

Composing the exact intertwining relation for each stage, with Ŵ\widehat W denoting the three actual protected pulses, yields the identity on the complete carrier:

Ŵ𝒥(ψAB⊗u)=𝒥(VγψAB⊗u). \boxed{\widehat W\,\mathcal J(\psi_{AB}\otimes u) =\mathcal J(V_\gamma\psi_{AB}\otimes u).} (3.10)

Thus the same relation holds for arbitrary mixed inputs and their entanglement with spectator records, without postselecting successful transfers. The sources and auxiliaries at both endpoints retain their original preparations and the mediator returns, while the target states may change and become entangled across the endpoints. For example, |10⟩|10\rangle becomes the coherent superposition of the two terms shown in the equation; a change of logical state does not mean that the complete carrier exits.

This example is calculated in the interaction picture at actual resonance. If the two modes are eigenstates of the local free generator, energy and charge balance within the code require

EA1−EA0=EB1−EB0=εv−εu=Δ,qA1qA0−1=qB1qB0−1=qvqu−1. \begin{gathered} E_{A1}-E_{A0}=E_{B1}-E_{B0}=\varepsilon_v-\varepsilon_u=\Delta,\\ q_{A1}q_{A0}^{-1}=q_{B1}q_{B0}^{-1}=q_vq_u^{-1}. \end{gathered} (3.11)

The charge equalities apply when the actual endpoints have definite group charges; otherwise covariance must be checked using matrix elements of the full representation. The energy condition within the code makes VγV_\gamma commute with the sum of the free energies at the two endpoints. Sufficient conditions for the complete two-arm action to conserve the same joint energy also include [Hfree,Xα]=[Hfree,Sα]=0[H_{\mathrm{free}},X_\alpha]=[H_{\mathrm{free}},S_\alpha]=0; energy conservation at the bare endpoint does not automatically ensure it for the reflected arm. If the actual controls do not satisfy these conditions, the energy supplied by the drive must be included, and shell energy cannot be directly identified with mass frequency.

When the maintenance action is retained and the above resonance conditions hold, free phases can be restored over the entire actual elapsed duration. If maintenance is paused during exchange, the pause still enters the frequency as prescribed in 2.4.6. For a forward middle stage γ≥0\gamma\ge0, the three-stage duration is Tex=π/(2ΩA)+γ/ΩB+π/(2ΩA)+TctrlT_{\mathrm{ex}}=\pi/(2\Omega_A)+\gamma/\Omega_B+\pi/(2\Omega_A)+T_{\mathrm{ctrl}}, with additional propagation, preparation, and recording time included in TctrlT_{\mathrm{ctrl}}. The final stage uses the actual inverse generator; if a different retrieval pulse is used, its action and duration must be recalculated.

For the specified input |10⟩|10\rangle, the middle-stage strength and readable transfer give

γ=gBβBTB,P10→01=sin⁡2γ,Δ⟨EB⟩=Δsin⁡2γ. \boxed{\gamma=g_B\beta_BT_B,\qquad P_{10\to01}=\sin^2\gamma,\qquad \Delta\langle E_B\rangle=\Delta\sin^2\gamma.} (3.12)

If the local 𝖡B\mathsf B_B uses the single-address effect of 7.1.3 and retains its specified auxiliary preparation, then βB=|Rθ|2/6\beta_B=|R_\theta|^2/6. This incorporates the spectral share into an actual exchange angle; the event probability remains sin⁡2γ\sin^2\gamma above, with interaction strength and duration retained. For a general port, βB\beta_B is obtained from the actual auxiliaries; a common character label cannot replace that calculation, nor can this example be taken as the unique realization of all force vertices.

When both endpoints use the same pattern Φ\Phi, they may also share one source. Take the joint embedding 𝒥shψ=ΦS⊗rA⊗rB⊗ψABC\mathcal J_{\mathrm{sh}}\psi=\Phi_S\otimes r_A\otimes r_B\otimes\psi_{ABC}, let each endpoint act only on the common source, its local auxiliaries, and its original logical port, and protect it with Pα,sh=PΦ⊗PrαP_{\alpha,\mathrm{sh}}=P_\Phi\otimes P_{r_\alpha}. The same two-arm cancellation gives Ĥα𝒥sh=𝒥shhα\widehat H_\alpha\mathcal J_{\mathrm{sh}}=\mathcal J_{\mathrm{sh}}h_\alpha, so the stagewise retrieval above remains valid and the source is counted only once. Local auxiliaries and complete records are retained; this identification is not made for different patterns or nonproduct permanent records.

No unretrieved path record is left while the relay temporarily stores the state. If the output is subsequently read, or thermal processing is added, retain these outcomes as a complete instrument. In particular, when each endpoint separately uses the thermal processing of 2.3.6, which is scalar on each survival history, let qA,qBq_A,q_B denote the survival shares at the endpoints and U0U_0 the free evolution retained over the actual elapsed duration. Summing all survival records gives

ℐlive(ρ)=qAqB𝒥ABU0VγρVγ†U0†𝒥AB†. \mathcal I_{\mathrm{live}}(\rho)=q_Aq_B\, \mathcal J_{AB}U_0V_\gamma\rho V_\gamma^\dagger U_0^\dagger \mathcal J_{AB}^\dagger. (3.13)

The shares in which only A exits, only B exits, and both exit are respectively (1−qA)qB(1-q_A)q_B, qA(1−qB)q_A(1-q_B), and (1−qA)(1−qB)(1-q_A)(1-q_B); together with the preceding expression they form the complete output. Two independent thermal processes are used here, with the same survival effect on every logical state employed; for a shared source, the operator associated with each thermal outcome acts as the identity on that source and both sets of auxiliaries. The same complete schedule is executed whichever endpoint exits; state-dependent exit or exit through a common environment must be calculated separately. Under the specified port, conservation, and record construction, exchange, retrieval, and subsequent survival of the two complete carriers are thereby connected into one set of finite processes.

3.1.3 Physical Readings of Exchange

The observed outcomes of exchange are determined by the actual pointers and their joint output. Include the actual pointers and other auxiliaries in environment ℰ, let 𝕌 denote the joint evolution including the necessary recording actions, and let η be its preparation. The joint final state yields both the reduced map on the two endpoints and the probability of event y:

Ωout=𝕌(ρAB⊗η)𝕌†,ΦAB(ρAB)=Tr⁡ℰΩout,qy=Tr⁡[(IAB⊗Qy)Ωout]. \begin{gathered}\Omega^{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb U(\rho_{AB}\otimes\eta)\mathbb U^\dagger,\\[3pt]\Phi_{AB}(\rho_{AB})=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal E}\Omega^{\mathrm{out}},\\[3pt]q_y=\operatorname{Tr}\![(I_{AB}\otimes Q_y)\Omega^{\mathrm{out}}].\end{gathered} (3.14)

Following the complete-record rule of Chapter 2, matrix elements of the actual joint evolution between the environment preparation and output basis give the Kraus actions for the outcomes 1112. Summing unread environment components within a single pointer class gives

ℐy(ρ)=∑aKyaρKya†,Ey=∑aKya†Kya,qy(ρ)=Tr⁡(ρEy),∑yEy=IAB. \begin{gathered}\mathcal I_y(\rho)=\sum_aK_{ya}\rho K_{ya}^{\dagger},\\[3pt]E_y=\sum_aK_{ya}^{\dagger}K_{ya},\\[3pt]q_y(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho E_y),\\[3pt]\sum_yE_y=I_{AB}.\end{gathered} (3.15)

Here aa combines unread preparation and output indices without specifying additional observable events; completeness follows from joint unitarity and normalized preparation. The correspondence between spectral response and coupling must be realized in these actual branches and their effects.

QyQ_{y} is an actual pointer projection satisfying the record conditions established in 2.3. The preceding final-state share becomes a recorded event probability only once the corresponding output distinction has been realized. When several paths enter the same event, combine them using the environment-overlap rule of 2.4.2; the return of C to the same prepared state means only that C retains no such distinction, while other parts of the environment may still contain records.

To quantify the effect on B, fix the input, environment preparation, and observation duration, and let Φ₀ be the baseline map with the exchange under discussion switched off. For an already calibrated observable OBO_{B}, the mean change caused by exchange is

Δ⟨OB⟩=Tr⁡[(IA⊗OB){ΦAB(ρAB)−Φ0(ρAB)}]. \Delta\langle O_B\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[(I_A\otimes O_B)\{\Phi_{AB}(\rho_{AB})-\Phi_0(\rho_{AB})\}\right]. (3.16)

Choosing a position, coherence, or momentum readout for OBO_{B} measures a distribution change, phase response, or momentum transfer, respectively. Only when momentum has been calibrated, with T denoting the actual elapsed duration of this comparison, does Δ⟨pB⟩/TΔ\langle p_{B}\rangle /T give the average mechanical force due to the exchange. The event probability qyq_{y}, the record rate per unit time, and this momentum response have different units and cannot share a numerical strength without a specified correspondence. Subsequent evaluation of resonance forces follows the established exchange process to determine its channels, response coefficients, and actual readings separately.

3.2 Structure of Resonance Channels

The preceding section connected transfer between directional endpoints to exchange and retrieval of selected complete carriers. We now fix the corresponding process and distinguish channels by changes in endpoint species: the propagation segment preserves the selected direction, while the endpoint transition is jointly balanced by the system and environment. Comparing the labels of the input and output states identifies which part of the phase structure participates in exchange, after which the corresponding actual action can be determined.

3.2.1 Channel Labels

Using the species-layer decomposition of 2.2, write p−1 as a product of pairwise coprime prime powers. Denote the order of the ith factor by nᵢ and the group of species labels by Γ:

p−1=∏i=1rni,ni=qibi,r=ω(p−1),Γ=∏i=1rℤ/niℤ. \begin{gathered}p-1=\prod_{i=1}^{r}n_i,\\[3pt]n_i=q_i^{b_i},\\[3pt]r=\omega(p-1),\\[3pt]\Gamma=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z.\end{gathered} (3.17)

The qᵢ are distinct, and ω counts the number of distinct prime factors. Once this CRT identification is fixed, the label ℓ=(ℓ₁,…,ℓᵣ) specifies the character χℓ=∏ᵢχℓᵢ⁽ⁱ⁾, and character multiplication is coordinatewise addition modulo nᵢ. The odd prime pp has not yet been assigned a value, and no specific particle or force names are assigned to the factors here.

Use the unit-shell average state e₀ as the trivial label |0⟩, and denote the remaining directions pulled back from the species layer by |ℓ⟩. These vectors are normalized as in 2.1 and span the species-layer subspace:

ℋsp=span⁡{|ℓ⟩:ℓ∈Γ}≃⨂i=1rℂni,|ℓ⟩↔|ℓ1⟩⊗⋯⊗|ℓr⟩,dim⁡ℋsp=p−1. \begin{gathered}\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sp}}=\operatorname{span}\{|\boldsymbol\ell\rangle:\boldsymbol\ell\in\Gamma\}\simeq\bigotimes_{i=1}^{r}\mathbb C^{n_i},\\[3pt]|\boldsymbol\ell\rangle\longleftrightarrow|\ell_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|\ell_r\rangle,\\[3pt]\dim\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sp}}=p-1.\end{gathered} (3.18)

This decomposes one layer of species degrees of freedom. The complete state space also contains other shells and directions of higher conductor; the dimension of the address space at depth K remains pᴷ. The trivial direction e₀ must be included in this tensor space, since transformations within a factor can mix nontrivial directions with it. Whether each nontrivial direction is a stable state under the specified response is still determined by the nonzero-eigenvalue condition of 2.1.

Fix the convention for the unit-group action so that the eigenvalue function of |ℓ⟩ is denoted by χℓ. When an endpoint changes from ℓ to ℓ′, the transition carries character χℓ′χℓ⁻¹, with label δ=ℓ′−ℓ. By the joint covariance of 3.1, a nonzero exchange matrix element between definite-charge input and output components satisfies

𝒜fi≠0⇒ΔℓA,i+ΔℓB,i+ΔℓC,i=0(mod⁡ni),i=1,…,r. \begin{gathered}\mathcal A_{fi}\ne0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\Delta\ell_{A,i}+\Delta\ell_{B,i}+\Delta\ell_{C,i}=0\pmod{n_i},\\[3pt]i=1,\ldots,r.\end{gathered} (3.19)

Here we first consider processes whose environment charges also belong to this species-layer character group; if the environment carries charge of higher conductor, balance must be imposed in the corresponding full group. When the input and output charges of C coincide, the label changes of A and B cancel coordinate by coordinate; when C retains a charge change, it carries the corresponding difference. Thus a coordinate at one endpoint may change, while conservation constrains the combined change of all participants.

The coordinates involved in the transition form its support S(δ)={i:δi≠0}S(δ)=\{i:δ_{i}≠0\}. If S is empty, the species label is unchanged, but the process may still change amplitude, phase, or records. If S contains one coordinate, the transition proceeds along one CRT factor; if S contains several, it changes several species components simultaneously. This classification covers arbitrary r and does not restrict multicoordinate changes to the case in which every coordinate is nonzero.

Joint conservation alone permits multicoordinate transitions. For example, the matrix unit Fℓ,δ=|ℓ+δ⟩⟨ℓ| carries charge χδ. If an environment operator B₋δ carries its inverse charge, a charge-conserving Hermitian action on the joint space can be formed:

D(u)Fℓ,𝜹D(u)†=χ𝜹(u)Fℓ,𝜹,DC(u)B−𝜹DC(u)†=χ𝜹(u)−1B−𝜹,V𝜹=gFℓ,𝜹⊗B−𝜹+g¯Fℓ,𝜹†⊗B−𝜹†. \begin{gathered}D(u)F_{\boldsymbol\ell,\boldsymbol\delta}D(u)^\dagger=\chi_{\boldsymbol\delta}(u)F_{\boldsymbol\ell,\boldsymbol\delta},\\[3pt]D_C(u)B_{-\boldsymbol\delta}D_C(u)^\dagger=\chi_{\boldsymbol\delta}(u)^{-1}B_{-\boldsymbol\delta},\\[3pt]V_{\boldsymbol\delta}=gF_{\boldsymbol\ell,\boldsymbol\delta}\otimes B_{-\boldsymbol\delta}+\overline g F_{\boldsymbol\ell,\boldsymbol\delta}^{\dagger}\otimes B_{-\boldsymbol\delta}^{\dagger}.\end{gathered} (3.20)

In each term the system and environment charges cancel, so Vδ commutes with the joint unit-group action without requiring δ to have only one nonzero coordinate. This construction checks charge conservation; its use as an actual vertex additionally requires the corresponding environment endpoints and energy balance. Single-factor channels must therefore be specified explicitly in the effective action.

3.2.2 Single-Factor Transitions

Following the single-factor step rule for formation paths, we organize elementary channels through effective transitions that act on only one CRT factor at a time and as the identity on all others. The matrix units of the ith family are

Xi(a,b)=I1⊗⋯⊗|a⟩i⟨b|⊗⋯⊗Ir,a,b∈ℤ/niℤ. \begin{gathered}X_i(a,b)=I_1\otimes\cdots\otimes|a\rangle_i\langle b|\otimes\cdots\otimes I_r,\\[3pt]a,b\in\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z.\end{gathered} (3.21)

For a≠b, this step carries charge whose only nonzero coordinate is a−b in position i; for a=b, it is a zero-charge diagonal action on that factor. This specifies both which labels change and the identity action on spectator factors. If a transition coefficient depends on labels of other factors, that conditional control must be retained; a single-coordinate label difference alone does not justify the above form.

These matrix units describe effective transitions within the species layer. The actual exchange vertices defined in 2.3 may also pass through the zero element and the environment, and the transfer of 3.1 also has intermediate states. Only after composing these steps and calculating the relevant matrix elements can one determine whether an effective channel is realized, together with its coefficient and phase. The trivial species-layer direction e₀ and the terminal zero element eKe_{K} belong to different shells and cannot be interchanged at this step.

Local matrix units on different factors commute. Every label difference also has a unique coordinate decomposition, so whenever all required local steps are available, a multicoordinate transition can be organized into a factor-by-factor path:

𝜹=∑i∈S(𝜹)δi𝒆i,χ𝜹=∏i∈S(𝜹)χδi𝒆i,[Xi(a,b),Xj(c,d)]=0(i≠j). \begin{gathered}\boldsymbol\delta=\sum_{i\in S(\boldsymbol\delta)}\delta_i\mathbf e_i,\\[3pt]\chi_{\boldsymbol\delta}=\prod_{i\in S(\boldsymbol\delta)}\chi_{\delta_i\mathbf e_i},\\[3pt][X_i(a,b),X_j(c,d)]=0\quad(i\ne j).\end{gathered} (3.22)

Here eᵢ is the unit vector of the label coordinates, not a shell-average state. The single-factor rule gives r families of local channels, and multicoordinate paths compose some of these families. Although the label decomposition is unique, the actual order is set by the process; complete exchanges sharing an environment need not commute, and their amplitudes also include intermediate states and records. Likewise, Rχ generally depends on the full character: the CRT decomposition does not imply factorwise multiplication of Dirichlet L-values.

3.2.3 Factor-Preserving Actions

Single-factor transitions determine the scope of actions within each factor. Extending these actions to arbitrary unitaries within each factor gives the factor-preserving unitary group, which organizes actions on the species layer that preserve the tensor-factor decomposition. Whether it also preserves a chosen spectral response must be checked by commutation with that response. This group is defined as the image of the tensor-product action:

𝒢fact={A1⊗⋯⊗Ar:Ai∈U(ni)}⊂U(ℋsp). \mathcal G_{\mathrm{fact}}=\{A_1\otimes\cdots\otimes A_r:A_i\in U(n_i)\}\subset U(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sp}}). (3.23)

A scalar phase can be factored out of each Aᵢ, leaving a determinant-one part; multiplying the scalars leaves only one overall phase. Hence the map Φ:(z,S₁,…,Sᵣ)↦z(S₁⊗⋯⊗Sᵣ) from U(1)×∏ᵢSU(nᵢ) onto this group is surjective. If its image is the identity, fixing eigenvectors of the other factors and comparing any two eigenvalues of the ith factor shows that Sᵢ must be scalar. The kernel is therefore completely characterized by

Si=ξiIi,ξini=1,z∏i=1rξi=1;ker⁡Φ≃∏i=1rμni≃ℤ/(p−1)ℤ. \begin{gathered}S_i=\xi_i I_i,\\[3pt]\xi_i^{n_i}=1,\\[3pt]z\prod_{i=1}^{r}\xi_i=1;\\[3pt]\ker\Phi\simeq\prod_{i=1}^{r}\mu_{n_i}\simeq\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z.\end{gathered} (3.24)

Here μₙ is the group of nth roots of unity. The final isomorphism uses the pairwise coprimality of the nᵢ; it also specifies the embedding of the central subgroup being quotiented out: each tuple ξᵢ determines z=(∏ᵢξᵢ)⁻¹. The resulting global group and Lie algebra are

𝒢fact≃U(1)×∏i=1rSU(ni)ℤp−1,𝔤fact≃𝔲(1)⊕⨁i=1r𝔰𝔲(ni). \begin{gathered}\mathcal G_{\mathrm{fact}}\simeq\frac{U(1)\times\prod_{i=1}^{r}SU(n_i)}{\mathbb Z_{p-1}},\\[3pt]\mathfrak g_{\mathrm{fact}}\simeq\mathfrak u(1)\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}\mathfrak{su}(n_i).\end{gathered} (3.25)

Each SU(nᵢ) factor is generated by i times the traceless Hermitian actions within that factor, including off-diagonal transitions and relative diagonal phases; it has nᵢ²−1 real generator directions. Scalar actions from all factors coincide as the same central U(1) on the tensor space. The Lie algebra thus has r+1 factors and total dimension 1+∑ᵢ(nᵢ²−1). This counts the structure of factor-preserving transformations on the species layer.

The central phase multiplies every vector in ℋspℋ_{\mathrm{sp}} by z, and every density operator satisfies (zI)ρ(zI)†=ρ; reading only the state within this space reveals no distinguishable change. It becomes a relative phase only if the actual process preserves coherence with another reference sector and applies the phase to the species layer alone. For example, take a reference subspace ℛ⊂ℋsp⟂ℛ⊂ℋ_{\mathrm{sp}}^{\perp} within the whole system, with projections PspP_{\mathrm{sp}} and PℛP_{ℛ}. On their direct sum,

Ũz=zPsp+Pℛ,PspŨzρŨz†Pℛ=zPspρPℛ. \begin{gathered}\widetilde U_z=zP_{\mathrm{sp}}+P_{\mathcal R},\\[3pt]P_{\mathrm{sp}}\widetilde U_z\rho\widetilde U_z^\dagger P_{\mathcal R}=zP_{\mathrm{sp}}\rho P_{\mathcal R}.\end{gathered} (3.26)

The corresponding observation must read this coherence block; if the preparation has no coherence across sectors, or recording has removed it, the action remains indistinguishable. The reference here is internal to the whole, and its preparation and phase action must be specified by the actual process. The central U(1) therefore does not correspond to a label difference with every coordinate nonzero: a scalar action preserves all labels, whereas a multicoordinate transition changes them.

3.2.4 Symmetries of a Fixed Response

The factor-preserving group also cannot be directly identified with the symmetry group of fixed dynamics. In the chosen character basis, let TspT_{\mathrm{sp}} be the restriction of the shell-preserving response to ℋspℋ_{\mathrm{sp}}, and denote all its eigenvalues by λℓ. For nontrivial labels, λℓ=Rχℓ; the shell-preserving response used here is projected onto direction space ℳ on both sides, so λ₀=0. This zero follows from the projection defining the directional response; the background in the complete cycle is still treated through the actual exchange. For an arbitrary unitary A, preservation of this fixed response requires

Tsp|ℓ⟩=λℓ|ℓ⟩,[A,Tsp]=0⇔(λℓ′−λℓ)⟨ℓ′|A|ℓ⟩=0(∀ℓ,ℓ′). \begin{gathered}T_{\mathrm{sp}}|\boldsymbol\ell\rangle=\lambda_{\boldsymbol\ell}|\boldsymbol\ell\rangle,\\[3pt][A,T_{\mathrm{sp}}]=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(\lambda_{\boldsymbol\ell^{\prime}}-\lambda_{\boldsymbol\ell})\langle\boldsymbol\ell^{\prime}|A|\boldsymbol\ell\rangle=0\quad(\forall\boldsymbol\ell,\boldsymbol\ell^{\prime}).\end{gathered} (3.27)

Thus only directions with identical complex eigenvalues can mix under this symmetry; equality of eigenvalue moduli alone is insufficient. Arbitrary unitary transformations are possible within each degenerate spectral block, while a simple spectrum leaves only phase transformations of the individual directions. A symmetry of the complete cycle must also be compatible with the actual exchanges, environment preparation, and readout; changing basis simultaneously for all states, operators, and pointers is a change of representation of the same process.

Under the specified single-factor effective step rule, this section obtains r families of local channels, together with r SU factors and one central U(1) from the tensor structure of the species layer. Identifying these r+1 structural factors with r+1 independent elementary resonance forces further requires the corresponding exchanges, readable responses, and their independence to be established individually; in particular, the central phase needs a specified relative reference. Specific force names and stable-state identities are fixed when channels are selected. Here we first calculate each channel’s coupling from its actual endpoints, participating directions, and environment output.

3.3 Couplings of Elementary Resonance Forces

After an exchange, environment records give the share of the selected outcome, while system readings give the change experienced by the stable state. Comparing the strengths of different resonance channels requires comparing responses of the same kind under common preparation and reference conventions. We first consider the direct action at an effective vertex, before incorporating repeated exchanges that leave and return, and call the corresponding dimensionless response coefficient the elementary coupling or bare coupling.

Using the notation of 3.2, δ denotes the species-label difference between input and output endpoints, while χ denotes the participating stable-state direction. The former determines the charge that the environment must balance in the exchange; the latter determines the spectral response used. Even processes carrying the same transfer charge may act on different stable states, so Rχ in the coupling must be evaluated for the direction that actually participates.

Fix the regular spectral point s*s_* used in 2.1, retain the full background spectral reference ζ*=ζ(s*)≠0\zeta_*=\zeta(s_*)\ne0, and abbreviate Lχ=L(s*,χ)L_\chi=L(s_*,\chi). By the directional response of 3.1, the squared response for input ρ and direction projection Pχ is |Rχ|2Tr⁡(ρPχ)|R_\chi|^2\operatorname{Tr}(\rho P_\chi). We now calculate how the actual preparation and endpoint matching determine this share.

3.3.1 Participating Labels

Once the directional response is fixed, the actual matching share remains to be calculated: an equal-weight preparation supplies orthogonal alternatives, of which the vertex accepts only one normalized direction, so the dimension of the alternative space is needed. To organize candidate exchanges in the species layer, write G=(ℤ/pℤ)×G=(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times and m=(p−1)/2m=(p-1)/2, and arrange the alternatives by relative unit-group action uu, negation-pair group jj, and conjugate orientation oo. First stipulate that these three labels vary independently. Then

Λχ=G×{0,…,m−1}×{+,−},m=p−12. \begin{gathered}\Lambda_\chi=G\times\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\times\{+,-\},\\[3pt]m=\frac{p-1}{2}.\end{gathered} (3.28)

Here j groups the species layer by {a,−a}\{a,-a\}; in deeper reductions it represents the entire group of lifts described in Supplementary Proof S4.2–Supplementary Proof S4.3, not the total number of point pairs at depth K. The label u describes the relative action, while j describes the group in which preparation or matching occurs. If the same address determines both in the actual process, the actually allowed subset of labels must be used, without multiplying their counts independently again.

We classify by the value of χ(u), retaining orientation when χ differs from its conjugate and combining the two orientations into one class when χ is real. Let ηχ(o) take values + and − in the former case and remain 0 in the latter. The classification map is

rχ(u,j,o)=(χ(u),ηχ(o)),ηχ(o)={o,χ≠χ‾,0,χ=χ‾. r_\chi(u,j,o)=(\chi(u),\eta_\chi(o)),\qquad \eta_\chi(o)=\begin{cases}o,&\chi\ne\bar\chi,\\0,&\chi=\bar\chi.\end{cases} (3.29)

This map first gives an algebraic classification. Realizing it as a record requires the corresponding internal reference and pointer; applying u to a pure character state produces only a common phase and does not by itself read χ(u). The following count also does not assume that these phases can be perfectly distinguished in a single readout.

Fix a class in the image of this map. For its phase value χ(u₀), the full preimage is u₀kerχ, giving |kerχ| choices of u; j has m choices; and orientation has cχ preimages, where cχ=1+[χ=χ̄]. With dχ=ordχ, the kernel–image relation for a group homomorphism gives the number of labels in this class:

Nχ=|ker⁡χ|mcχ=(p−1)22dχcχ,dχ=ord⁡χ,cχ=1+𝟏{χ=χ‾}. \begin{gathered}N_\chi=|\ker\chi|\,m\,c_\chi=\frac{(p-1)^2}{2d_\chi}\,c_\chi,\\[3pt]d_\chi=\operatorname{ord}\chi,\\[3pt]c_\chi=1+\mathbf1_{\{\chi=\bar\chi\}}.\end{gathered} (3.30)

Here Nχ counts label preimages within the same accepted class, with its three factors coming from relative action, point-pair group, and orientation. To use this count for an actual matching share, the preparation or environment must contain corresponding independent alternatives carrying these labels. In particular, the factor 2 in the self-conjugate case requires two actual orientation alternatives; if forward and reverse are merely two descriptions of the same complete state, they are counted once. If they are two coherent histories leading to the same joint final state, amplitudes are combined first, and their strength is determined jointly by phase and environment overlap.

3.3.2 Endpoint Matching

Suppose that all labels in the selected class are indeed carried by Nχ orthogonal preparation alternatives, with label space ℒχ. Take the equal-weight mixed preparation σχ=Iℒχ/Nχ and suppose this vertex matches only one normalized direction vχ, with normalized matched output fχ. Following the spectral-response assignment, specify the unnormalized action of this vertex as Aχ=Lχ|fχ⟩⟨vχ|. Any normalized input ξ first enters the matched direction with overlap ⟨vχ|ξ⟩ and then acquires the spectral factor Lχ; averaging over the prepared state gives

Aχ|ξ⟩=Lχ⟨vχ|ξ⟩|fχ⟩,Pvχ=|vχ⟩⟨vχ|,Aχ†Aχ=|Lχ|2Pvχ,Tr⁡(σχAχ†Aχ)=|Lχ|2Nχ. \begin{gathered}A_\chi|\xi\rangle=L_\chi\langle v_\chi|\xi\rangle|f_\chi\rangle,\\[3pt]P_{v_\chi}=|v_\chi\rangle\langle v_\chi|,\\[3pt]A_\chi^\dagger A_\chi=|L_\chi|^2P_{v_\chi},\\[3pt]\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\chi A_\chi^\dagger A_\chi)=\frac{|L_\chi|^2}{N_\chi}.\end{gathered} (3.31)

The last step uses only Tr(Pvχ)=1. Thus the denominator comes from the share of an equal-weight preparation lying in one matched direction. Dividing this mean response by the specified squared background spectral response gives the bare coupling:

αχ(0):=Tr⁡(σχAχ†Aχ)|ζ*|2=|Rχ|2Nχ=2dχ(p−1)2cχ|L(s*,χ)ζ(s*)|2. \alpha_\chi^{(0)}:=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\chi A_\chi^\dagger A_\chi)}{|\zeta_*|^2}=\frac{|R_\chi|^2}{N_\chi}=\frac{2d_\chi}{(p-1)^2c_\chi}\left|\frac{L(s_*,\chi)}{\zeta(s_*)}\right|^2. (3.32)

The superscript (0) indicates that repeated exchange has not yet been included. Equal-weight labels can be realized by thermal preparation in the equal-energy block HL=ϵIH_L=\epsilon I, whose conditional Gibbs state is I/NχI/N_\chi 13. For a general normalized preparation σχ\sigma_\chi, retaining a common spectral amplitude on the actual matching subspace, namely Aχ†Aχ=|Lχ|2PmatchA_\chi^\dagger A_\chi=|L_\chi|^2P_{\mathrm{match}}, gives

αχ(0)=|Rχ|2Tr⁡(σχPmatch);σχ=I/Nχ,rank⁡Pmatch=q⇒αχ(0)=q|Rχ|2Nχ. \begin{gathered}\alpha_\chi^{(0)}=|R_\chi|^2\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\chi P_{\mathrm{match}});\\[3pt]\sigma_\chi=I/N_\chi,\ \operatorname{rank}P_{\mathrm{match}}=q\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\alpha_\chi^{(0)}=\frac{q|R_\chi|^2}{N_\chi}.\end{gathered} (3.33)

Thus the denominator counts the share of the equal-weight input lying in the matching subspace; summation of orthogonal outcomes and amplitude combination of coherent paths are treated separately as in 2.4.2.

3.3.3 Actual Events

The bare coupling is a squared-response ratio relative to a reference; actual events must still be specified by a normalized instrument. For a single matched direction, choose κ>0 such that κ²|Rχ|²≤1 and set, on the same label space,

Mχ=κRχ|fχ⟩⟨vχ|,M⌀=(I−κ2|Rχ|2Pvχ)1/2,Mχ†Mχ+M⌀†M⌀=I. \begin{gathered}M_\chi=\kappa R_\chi|f_\chi\rangle\langle v_\chi|,\\[3pt]M_\varnothing=(I-\kappa^2|R_\chi|^2P_{v_\chi})^{1/2},\\[3pt]M_\chi^\dagger M_\chi+M_\varnothing^\dagger M_\varnothing=I.\end{gathered} (3.34)

The record χ\chi and remaining outcomes ⌀\varnothing complete the output; κ\kappa calibrates the interaction amplitude, and the event share of the equal-weight input is κ2αχ(0)\kappa^2\alpha_\chi^{(0)}. For a given exchange, checking whether its actual effect equals κ2|Rχ|2Pmatch\kappa^2|R_\chi|^2P_{\mathrm{match}} determines whether it realizes this response. The criterion for all inputs and its short proof are given in Supplementary Proof S5.1.

For the transfer from a unit-shell direction to the terminal zero element already specified in Supplementary Proof S5.1, this connection can be expressed directly as cycle data. In this section θ denotes the exchange angle, to distinguish it from coupling α. Let aKχ be the corresponding preparation share, θKχ the exchange angle, and tu,Kχ the environment upper-state weight. Then

ϵKχ=aKχtu,Kχsin⁡2θKχ;aKχsin⁡2θKχ=αχ(0)⇒ϵKχ=tu,Kχαχ(0). \begin{gathered}\epsilon_{K\chi}=a_{K\chi}t_{u,K\chi}\sin^2\theta_{K\chi};\\[3pt]a_{K\chi}\sin^2\theta_{K\chi}=\alpha_\chi^{(0)}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\epsilon_{K\chi}=t_{u,K\chi}\alpha_\chi^{(0)}.\end{gathered} (3.35)

This realization carries the bare coupling through a combination of preparation share and exchange angle, while the actual event probability also contains the thermal environment weight. When several directions share one preparation, their aKχ obey a sum constraint. Supplementary Proof S5.1 provides a common construction when S=∑χαχ⁽⁰⁾<1: the background share is strictly positive, the exchange angles take nonendpoint values, and the spectral evaluations of all directions are realized by the same normalized instrument. Specific values are checked within this range.

The persistent port of 3.1.2 places the single-address mean βB=αEM(0)\beta_B=\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}^{(0)} in angle γ=gBTBβB\gamma=g_BT_B\beta_B, giving probability sin⁡2γ\sin^2\gamma; the one-shot acceptance instrument of this section places the spectral response in the amplitude, giving κ2α(0)\kappa^2\alpha^{(0)} for an equal-weight input. The former scales as (α(0))2(\alpha^{(0)})^2 at short times, whereas the latter scales linearly with α(0)\alpha^{(0)}. These use different actual endpoints and show that the location at which a spectral share enters an operator determines its reading.

3.3.4 Comparison of Couplings

With the same spectral parameter and reference, equal-weight preparations, and one matched direction each, the ratio of two nonzero elementary couplings is

αχ(0)αψ(0)=|L(s*,χ)L(s*,ψ)|2NψNχ. \frac{\alpha_\chi^{(0)}}{\alpha_\psi^{(0)}}=\left|\frac{L(s_*,\chi)}{L(s_*,\psi)}\right|^2\frac{N_\psi}{N_\chi}. (3.36)

Relative strength is determined jointly by spectral response and matching share. Character order determines the kernel size and thus enters the participation count; the L-value also depends on the particular phases of that character at each integer, so ordering by character order cannot replace calculation of response magnitudes. If two processes have different thermal environment weights or matching ranks, these factors must also be retained when comparing actual recorded shares.

A response bound must also specify the range of the spectral parameter. For real s>1, absolute convergence of the Dirichlet series and the triangle inequality give

|L(s,χ)|≤∑p∤nn−s=(1−p−s)ζ(s),|Rχ(s)|≤1−p−s(s>1). \begin{gathered}|L(s,\chi)|\le\sum_{p\nmid n}n^{-s}=(1-p^{-s})\zeta(s),\\[3pt]|R_\chi(s)|\le1-p^{-s}\quad(s>1).\end{gathered} (3.37)

When evaluation at s₀=1/2 uses analytic continuation, this proof no longer guarantees the above maximal-response bound. In that case |ζ(s₀)|² serves as the specified spectral reference, while preparation and the instrument control the range of actual probabilities. Each elementary coupling is thereby connected to a definite direction, participating labels, and matching endpoint. If repeated exchange changes accessible paths or final-state records, the response must be recombined from those actual actions.

3.4 Virtual Processes and Effective Couplings

When a stable state participates in an exchange, the excitation may reach the selected endpoint directly, or first enter an intermediate direction and then return to the original direction or reach the same endpoint. Such round trips change both the amplitude reaching the endpoint and the preparation share. For processes that preserve the spectral vertex, virtual corrections change the matching share of the same direction, replacing the participation count in the bare-coupling denominator with an effective matching denominator. If the spectral vertex or matched direction also changes with the process, those changes must be included in the complete response.

Here intermediate round trips that are not read as independently terminating events are called virtual processes. Direct and round-trip paths are combined using the environment-overlap formula of 2.4.2, and the resulting complete output becomes the input to the next round. Virtual processes thus change both endpoint response and subsequent preparation; these changes are calculated separately below.

3.4.1 Effective Matching Share

First consider a case admitting an exact effective-denominator form: intermediate actions change the preparation at the matching endpoint while leaving the response Aχ and matched direction vχ specified in 3.3 unchanged. Let Γχ≥0 be a nonzero unnormalized preparation on this label space, with σχ=Γχ/Zχ and Zχ=TrΓχ; write hχ=⟨vχ|Γχ|vχ⟩>0 and wχ=|Rχ|²>0. Since Aχ†Aχ=|Lχ|²Pvχ,

αχeff:=Tr⁡(σχAχ†Aχ)|ζ*|2=wχhχZχ=wχNχeff,Nχeff:=Zχhχ≥1,ΔNχ:=Nχeff−Nχ,αχeff=wχNχ+ΔNχ. \begin{gathered}\alpha_\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}:=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\chi A_\chi^\dagger A_\chi)}{|\zeta_*|^2}=w_\chi\frac{h_\chi}{Z_\chi}=\frac{w_\chi}{N_\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}},\\[3pt]N_\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}:=\frac{Z_\chi}{h_\chi}\ge1,\\[3pt]\Delta N_\chi:=N_\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}-N_\chi,\\[3pt]\alpha_\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{w_\chi}{N_\chi+\Delta N_\chi}.\end{gathered} (3.38)

The inequality follows from 0≤Pvχ≤I, which gives hχ≤Zχ. The equal-weight preparation can be represented by Γχ=I, giving Zχ=Nχ and hχ=1 and recovering the bare coupling. If hχ=0, the preparation has no matching share and the coupling vanishes; the effective denominator can only be understood as an infinite limit. Multiplying Γχ by an overall positive scalar does not change the ratio.

Thus the bare value Nχ may come from a structural label count, whereas Nχᵉᶠᶠ is the ratio of total preparation weight to matching weight and is generally no longer an integer. An intermediate process that increases the matching share decreases the effective denominator; one that relatively increases other preparation shares increases it. If the actual correction also changes Aχ, the matched direction, or coherent paths, first recalculate Tr(σχAχ†Aχ), without presuming that all changes enter the denominator.

The link between this response and event probability still uses the actual calibration of 3.3. For example, if the conditional operator of the selected outcome is Mχ=κAχ/ζ＊, with κ fixed and satisfying Mχ†Mχ≤I, then pχ(σχ)=κ²αχᵉᶠᶠ. Preparation dependence, the calibration factor, and the duration of each round are all retained explicitly. To turn a spectral-response ratio into a stationary record rate, one must additionally use the actual stationary input and divide by τ.

Now calculate the first-order correction near the equal-weight preparation. Let a real parameter λ control the added action, and suppose Γχ(λ)=I+λGχ+O(λ²), where Gχ is self-adjoint and Γχ remains positive in a neighborhood. Writing γχ=TrGχ and gχ=⟨vχ|Gχ|vχ⟩, direct expansion of the above ratio gives

Nχeff(λ)=Nχ+λγχ+O(λ2)1+λgχ+O(λ2)=Nχ+λ(γχ−Nχgχ)+O(λ2),αχeff(λ)=αχ(0)[1+λ(gχ−γχNχ)+O(λ2)]. \begin{gathered}N_\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)=\frac{N_\chi+\lambda\gamma_\chi+O(\lambda^2)}{1+\lambda g_\chi+O(\lambda^2)}=N_\chi+\lambda(\gamma_\chi-N_\chi g_\chi)+O(\lambda^2),\\[3pt]\alpha_\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)=\alpha_\chi^{(0)}\left[1+\lambda\left(g_\chi-\frac{\gamma_\chi}{N_\chi}\right)+O(\lambda^2)\right].\end{gathered} (3.39)

The quantity γχ measures the change in total weight, while gχ measures the change at the matching endpoint; their relative sizes determine the sign of the correction. Even for an exactly linear preparation Γχ=I+λGχ, the effective denominator remains (Nχ+λγχ)/(1+λgχ) and does not automatically truncate to a linear expression.

3.4.2 Virtual-Process Corrections

Finding Gχ requires tracing how the added action changes total preparation weight and endpoint matching weight. Structural labels first constrain the directions through which these contributions can pass: if the system operator Xχ of a step carries definite character charge χ under the unit-group action, then composing it twice in the same direction gives

D(u)XχD(u)†=χ(u)Xχ⇒D(u)Xχ2D(u)†=χ(u)2Xχ2. D(u)X_\chi D(u)^\dagger=\chi(u)X_\chi\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D(u)X_\chi^2D(u)^\dagger=\chi(u)^2X_\chi^2. (3.40)

The environment must still balance this system charge in the joint exchange. Thus a nonzero matrix element sends system label η to ηχ²; the composite operator may also vanish through endpoint mismatch. For nontrivial χ, χ²=1 if and only if ord χ=2, and χ²=χ̄ if and only if ord χ=3. Other squares lie in other nontrivial directions. The class whose same-direction square is the trivial character is called Type II; the remaining class is called Type I. This classification first specifies the destination of the composite charge.

Since G is cyclic of even order, the nontrivial quadratic character χq is unique. But any χ multiplied by χ̄ also gives 1, so this does not imply a unique neutral round trip. For order 3, {1,χ,χ¯}\{1,χ,\overline{χ}\} is closed under label multiplication; higher-order characters also have finite multiplicative closures and can form longer return paths. Which paths occur depends on the actual vertices, shells, energy balance, and environment output.

For Type I, the first-order effective-denominator shift equals V₀−2wχ provided the actual correction satisfies γχ−Nχgχ=V₀−2wχ. If the total-weight term and endpoint-enhancement term are further specified separately as γχ=V₀ and gχ=2wχ/Nχ, then

γχ=V0,gχ=2wχNχ⇒Nχeff=Nχ+λ(V0−2wχ)+O(λ2). \begin{gathered}\gamma_\chi=V_0,\\[3pt]g_\chi=\frac{2w_\chi}{N_\chi}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N_\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}=N_\chi+\lambda(V_0-2w_\chi)+O(\lambda^2).\end{gathered} (3.41)

V₀ must be calculated from the actual preparation and operator of the selected background fluctuation. If a connected fluctuation is defined as ⟨B†B⟩−|⟨B⟩|², B and the state in which the expectation is taken must be specified; identifying it with |Rχq|² remains an additional correspondence. The coefficient 2 must likewise come from two actual contributions and their coherence relation, and cannot be inferred merely from passage through two vertices.

Equation (3.41) determines a first-order shift. To use this shift in a finite corrected denominator, write ΔNχ,I=V0−2wχ\Delta N_{\chi,\mathrm I}=V_0-2w_\chi and take, in the range Nχ+ΔNχ,I≥1N_\chi+\Delta N_{\chi,\mathrm I}\ge1,

ΔNχ,I=V0−2wχ,Nχ,Ifin=Nχ+ΔNχ,I,αχ,Ifin=wχNχ+V0−2wχ. \begin{gathered}\Delta N_{\chi,\mathrm I}=V_0-2w_\chi,\\[3pt]N_{\chi,\mathrm I}^{\mathrm{fin}}=N_\chi+\Delta N_{\chi,\mathrm I},\\[3pt]\alpha_{\chi,\mathrm I}^{\mathrm{fin}} =\frac{w_\chi}{N_\chi+V_0-2w_\chi}.\end{gathered} (3.42)

The superscript fin\mathrm{fin} denotes the finite-correction prescription used here. It retains the above first-order coefficient; the first-order expansion has not determined higher-order changes in the actual preparation. The connected background contribution increases the effective denominator, while the two endpoint enhancements decrease it; their net effect determines whether the coupling is enhanced or reduced relative to its bare value. The common spectral factor wχw_\chi remains unchanged at this step.

The same applies to cross-direction actions in Type II. Only if the actual routing calculation gives first-order coefficients εχψ and a self-conjugate-alternative contribution cχwχ can one write

Nχeff=Nχ+λ(∑ψϵχψwψ+cχwχ)+O(λ2),wψ=|Rψ|2. \begin{gathered}N_\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}=N_\chi+\lambda\left(\sum_{\psi}\epsilon_{\chi\psi}w_\psi+c_\chi w_\chi\right)+O(\lambda^2),\\[3pt]w_\psi=|R_\psi|^2.\end{gathered} (3.43)

The sum covers the directions that actually participate. Only mutually orthogonal alternatives with equal response weights directly give integer multiplicities; coherently combined paths require their cross terms to be retained. Each correction must be realized as a change in total preparation weight or matching weight. Under the same finite-correction prescription, denote the sum of these contributions by ΔNχ,II\Delta N_{\chi,\mathrm {II}} and require the resulting denominator to be at least one. Then

ΔNχ,II=∑ψϵχψwψ+cχwχ,Nχ,IIfin=Nχ+ΔNχ,II,αχ,IIfin=wχNχ+∑ψϵχψwψ+cχwχ. \begin{gathered}\Delta N_{\chi,\mathrm {II}} =\sum_\psi\epsilon_{\chi\psi}w_\psi+c_\chi w_\chi,\\[3pt]N_{\chi,\mathrm {II}}^{\mathrm{fin}}=N_\chi+\Delta N_{\chi,\mathrm {II}},\\[3pt]\alpha_{\chi,\mathrm {II}}^{\mathrm{fin}} =\frac{w_\chi}{N_\chi+\sum_\psi\epsilon_{\chi\psi}w_\psi+c_\chi w_\chi}.\end{gathered} (3.44)

Both classes of formulas express corrections as the matching share at the same endpoint. Type I retains the connected background contribution and endpoint enhancement in the given direction; Type II additionally includes redistribution across directions obtained from the actual routing. Signs and multiplicities of correction terms are determined by the corresponding actions and complete output, with the conditions for adopting a finite denominator kept distinct from the first-order expansion.

3.4.3 Composition of Repeated Processes

Higher-order responses from repeated round trips can be obtained directly from the actual intermediate actions. First consider a coherence-preserving process: paths of different lengths are indeed indistinguishable in the same final readout, and their propagation phases and durations are included in their amplitudes. Let b be the amplitude vector entering the intermediate space, C the linear action from that space to the selected endpoint, and B the amplitude action for one further round trip within it. Denote the total amplitude combining all intermediate paths by ainta_{\mathrm{int}}. Splitting according to whether another round trip occurs gives aint=b+Bainta_{\mathrm{int}}=b+B a_{\mathrm{int}}. When the spectral radius satisfies spr(B)<1, this relation has a unique solution, hence

aint=(I−B)−1b,Caint=∑n=0∞CBnb,𝒜eff=𝒜dir+C(I−B)−1b. \begin{gathered}a_{\mathrm{int}}=(I-B)^{-1}b,\\[3pt]Ca_{\mathrm{int}}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}CB^n b,\\[3pt]\mathcal A_{\mathrm{eff}}=\mathcal A_{\mathrm{dir}}+C(I-B)^{-1}b.\end{gathered} (3.45)

In finite dimensions, the spectral-radius condition ensures that Bⁿ tends to zero; multiplying the finite sum by I−B gives I−Bⁿ⁺¹, and taking the limit yields the formula. Here ainta_{\mathrm{int}} is the total path amplitude under the common terminal readout, not a separately normalized intermediate or stationary state. C, B, and b contain the actual matrix elements and propagation factors. The coupling correction is obtained only after substituting the effective amplitude into a response comparison with the same preparation and spectral reference; if different durations have left orthogonal time records, one must instead sum recorded outcomes.

A scalar alternating series is only one special case: the corrected amplitude becomes its first term divided by 1+r only if the accessible intermediate mode is actually multiplied by −r at each repetition and |r|<1. Orientation reversal alone does not fix this sign. For example, on a conjugate pair let S exchange the two orientations, with S²=I. If B=rS, then

(I−rS)−1=I+rS1−r2=P+1−r+P−1+r,P±=I±S2,|r|<1. \begin{gathered}(I-rS)^{-1}=\frac{I+rS}{1-r^2}=\frac{P_+}{1-r}+\frac{P_-}{1+r},\\[3pt]P_\pm=\frac{I\pm S}{2},\\[3pt]|r|<1.\end{gathered} (3.46)

The factor 1/(1+r) remains alone only when the component actually entered and read out lies in the antisymmetric mode. If both modes participate, both terms must be retained. Label closure for a character of order 3 does not by itself determine which mode is entered, the magnitude of the repetition ratio r, or whether the environment retains a distinction.

When the environment has recorded the intermediate outcomes, repeated processes are instead composed through completely positive actions. Let 𝒬 denote the conditional action in which the exchange has not yet terminated, and 𝒥χ the action terminating with the selected outcome; all terminating outcomes together with 𝒬 form a complete trace-preserving one-step action. If spr(𝒬)<1, the probability of eventually obtaining a χ-class outcome from normalized initial state ρ is

pχend=∑n=0∞Tr⁡𝒥χ𝒬n(ρ)=Tr⁡[𝒥χ(I−𝒬)−1(ρ)]. p_\chi^{\mathrm{end}}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal J_\chi\mathcal Q^n(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\mathcal J_\chi(I-\mathcal Q)^{-1}(\rho)\right]. (3.47)

The terms correspond to different termination rounds and are individually nonnegative; summing over every terminating outcome gives 1 under the above termination condition. This probability calculation and coherent amplitude summation describe different recording arrangements. To calculate strength per unit time, the actual duration of each path must also be included; a termination probability cannot be directly treated as a count rate.

To compare different corrections, fix the preparation procedure, spectral reference, and outcome read. Let {ℐr}\{ℐ_{r}\} be the one-round instrument including all intermediate actions, ℱ the complete cycle, and ℐχ the instrument for the selected terminal-record class. Each round uses the same fresh environment preparation and has actual period τ. Then

∑rℐr=ℱ,pχ(ρ)=Tr⁡ℐχ(ρ),ρ*=ℱ(ρ*),ℛχ,*=pχ(ρ*)τ. \begin{gathered}\sum_r\mathcal I_r=\mathcal F,\\[3pt]p_\chi(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal I_\chi(\rho),\\[3pt]\rho_* =\mathcal F(\rho_*),\\[3pt]\mathscr R_{\chi,*}=\frac{p_\chi(\rho_*)}{\tau}.\end{gathered} (3.48)

Under the positive-exchange and restoration conditions in §4.4 of Ref. 2, iteration of the original thermal cycle converges to ρ＊, and the expected cumulative event count divided by total duration tends to ℛχ,＊ as the number of cycles grows. This result for the expected count rate does not require events in successive rounds to be independent (Hu, 2026, §§4.4 and 6.6) 2. Stationary occupation is determined jointly by preparation and exchange, so the stationary record rate generally also contains stable-state occupation and thermal environment weights. Couplings must be compared using the same input and calibration; if stationary inputs are used instead, their dependence must be retained as well.

The pχ above is the share of rounds producing the selected terminal outcome and lies between 0 and 1. If several χ-class events are actually recorded within one round, their mean number is ∑h nχ(h)Pr(h), where h denotes a distinguishable complete record history. This may exceed 1 and differs from the probability of at least one occurrence in the round. Coherent paths that leave no distinction are combined at the amplitude level and are not counted among these additive histories.

3.4.4 Corrected Couplings

Combining coherent paths and recorded histories determines how repeated processes enter the actual response. If these actions preserve the spectral vertex, matched direction, and comparison reference, their changes to the same effective denominator can be examined further. Let δNn\delta N_n be the added denominator contribution from repetition nn, with first term ΔNχfin\Delta N_\chi^{\mathrm{fin}} chosen as the finite-correction shift of Type I or Type II above. For a fixed real number rr, when the actual denominator increments satisfy the following recurrence and |r|<1|r|<1, their sum and the corresponding coupling are

δNn+1=−rδNn,δN0=ΔNχfin,r∈ℝ,|r|<1,Nχfull=Nχ+∑n=0∞δNn=Nχ+ΔNχfin1+r,αχfull=wχNχfull=wχNχ+ΔNχfin/(1+r). \begin{gathered} \delta N_{n+1}=-r\delta N_n,\qquad \delta N_0=\Delta N_\chi^{\mathrm{fin}},\qquad r\in\mathbb R,\quad |r|<1,\\[3pt] N_\chi^{\mathrm{full}}=N_\chi+\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\delta N_n =N_\chi+\frac{\Delta N_\chi^{\mathrm{fin}}}{1+r},\\[3pt] \alpha_\chi^{\mathrm{full}}=\frac{w_\chi}{N_\chi^{\mathrm{full}}} =\frac{w_\chi}{N_\chi+\Delta N_\chi^{\mathrm{fin}}/(1+r)}. \end{gathered} (3.49)

Induction on the recurrence gives δNn=(−r)nΔNχfin\delta N_n=(-r)^n\Delta N_\chi^{\mathrm{fin}}. The sum of the first J+1J+1 terms is ΔNχfin[1−(−r)J+1]/(1+r)\Delta N_\chi^{\mathrm{fin}}[1-(-r)^{J+1}]/(1+r); under |r|<1|r|<1 the remainder tends to zero, yielding the effective denominator. Dividing the same spectral response wχw_\chi by this denominator gives the corrected coupling. The resulting NχfullN_\chi^{\mathrm{full}} must still be at least one and compatible with probability normalization of the actual instrument; when r=0r=0, this formula recovers the preceding finite-correction prescription.

This resummation acts on the increments of the denominator, leaving the bare denominator NχN_\chi unchanged. The denominator recurrence must be established separately from the corresponding process and cannot be replaced directly by a geometric amplitude series: taking a coherent amplitude’s squared modulus generates cross terms, and preparation normalization also generates higher-order terms. The sum is exact once the recurrence is given; the finite prescription for its first term and the repetition ratio retain their respective physical-correspondence conditions. Here full\mathrm{full} denotes the complete sum of this specified correction sequence.

Exact normalization may also arise from ratio preservation in a recorded process. Independently prepare a state on a fixed output auxiliary space. Let the continuation branch leave that auxiliary system untouched and apply two types of filtering only at the first terminal event. If the two endpoint effects have the same ratio for every input, every segment of continuation evolution applies the same linear map to them, preserving the ratio segment by segment. Summing histories that have already been distinguished also preserves it. Retries therefore change the total delivery probability and waiting time, while the two conditional mixture shares after delivery remain unchanged, as does the matching denominator of the output state. Supplementary Proof S8 gives the complete proof and the realization used in Chapter 7.

This reveals another structural stability of effective coupling: repeated processes may change when delivery occurs and how much is delivered while preserving how the delivered directions are mixed. The denominator recurrence and this fixed-ratio mechanism are each used according to the actual process; they connect the composition laws of the complete output back to calculable matching shares.

3.5 Emergent Resonance Forces

An emergent state describes a collective excitation through a pattern involving the entire space. In resonance, exchange may occur between two collective excitations or connect a collective pattern with an elementary direction. Calculating this interaction requires identifying the actual ports through which the collective pattern participates, the distinguishable outcomes left by exchange, and their total response relative to the same background reference.

3.5.1 Ports of the Collective Pattern

First consider the collective pattern itself. In 2.1, b is invariant under every multiplicative pullback and has full spectral response ζ(s)b, while an elementary direction has response L(s,χ)ψχ. Thus, at a spectral point where ζ＊=ζ(s＊) is finite and nonzero and the corresponding L-values are well defined, their spectral factors relative to the collective reference are respectively 1 and Rχ=L(s＊,χ)/ζ＊. These factors describe responses to a specified spectral action. Actual exchange also contains port overlaps, exchange angles, propagation phases, and environment shares, which must be calculated with the process.

The absence of a nontrivial unit-group character in the collective pattern does not remove these exchange factors. For example, using the zero-element vertex of 2.4.1, take a normalized nontrivial unit-shell direction ψχ and let eK be the normalized zero-element state. Then

V0,χ=|eK⟩⟨ψχ‾|−χ(−1)|ψχ⟩⟨eK|,V0,χb=−χ(−1)p−K/2ψχ,|⟨ψχ|V0,χ|b⟩|2=p−K. \begin{gathered}V_{0,\chi}=|e_K\rangle\langle \psi_{\bar\chi}|-\chi(-1)|\psi_\chi\rangle\langle e_K|,\\[3pt]V_{0,\chi}b=-\chi(-1)p^{-K/2}\psi_\chi,\\[3pt]|\langle \psi_\chi|V_{0,\chi}|b\rangle|^2=p^{-K}.\end{gathered} (3.50)

The first term vanishes because ψχ̄ is orthogonal to b, while the second extracts the zero-element component of b. This calculates a vertex matrix element; the complete joint exchange must still satisfy energy and charge balance and include the actual interaction duration. If this vertex enters the selected channel, its p⁻ᴷ share must remain in that channel’s weight. Moreover, b contains coherent components of different shell energies, so resonance conditions in the actual cycle are still determined by phase and exchange as in 3.1; the trivial character alone does not establish zero-frequency resonance.

3.5.2 Affine Channels

The collective pattern may participate in exchange through different ports, requiring a set of operation labels to organize these paths. Addition and unit multiplication supply such candidates: at the species layer, composing translations x↦x+b with scalings x↦ax gives the affine group. Whether different operations produce distinguishable exchange outputs also depends on the actual input and environment. To distinguish it from the unit group G used above, denote this group by Gaff:

Gaff=Aff⁡(𝔽p)={(a,b):a∈𝔽p×,b∈𝔽p},(a,b)(a′,b′)=(aa′,b+ab′),|Gaff|=p(p−1). \begin{gathered}G_{\mathrm{aff}}=\operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb F_p)=\{(a,b):a\in\mathbb F_p^\times,\ b\in\mathbb F_p\},\\[3pt](a,b)(a',b')=(aa',\,b+ab'),\\[3pt]|G_{\mathrm{aff}}|=p(p-1).\end{gathered} (3.51)

Here b as the second coordinate of a group element denotes a translation amount; the pattern b written on its own still denotes the constant function on the full space. For K≥2, affine operations admit a nonredundant identification with unit addresses at depth two. Let U₂=(ℤ/p²ℤ)× and let [a] be the multiplicatively compatible Teichmüller representative. Specify the following action on U₂:

Fa,b(x)=[a]x+pb(mod⁡p2),Fa,b∘Fa′,b′=Faa′,b+ab′. \begin{gathered}F_{a,b}(x)=[a]x+pb\pmod{p^2},\\[3pt]F_{a,b}\circ F_{a',b'}=F_{aa',\,b+ab'}.\end{gathered} (3.52)

If Fₐ,ᵦ fixes a unit address, reduction modulo p first gives a=1, and reduction modulo p² then gives b=0. Thus no nonidentity operation fixes that address; since both the operation count and address count are p(p−1), the action is free and transitive. Choosing reference address x₀=1 associates each operation with a unique Fₐ,ᵦ(x₀), and every other address occurs exactly once. This is an affine action on the set U₂; the multiplicative group of U₂ itself is abelian, and the two group structures are used separately. If the original state space has depth K greater than two, using these labels additionally requires specifying reduction to U₂ and the preparation of deeper addresses; all positions of the entire unit shell cannot be counted as this label set.

The same set of operations can produce very different results on different inputs. These address permutations all preserve the uniform vector on U₂, so every operation sends the same uniform input to the same vector. Conversely, applying these permutations to a chosen point state produces mutually orthogonal address states.
