The first case shows that operation count does not equal output count; the second provides a preparation realizing all address distinctions. The actual channels of an emergent state must be determined from its own joint exchange.

3.5.3 Combination of Complete Outputs

Suppose the same normalized matched input v produces complete output FgF_{g} along candidate path g, where FgF_{g} already includes both system and environment and is individually normalized, and the path amplitude is cgc_{g}. For the selected exchange outcome, the intensity of the complete response is

∥∑gcgFg∥2=∑g,hcg¯ch⟨Fg|Fh⟩. \left\|\sum_g c_gF_g\right\|^2=\sum_{g,h}\overline{c_g}c_h\langle F_g|F_h\rangle. (3.53)

The Gram matrix of the complete outputs determines the total response of this exchange; subsequent return also depends on the output states. Retaining a separate record for each path and retaining only a common record for a group of paths can give the same outcome effect while preserving different coherence within the group. Supplementary Proof S4.4 shows how this difference changes the input occupation at the same return vertex.

In the additive case, fix an exchange class, a matched input v, and mutually orthogonal actual complete outputs FgF_{g}. Suppose every channel has the same spectral factor r, with the remaining input, propagation, and exchange factors included in cgc_{g}. The channel response normalized by the collective spectral reference is Bg,r=rcg|Fg⟩⟨v|B_{g,r}=r c_{g}\vert F_{g}\rangle \langle v\vert. The response operator of each output satisfies Bg,r†Bg,r=|r|2|cg|2|v⟩⟨v|B_{g,r}^{\dagger}B_{g,r}=\vert r\vert ^{2}\vert c_{g}\vert ^{2}\vert v\rangle \langle v\vert; taking the trace against input preparation ρ and summing all actual orthogonal outputs gives

Bg,r=rcg|Fg⟩⟨v|,Waff:=∑g|cg|2,hv(ρ):=⟨v|ρ|v⟩,αr(ρ):=∑gTr⁡(Bg,rρBg,r†)=|r|2Waffhv(ρ). \begin{gathered}B_{g,r}=r c_g|F_g\rangle\langle v|,\\[3pt]W_{\mathrm{aff}}:=\sum_g|c_g|^2,\\[3pt]h_v(\rho):=\langle v|\rho|v\rangle,\\[3pt]\alpha_r(\rho):=\sum_g\operatorname{Tr}(B_{g,r}\rho B_{g,r}^\dagger)=|r|^2W_{\mathrm{aff}}h_v(\rho).\end{gathered} (3.54)

Waff is the total channel weight of this process. For matched input ρ=|v⟩⟨v|, hv=1h_{v}=1. Only if all p(p−1) labels are actually realized and every channel has |cg|2=1\vert c_{g}\vert ^{2}=1 in the same response units does Waff=p(p−1). If g is merely a preparation label randomly chosen with probability aga_{g}, then cgc_{g} already contains ag\sqrt{a_{g}}; when every other per-channel response is one and ∑gag=1\sum _{g} a_{g}=1, the total weight is one. Adding alternative labels to a normalized preparation does not automatically increase total response.

For an interaction between emergent states, take r=1 above if the unnormalized spectral response of each channel is ζ*cgζ_{*}c_{g}. For an interaction between an emergent state and elementary direction χ, take r=Rχ if the per-channel response is L(s*,χ)cgL(s_{*},χ)c_{g}. Only when these two processes have the same total channel weight and are each compared at their matched input are their couplings respectively

αemg=Waff,αmix(χ)=Waff|Rχ|2. \begin{gathered}\alpha_{\mathrm{emg}}=W_{\mathrm{aff}},\\[3pt]\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}(\chi)=W_{\mathrm{aff}}|R_\chi|^2.\end{gathered} (3.55)

These formulas make explicit the roles of the common weight and the spectral factor. Having collective states at both endpoints does not alone fix the spectral factor of an exchange vertex: if the actual exchange passes through elementary direction χ, its response must still be retained. If a mixed process adds a zero-element input, directional filtering, or a different environment preparation, these factors must enter its own cgc_{g} before Waff is calculated. For example, entry from b into fχ through a zero-element vertex carries amplitude p⁻ᴷᐟ²; a comparison conditional on the selected zero-element component must separately state the probability of that condition.

To use the response for a one-round event, normalize with a common coefficient κ\kappa as in 3.3.3 and complete the output with the no-exchange outcome. Let Pv=|v⟩⟨v|P_v=|v\rangle\langle v|. The total-effect condition in this section is κ2|r|2WaffPv≤I\kappa^2|r|^2W_{\mathrm{aff}}P_v\le I, and the event share is pr(ρ)=κ2αr(ρ)p_r(\rho)=\kappa^2\alpha_r(\rho). If the two exchange classes are alternative outcomes in the same round, their effects must be added before checking this bound. Evaluating the share at the actual stationary input and dividing by the complete cycle period gives the event count rate.

3.5.4 Node Weights

The channel sum reduces total response to the individual path coefficients cgc_g. When layer labels are used to assign node weights, one must first count how often each node occurs in the specified layer product and then connect that product to actual channel weights. Representations of the affine group in characteristic pp organize these multiplicities; their layer chain counts labels, while actual quantum propagation is still determined by joint operators on the complex state space. In characteristic pp, the group order contains the factor pp, so a representation need not split into a direct sum of simple modules. Let A=𝔽p[Gaff]A=\mathbb F_p[G_{\mathrm{aff}}], let U=𝔽p×U=\mathbb F_p^\times be the scaling subgroup, and induce from its trivial module to obtain P0P_0. Denoting unit translation by tt, we may write

P0=A⊗𝔽p[U]𝟏≃𝔽p[t]/((t−1)p),z=t−1,rad⁡kP0=zkP0,dim⁡𝔽pzkP0=p−k(0≤k≤p). \begin{gathered}P_0=A\otimes_{\mathbb F_p[U]}\mathbf1\simeq\mathbb F_p[t]/((t-1)^p),\\[3pt]z=t-1,\\[3pt]\operatorname{rad}^kP_0=z^kP_0,\\[3pt]\dim_{\mathbb F_p}z^kP_0=p-k\quad(0\le k\le p).\end{gathered} (3.56)

The element t satisfies tᵖ=1, and in characteristic p, tᵖ−1=(t−1)ᵖ. Every submodule must first be translation-invariant and hence an ideal of this truncated polynomial ring; these ideals are precisely (zᵏ), and all are scaling-invariant. They form the unique successive inclusion chain, with one-dimensional successive quotients. This is the Loewy-layer structure used here. 14 Since the order p−1 of U is invertible in 𝔽p, its trivial module is projective; induction preserves projectivity, and P₀ has the trivial module as its unique simple top, so it is the projective cover of the trivial module.

Scaling by a sends t to tᵃ, with tᵃ−1≡a(t−1) mod (t−1)². It therefore acts on the kth successive quotient by multiplication by aᵏ:

zkP0/zk+1P0≃χnatk,χnat(a)=a,k=0,…,p−1. \begin{gathered}z^kP_0/z^{k+1}P_0\simeq\chi_{\mathrm{nat}}^k,\\[3pt]\chi_{\mathrm{nat}}(a)=a,\\[3pt]k=0,\ldots,p-1.\end{gathered} (3.57)

Thus every nontrivial character occurs exactly once in the intermediate layers, while the trivial character occurs at both ends. This chain has p layers and P₀ has dimension p; the earlier p(p−1) counts all affine operations, a different quantity. To associate these layer labels with complex spectral directions, first choose a label convention from 𝔽p× to complex roots of unity, consistent with the orientation of the pullback action used above. This associates character labels; it does not turn the nonsplit chain over 𝔽p into a quantum propagation chain in the complex state space. A complex representation decomposes using an invariant inner product, and actual transitions between layers must still be supplied by joint operators.

The layer structure determines the multiplicities of a given node prescription rigorously. Retain the decomposition p−1=∏inip-1=\prod _{i} n_{i} of 2.2, where the nin_{i} are pairwise coprime prime powers and characters are labeled by coordinates ℓi(χ)∈ℤ/niℤℓ_{i}(χ)∈ℤ/n_{i}ℤ. Now explicitly specify an evaluation prescription: assign a positive factor tit_{i} when coordinate i is zero and one otherwise; take the product of these factors for each nontrivial layer, then multiply over all nontrivial layers. Denoting the total factor by ℒp gives

𝒯χ=∏i:ℓi(χ)=0ti,ℒp:=∏χ≠1𝒯χ=∏iti(p−1)/ni−1. \begin{gathered}\mathcal T_\chi=\prod_{i:\ell_i(\chi)=0}t_i,\\[3pt]\mathcal L_p:=\prod_{\chi\ne1}\mathcal T_\chi=\prod_i t_i^{(p-1)/n_i-1}.\end{gathered} (3.58)

The proof is a count: fixing coordinate i to zero leaves (p−1)/ni(p-1)/n_{i} choices for the other coordinates; after removing the fully trivial label, the remaining (p−1)/ni−1(p-1)/n_{i}-1 nontrivial layers each contribute one factor tit_{i}. Multiplying the contributions of all factors gives the formula. Conjugating all labels negates every coordinate and leaves the zero-coordinate counts unchanged.

This theorem determines multiplicities; the physical values of the node factors must be established as in Supplementary Proof S4.2 and Supplementary Proof S5.1. The factor ni−1/2n_{i}^{-1/2} is the single-point amplitude of a uniform vector; its square is the corresponding probability. The total share of nin_{i} orthogonal, equally weighted outcomes is instead obtained by addition. Connecting these quantities to the same layer weight tit_{i} requires specifying the input, endpoint, spectral reference, and whether the final quantity is an amplitude or a share. If consecutive layers represent successive recorded exchanges, their joint probability must be obtained by sequentially composing conditional instruments; only when the actual composition yields scalar factors may it be replaced by the product of those factors.

Using this layer product as the denominator of emergent channel weight corresponds to the assignment

Waff=p(p−1)ℒp⇒αemg=p(p−1)ℒp,αmix(χ)=p(p−1)ℒp|Rχ|2. \begin{gathered}W_{\mathrm{aff}}=\frac{p(p-1)}{\mathcal L_p}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \alpha_{\mathrm{emg}}=\frac{p(p-1)}{\mathcal L_p},\\[3pt]\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}(\chi)=\frac{p(p-1)}{\mathcal L_p}|R_\chi|^2.\end{gathered} (3.59)

For example, this total weight is realized if all affine channels are orthogonal, have equal responses, and actually each take |cg|2=1/ℒp\vert c_{g}\vert ^{2}=1/ℒ_{p}. But the Loewy chain alone does not prove that actual exchange uses these cgc_{g}. Choosing P₀ as the emergent evaluation object, prescribing multiplication of node weights along its layers, and placing the resulting product in the channel denominator are all conditions retained in this evaluation correspondence. The integer number of group elements remains p(p−1); it is the response weight that changes. General positive factors tit_{i} do not guarantee ℒp>1, so the correction may enhance or suppress response and cannot universally be interpreted as removal of channels.

Comparisons of responses at different spectral parameters s must retain these preparation and weight conditions. Only with matched inputs, fixed cgc_{g}, and its fixed evaluation correspondence can all variation of the mixed response be assigned to Rχ(s), while the purely emergent response remains the same Waff. The spectral parameter s, inverse environment temperature β, and actual time are distinct variables. Interpreting parameter variation as time evolution further requires a relation between that parameter and time, together with calculation of changes in preparation and exchange. Finite thermal preparations always use finite partition sums; the pole of the infinite ζ partition sum at β=1 does not directly imply divergence of a one-event probability.

The physical process of a resonance force consists of actual exchange between two carriers: an excitation passes through compatible endpoints and a common environment, allowing a change in one carrier to enter the state evolution of the other. In the constructed protection and retrieval process, the sources and auxiliaries retain their original preparations and the mediator returns, while the two targets may still undergo transfer and become entangled. Exchange strength is calculated along the same process: matching shares at elementary vertices give Eq. (3.33); repeated round trips modify the response according to coherence and record relations of the complete output; and collective exchange sums to Eq. (3.54) when outputs are orthogonal. Actual instruments realize these responses as event shares, while momentum changes with the same input, reference, and elapsed duration give the corresponding mechanical readings.

Chapter 4. Metric Forces

Matter changes the local state of the background; this change propagates through the background and alters the maintenance of other stable states. The resulting rate of momentum change is called a metric force.

Persistent exchange by a stable state both changes background occupation and is modulated by background availability. Source writing and the maintenance response are therefore parts of one process: background propagation carries local occupation changes to other positions, where they alter the complete maintenance generator. Metric action connects stable states through this shared background, and its universal part comes from this common modulation. This chapter calculates the response for a fixed source at rest and a passively moving carrier. The source, background resource units, and test carrier share actual positions, with time and distance calibrated by the same process.

4.1 Matter Sources

A matter source must be produced by the stable state’s own action. Connecting the persistent generator of the complete carrier to the local background makes paths, nodes, and formation shares determine the writing through the same operator; source strength is thereby connected to maintenance phase. We first describe a source process that retains fresh outputs by refreshing pointers, then connect the common matching of Chapter 2 into a reversible occupation round trip. Both obtain the source from the actual joint action, with definite forms for the background and return histories left behind.

Denote the isometric embedding of the protected carrier by JfJ_f, with complete action satisfying ĤfJf=Jf𝖧f\widehat H_fJ_f=J_f\mathsf H_f, where both generators are measured in frequency units. During a readout window with displacement paused, prepare a fresh pointer in |0⟩B|0\rangle_B, implement Uread=exp⁡(−itreadĤf⊗σyB)U_{\mathrm{read}}=\exp(-it_{\mathrm{read}}\widehat H_f\otimes\sigma_y^B) for effective readout duration treadt_{\mathrm{read}}, then read the pointer in the σxB\sigma_x^B basis. Adding and subtracting the amplitudes of its two components gives the operators within the code:

k±=cos⁡(tread𝖧f)±sin⁡(tread𝖧f)2,E±=k±†k±=I±sin⁡(2tread𝖧f)2,E++E−=I. \begin{gathered} k_\pm=\frac{\cos(t_{\mathrm{read}}\mathsf H_f)\pm\sin(t_{\mathrm{read}}\mathsf H_f)}{\sqrt2},\\ E_\pm=k_\pm^\dagger k_\pm =\frac{I\pm\sin(2t_{\mathrm{read}}\mathsf H_f)}2, \qquad E_++E_-=I. \end{gathered} (4.1)

Completeness shows that every outcome is included. The readout preserves rest-frame eigenbranches and their degenerate subspaces; after tracing out the pointer, coherence between distinct eigenvalues generally decays. The field source below is a fixed rest-frame eigenbranch and is not replaced by an arbitrary unknown superposition.

A fixed positive source can be produced by an already formed carrier. Using the common return column of 2.5.3 and Supplementary Proof S6, with input z0z_0, normalized bright output ee, and target orientations Q=Q†Q=Q^\dagger and Q2=IQ^2=I, the complete rest-frame vertex is FW=μWσx⊗QF_W=\mu_W\sigma_x\otimes Q, where μW=(gcol/Λ)Wlog⁡W>0\mu_W=(g_{\mathrm{col}}/\Lambda)\sqrt W\log W>0 is the half-gap during loading. Pause displacement and isolate resource gating; after a quarter pulse, apply phase ii at the output to obtain

U+=Die−iπFW/(4μW),𝒥+ψ=U+(z0⊗ψ)=z0⊗ψ+e⊗Qψ2,𝒥+†𝒥+=I,FW𝒥+=μW𝒥+. \boxed{\begin{gathered} U_+=D_i e^{-i\pi F_W/(4\mu_W)},\qquad \mathcal J_+\psi=U_+(z_0\otimes\psi) =\frac{z_0\otimes\psi+e\otimes Q\psi}{\sqrt2},\\ \mathcal J_+^\dagger\mathcal J_+=I,\qquad F_W\mathcal J_+=\mu_W\mathcal J_+. \end{gathered}} (4.2)

Target information is retained in correlations between port and orientation, and the isometry also preserves arbitrary entanglement with subsystems not participating in this action. The definite preparation already formed in Chapter 2 has an actual inverse procedure; in the same ready layout, first invert back to the preparation input and then execute U+U_+, so every accepted history still yields the same 𝒥+\mathcal J_+. The total acceptance probability remains the original QMQ_M, without an additional positive-branch share. Different layouts require an actual input conversion and inclusion of its duration; the complete proof of delivery is given in Supplementary Proof S9.1.

Source writing is a function of the complete generator, so the operator associated with each outcome is a scalar multiple of the identity on this positive-source code subspace and preserves target logic. The same-vertex procedure below also includes the common maintenance phase without changing these outcome probabilities. The object prepared here is a source at rest; displacement generally couples positive and negative carriers, so rest-frame preservation does not directly establish preservation of the same code in motion. The loading half-gap and the mass read over the complete operating cycle are also read separately.

Place an identical local two-state background resource unit at each actual propagation position, with Ni=|1⟩⟨1|N_i=|1\rangle\langle1| projecting onto its unavailable state. With input-independent probability εi\varepsilon_i, perform the entire readout segment, load outcomes +,−+,- into endpoints 1 and 0 of a fresh resource unit, respectively, and swap it into the background position. If the segment is not performed, retain the old resource unit; old outputs and outcome records remain within the joint process. For eigenvalue λi\lambda_i of source generator 𝖧f\mathsf H_f, let

ξi=⟨Ni⟩−12,bi=12sin⁡(2treadλi),Δξi=−εiξi+εibi. \xi_i=\langle N_i\rangle-\frac12,\qquad b_i=\frac12\sin(2t_{\mathrm{read}}\lambda_i),\qquad \boxed{\Delta\xi_i=-\varepsilon_i\xi_i+\varepsilon_i b_i.} (4.3)

The executed branch replaces resource unit occupation with the reading E+E_+, while the bypass retains the old occupation, so this update includes both writing and replenishment. The half-occupied reference is realized by unbiased supply with equal probabilities for the two states and boundary preparation; it is not a constant subtracted afterward from an arbitrary background. A weak source gives bi=treadλi+O((treadλi)3)b_i=t_{\mathrm{read}}\lambda_i+O((t_{\mathrm{read}}\lambda_i)^3) without removing the replenishment term.

The local source thus has a definite physical meaning: the stable state’s action changes the unavailable share of background resource units, while replenishment in the same update limits its accumulation. When 0<treadλi≪10<t_{\mathrm{read}}\lambda_i\ll1, source writing increases the unavailable share and reduces the available share relative to the unbiased reference; background exchange then conveys this local change to other positions.

The matter source can also be realized directly by the same complete matching of 2.5.3. Write occupation using an already formed carrier: the matter action is still given by Hs=gME/4H_s=g_ME/4, and the written occupation share is also determined by E, rather than by a separately specified source coefficient. After entry into the common positive bright carrier, the mean resource occupation is ne=Ne/2n_e=Ne/2, and the available bright-channel amplitude rer_e relative to zero blockage r0=sr_0=\sqrt s satisfies

re2r02=1−e=1−2neN. \boxed{\frac{r_e^2}{r_0^2}=1-e=1-\frac{2n_e}{N}.} (4.4)

Formation preparation can connect directly to this occupation without a separately specified post-formation input. Denote the actual formation acceptance column by K5K_5 and its pre-formation acceptance effect by DF=K5†K5D_F=K_5^\dagger K_5. In the connection where the same formation column supplies subsequent matching, the post-formation effect is ERO=K5K5†E_{\mathrm{RO}}=K_5K_5^\dagger and the complete matching is E=q0EROE=q_0E_{\mathrm{RO}}. Hence K5†EROK5=DF2K_5^\dagger E_{\mathrm{RO}}K_5=D_F^2: matching once more after formation makes the occupation effect on the pre-formation input contain DF2D_F^2. Available, occupied, old-failure, and unformed outputs together complete the identity, showing that this occupation indeed comes from the same formation–exchange process.

The original formation reflection preserves the matter action over the entire pattern; its available component carries the same matter phase into background exchange, and the positive bright-channel amplitude is determined by the norm of this actual available column. Once the positive bright carrier is actually loaded, equal halves at the two outer ports also give the resource-occupation relation in Eq. (4.4). The pre- and post-formation domains, complete normalization, and common intertwining are given in Supplementary Proof S7.1.

The same matching determines both source phase and occupation share, connecting persistent matter matching to a change in background availability. We first calculate field establishment and motion using continual refreshing with fresh pointers; the realization in which the same resource packet returns along its original path is developed in 4.5.7, where complete histories determine both resource occupation at the end of a round and accumulation along the path.

4.2 Background Propagation

Exchange between background resource units conveys the local bias already produced. Propagation paths are determined by resource unit pairs that can actually exchange, while time and distance are calibrated by the corresponding process readings.

Observational geometry and reading structure follow the observation construction in Dynamics of the Bost–Connes State Space 2: the complex matrix algebra of nonzero observation units and its positivity give observational spacetime of signature (1,3)(1,3), while cycle duration and logarithmic coordinates of integer representatives provide time and position readings, respectively. The original proofs are in §§5.1–5.2, §5.4, and §§2.6 and 5.5 of that paper. Specific propagation further requires common positions, adjacency, and lengths for resource units and the test carrier. Here we fix actual position projections PiP_i, neighboring displacements, and supply boundaries, with pointwise correspondence between the two. Using the position ring already realized in Chapter 2, calibrate adjacent length as ℓx\ell_x; periodic wraparound is also an actual edge. The background is transported along this adjacency, with distant exchange against unbiased resource units through supply branches.

After source updating in each round, choose a complete swap of neighboring identical resource units or an idle step with specified probabilities. Let RR be the first-moment transport matrix. Writing Dε=diag⁡(εi)D_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon_i), the round recurrence, with refreshing followed by transport, and its stationary solution are

ξ′=R(I−Dε)ξ+RDεb,ξ*=[I−R(I−Dε)]−1RDεb. \boxed{\begin{aligned} \xi'&=R(I-D_\varepsilon)\xi+RD_\varepsilon b,\\ \xi_*&=[I-R(I-D_\varepsilon)]^{-1}RD_\varepsilon b. \end{aligned}} (4.5)

This is a finite mixing process: each connected component can reach an unbiased supply endpoint, and an idle step has positive probability. The resulting contraction makes the inverse exist, and the initial bias converges to the unique solution over successive rounds. The full configuration may still have correlations; closure of first moments follows from the chosen swaps and repreparations and does not require the biased stationary state to be a product.

When every internal edge and supply branch has common selection probability cc, R=I−cLR=I-cL, where LL is the graph Laplacian including the supply boundary. Let ξ+=(I−Dε)ξ+Dεb\xi^+=(I-D_\varepsilon)\xi+D_\varepsilon b denote the stationary bias after refreshing and before transport. Then

cLξ+=Dε(b−ξ),ξ=Rξ+. \boxed{cL\xi^+=D_\varepsilon(b-\xi),\qquad \xi=R\xi^+.} (4.6)

The first relation follows directly from ξ+−ξ=Dε(b−ξ)\xi^+-\xi=D_\varepsilon(b-\xi). Interior regions without matter refreshing satisfy Lξ+=0L\xi^+=0; the post-transport ξ\xi is also harmonic away from refreshing sites and their neighbors. With only conservative transport outside the source, there is no additional bulk decay term; refreshing throughout the bulk changes the equation and field profile.

Actual adjacency determines where this change propagates, while boundary supply and source replenishment determine its stationary distribution. The three spatial axes specify observational geometry, and the position ring retains its actual circular adjacency. Spectral addresses nn and their logarithmic distances are used separately from propagation positions ii; using the former for this process additionally requires specifying a correspondence between them.

The position kernel and coherent memory of the original joint thermal cycle are given in Supplementary Proofs S9.2–S9.3; this section uses the explicitly specified resource-unit swaps and supply boundaries above.

The resulting ξ*,i\xi_{*,i} describes background occupation bias relative to the unbiased reference at every position in the presence of the source. The action felt by the test carrier must still be determined from the actual role of these resource units in its maintenance process.

4.3 Maintenance Response

Local background changes enter matter through the original maintenance action. Chapter 2 has already placed matter phase and background gradient in the same carrier; when local resources constrain this common exchange, both responses acquire the same availability factor. Spatial differences caused by the source thus change the local rhythm of stable states relative to the shared background, and position gradients become impulses through actual motion. We first formulate a complete cycle using single-resource-unit gating, then explain how collective configurations produce finite common modulation. The source remains a fixed rest-frame eigenbranch, and the test carrier writes no additional source record during this round.

Let 𝒏=(ni)\mathbf n=(n_i) denote the resource configuration in a round. Single-resource-unit availability response is hi(𝒏)=1−nih_i(\mathbf n)=1-n_i. If πb\pi_b is the stationary configuration distribution produced by all source updates and transport, then

h‾i=∑𝒏πb(𝒏)hi(𝒏)=12−ξ*,i,h0=12. \bar h_i=\sum_{\mathbf n}\pi_b(\mathbf n)h_i(\mathbf n) =\frac12-\xi_{*,i},\qquad h_0=\frac12. (4.7)

This holds exactly for any admissible finite bias. Multiple-resource-unit response is generally a square-root function whose mean must be calculated from the full configuration distribution, not replaced by the square root of mean occupation. We fix a single resource unit here to retain a complete calculation of the same process.

This available share enters maintenance through an actual response port. Use mutually orthogonal normalized input |zi⟩|z_i\rangle and output direction |ai⟩|a_i\rangle of the background port, and let rv>0r_v>0 be the spectral-response coefficient fixed at full availability. An unavailable single resource unit switches off this response. For a fixed configuration, the port action and preparation are

Xi(𝒏)=rv(1−ni)(|ai⟩⟨zi|+|zi⟩⟨ai|),|χi(𝒏)⟩={(|zi⟩+|ai⟩)/2,ni=0,|zi⟩,ni=1,Xi(𝒏)|χi(𝒏)⟩=rvhi(𝒏)|χi(𝒏)⟩. \begin{gathered} X_i(\mathbf n)=r_v(1-n_i) (|a_i\rangle\langle z_i|+|z_i\rangle\langle a_i|),\\ |\chi_i(\mathbf n)\rangle= \begin{cases} (|z_i\rangle+|a_i\rangle)/\sqrt2,&n_i=0,\\ |z_i\rangle,&n_i=1, \end{cases} \qquad X_i(\mathbf n)|\chi_i(\mathbf n)\rangle =r_vh_i(\mathbf n)|\chi_i(\mathbf n)\rangle. \end{gathered} (4.8)

The final equality follows directly from exchange between the two endpoints. When unavailable, the port uses a zero-response input without normalizing a zero vector. This realizes control of an actual interaction edge by the same resource unit, making hih_i an interaction coefficient.

On the matter side, reuse the two-arm protection of Chapter 2, denoting its dimensionless action by 𝖥̂t\widehat{\mathsf F}_t with 𝖥̂tJt=Jt𝖥t\widehat{\mathsf F}_tJ_t=J_t\mathsf F_t. Multiply both arms by the local XiX_i and prepare working array |Ξ𝒏⟩=⨂i|χi(𝒏)⟩|\Xi_{\mathbf n}\rangle=\bigotimes_i|\chi_i(\mathbf n)\rangle at all positions. Take joint embedding 𝒥𝒏(ψ⊗|i⟩)=(Jtψ⊗|i⟩)⊗|Ξ𝒏⟩\mathcal J_{\mathbf n}(\psi\otimes|i\rangle)=(J_t\psi\otimes|i\rangle)\otimes|\Xi_{\mathbf n}\rangle. This array depends on resource configuration, independently of the position occupied by the test carrier.

Let gTg_T be the bare maintenance strength and ν\nu the displacement strength. Acting as the identity on other working factors, the actual maintenance action and compression relations for the two terms are

ĤH(𝒏)=gT∑i(𝖥̂t⊗Pi)⊗Xi(𝒏),ĤH(𝒏)𝒥𝒏=𝒥𝒏(gTrv𝖥t⊗h(𝒏)),h(𝒏)=∑ihi(𝒏)Pi,Ĥx𝒥𝒏=𝒥𝒏(νZ⊗Dx),Dx=S†−S2i. \begin{gathered} \widehat H_H(\mathbf n) =g_T\sum_i(\widehat{\mathsf F}_t\otimes P_i)\otimes X_i(\mathbf n),\\ \widehat H_H(\mathbf n)\mathcal J_{\mathbf n} =\mathcal J_{\mathbf n}(g_Tr_v\mathsf F_t\otimes h(\mathbf n)),\qquad h(\mathbf n)=\sum_i h_i(\mathbf n)P_i,\\ \widehat H_x\mathcal J_{\mathbf n} =\mathcal J_{\mathbf n}(\nu Z\otimes D_x),\qquad D_x=\frac{S^\dagger-S}{2i}. \end{gathered} (4.9)

For input ψ⊗|i⟩\psi\otimes|i\rangle, PiP_i in the first term selects the local response; Eq. (4.8) and matter-side intertwining then give coefficient gTrvhig_Tr_vh_i. The original displacement SS changes only position and acts as the identity on the working array, so it still preserves the same 𝒥𝒏\mathcal J_{\mathbf n}. This explains the preparation of an all-position array: if only a position-dependent working state were attached, the original bare displacement would generally fail to preserve that carrier.

Both terms can therefore act simultaneously on the same object. Let the test action have the pair of eigenvalues ±ft\pm f_t, with the original motion orientation satisfying Z2=IZ^2=I and {Z,𝖥t}=0\{Z,\mathsf F_t\}=0. Denote the accumulated coefficients during the active window by aH=∫gT(t)rvdta_H=\int g_T(t)r_v\,dt and ax=∫ν(t)dta_x=\int\nu(t)\,dt. If the two terms are constant or share an envelope, the activity and accumulated generator are

U𝒏=e−iK𝒏,K𝒏=aH𝖥t⊗h(𝒏)+axZ⊗Dx. \boxed{U_{\mathbf n}=e^{-iK_{\mathbf n}},\qquad K_{\mathbf n}=a_H\mathsf F_t\otimes h(\mathbf n) +a_xZ\otimes D_x.} (4.10)

Different temporal schedules require the actual time-ordered propagator. In each round, freeze the configuration after resource updating, prepare the array, run this action, then reverse the working preparation. Preparation and its inverse do not change logical position; the common period τ\tau includes all array preparation, source readout, transport, and waiting.

Let P(𝒏′|𝒏;b)P(\mathbf n'|\mathbf n;b) be the transition probability of the full resource configuration. At the cycle stage where the joint state is block diagonal in the resource-configuration basis, one round acts on any classically correlated resource–carrier blocks ρ𝒏\rho_{\mathbf n} as

ρ̃𝒏′=∑𝒏P(𝒏′|𝒏;b)ρ𝒏,ρ𝒏′′=U𝒏′ρ̃𝒏′U𝒏′†. \boxed{\begin{aligned} \widetilde\rho_{\mathbf n'} &=\sum_{\mathbf n}P(\mathbf n'|\mathbf n;b)\rho_{\mathbf n},\\ \rho'_{\mathbf n'}&=U_{\mathbf n'}\widetilde\rho_{\mathbf n'}U_{\mathbf n'}^\dagger. \end{aligned}} (4.11)

Its Kraus operators are P(𝒏′|𝒏;b)|𝒏′⟩⟨𝒏|⊗U𝒏′\sqrt{P(\mathbf n'|\mathbf n;b)}|\mathbf n'\rangle\langle\mathbf n|\otimes U_{\mathbf n'}. Each probability column sums to 1, so the process preserves trace and retains all resource outcomes; it does not require decorrelating the carrier from the background anew in every round.

Equation (4.11) places source updating and background transport from the preceding sections in the same round as maintenance and motion. Each resource outcome corresponds to an actual action U𝒏U_{\mathbf n}; correlations generated between background and carrier enter the next round, allowing changes in carrier motion to be calculated directly.

Multiple-resource-unit configurations can modulate frequency through the same port structure. Suppose NCN_C configurations are coherently produced with equal weights from one input, and occupation projection OO blocks only the configuration matching the incoming resource packet label. The Gram operator of the complete available column is βC2(I−O/NC)\beta_C^2(I-O/N_C), where βC=WC/ΛC\beta_C=\sqrt{W_C}/\Lambda_C. Its positive square root is the bright-channel coupling operator, giving βC(I−δCO)\beta_C(I-\delta_CO) and δC=1−1−1/NC\delta_C=1-\sqrt{1-1/N_C}. Matching first changes the norm of the output column and thereby the persistent frequency.

When the original matter and background gradient share this bright carrier and motion transports the entire loaded working system, this bright-channel coupling operator modulates the complete generator in common. Forward and inverse loading return the auxiliaries while retaining the holding phase, as proved in Supplementary Proof S6.5. The coupling operator and loading duration both enter the background calibration of this realization.

4.4 Motion and Force

4.4.1 Momentum Change

Within the active window of each fixed configuration, first consider how the carrier moves between positions. Let u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1] be normalized elapsed time in the window, and denote the position blocks of the carrier by ρij(u)\rho_{ij}(u) and pi=Tr⁡ρiip_i=\operatorname{Tr}\rho_{ii}. From ∂uρ=−i[K𝒏,ρ]\partial_u\rho=-i[K_{\mathbf n},\rho],

Ji(u)=axRe⁡Tr⁡(Zρi,i+1(u)),∂upi=Ji−1−Ji. J_i(u)=a_x\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(Z\rho_{i,i+1}(u)),\qquad \partial_up_i=J_{i-1}-J_i. (4.12)

The local maintenance term cancels in the position trace, while neighboring displacement gives incoming and outgoing probability currents, conserving total probability around the ring. Background action changes coherence between orientation and position, thereby changing subsequent probability flow; background-occupation differences alone do not determine the carrier’s actual motion.

Take the finite-difference momentum operator Πx=I⊗Dx/ℓx\Pi_x=I\otimes D_x/\ell_x on the same position ring. Resource updating does not change test-carrier momentum, and the displacement term also commutes with Πx\Pi_x. Integrating the Heisenberg equation for each configuration gives the exact finite-round relation

Δ⟨Πx⟩=∑𝒏Tr⁡(ρ̃𝒏ℐ𝒏),ℐ𝒏=∫01eiuK𝒏iaH[𝖥t⊗h(𝒏),Πx]e−iuK𝒏du. \boxed{\begin{aligned} \Delta\langle\Pi_x\rangle &=\sum_{\mathbf n}\operatorname{Tr}(\widetilde\rho_{\mathbf n}\,\mathcal I_{\mathbf n}),\\ \mathcal I_{\mathbf n} &=\int_0^1e^{iuK_{\mathbf n}}\,ia_H [\mathsf F_t\otimes h(\mathbf n),\Pi_x] e^{-iuK_{\mathbf n}}\,du. \end{aligned}} (4.13)

The proof uses only ddu(eiuKΠxe−iuK)=eiuKi[K,Πx]e−iuK\frac d{du}(e^{iuK}\Pi_xe^{-iuK})=e^{iuK}i[K,\Pi_x]e^{-iuK}. It does not assume that finite position and momentum satisfy the canonical commutation relation of infinite space, and it includes the periodic wraparound edge. The mean metric force per round is therefore F¯x=Δ⟨Πx⟩/τ\overline F_x=\Delta\langle\Pi_x\rangle/\tau. Spatial background differences generate impulse through the commutator of maintenance with momentum, completing the connection from local background change to actual force; a uniform maintenance term contributes zero here.

4.4.2 Potential Energy and Acceleration

The background changes maintenance frequency, appearing in slow motion as position-dependent potential energy. Since resources still fluctuate each round, the range in which a mean action is valid must first be determined from the complete channel.

Fix a finite mixing resource process with stationary distribution πb\pi_b and per-round accumulation K𝒏=ηB𝒏K_{\mathbf n}=\eta B_{\mathbf n}, where B𝒏B_{\mathbf n} is bounded and η\eta sufficiently small. Starting from a stationary product input, the complete channel retains correlations generated subsequently; finite mixing makes their correction to the reduced motion per round O(η2)O(\eta^2), so within Nη≤TN\eta\le T,

supNη≤T∥ρ(N)−e−iNηB‾ρ(0)eiNηB‾∥1≤CTη. \boxed{\sup_{N\eta\le T} \left\|\rho^{(N)}-e^{-iN\eta\bar B}\rho^{(0)}e^{iN\eta\bar B}\right\|_1 \le C_T\eta.} (4.14)

The constant depends on the mixing rate and operator bounds of the fixed resource process, and actual elapsed duration is NτN\tau; see Supplementary Proof S9.8. Within this window, converting to rates using the complete cycle period gives the mean generator and the source-induced change:

Hav=aHτ𝖥t⊗∑ih‾iPi+axτZ⊗Dx,δH=aHτ𝖥t⊗∑i(h‾i−h0)Pi. \begin{gathered} H_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{a_H}{\tau}\mathsf F_t\otimes\sum_i\bar h_iP_i +\frac{a_x}{\tau}Z\otimes D_x,\\ \boxed{\delta H=\frac{a_H}{\tau}\mathsf F_t\otimes \sum_i(\bar h_i-h_0)P_i.} \end{gathered} (4.15)

Hloc(x,k)=mt[1+Φ(x)]βt+axτZsin⁡(kℓx),Hloc(x,k)2={mt2[1+Φ(x)]2+ax2τ2sin⁡2(kℓx)}I. \begin{gathered} H_{\mathrm{loc}}(x,k)=m_t[1+\Phi(x)]\beta_t +\frac{a_x}{\tau}Z\sin(k\ell_x),\\ H_{\mathrm{loc}}(x,k)^2 =\left\{m_t^2[1+\Phi(x)]^2+ \frac{a_x^2}{\tau^2}\sin^2(k\ell_x)\right\}I. \end{gathered} (4.16)

Cross terms cancel by anticommutation. The first term is the baseline rest energy, the second the background-induced energy change, and the third the kinetic energy k2/(2Min,t)k^2/(2M_{{\mathrm{in}},t}). This identifies both Min,t=mt/c02M_{{\mathrm{in}},t}=m_t/c_0^2 and

Vt(i)=mtΦi,Φi=h‾i−h0h0=−2ξ*,i. \boxed{V_t(i)=m_t\Phi_i,\qquad \Phi_i=\frac{\bar h_i-h_0}{h_0} =-2\xi_{*,i}.} (4.18)

To compare source and test carrier, first use the same fixed frequency scale ν*>0\nu_*>0 to write Ĥs=ν*𝖥̂s\widehat H_s=\nu_*\widehat{\mathsf F}_s, and let fs=λs/ν*f_s=\lambda_s/\nu_* and θ=ν*tread\theta=\nu_*t_{\mathrm{read}}. For a fixed source and process, both the field’s spatial structure and strength come from the same return kernel 𝒬\mathcal Q.

4.4.3 Continuous Survival and Energy Balance

Continuous survival of matter and the stationary distribution of the background field describe different objects. The channel above preserves source and test carrier within the protected study window; if the actual cycle also performs thermal processing, the complete process must specify how the original carrier is stored during that processing, when it returns, and when it exits.

One existing pattern-preserving realization uses an auxiliary copy with the same spectrum and group representation as the system. A full swap first stores the unknown carrier and its correlations in the copy, while the original thermal processing acts on a known system input; after successful filtering, the inverse swap returns the carrier. The full swap commutes with the sum of the two bare energies. Activity is switched off during thermal processing, and the bare free phases of system and copy are actually compensated. If the success outcomes at the fixed input act on the carrier as rηI\sqrt{r_\eta}I, with total survival probability qT=∑ηrηq_T=\sum_\eta r_\eta, then the protected activity UU satisfies

𝒬T(ρ)=qTUρU†,Tr⁡𝒬T(ρ)+Tr⁡𝒳T(ρ)=Tr⁡ρ. \mathcal Q_T(\rho)=q_TU\rho U^\dagger,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}\mathcal Q_T(\rho)+\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal X_T(\rho) =\operatorname{Tr}\rho. (4.21)

The exit map 𝒳T\mathcal X_T retains failed outputs and the stored unknown state. Envelope and phase evolution of the successful component are thereby separated: survival probability changes the envelope, while frequency must also be divided by the complete cycle period including storage, thermal exchange, filtering, compensation, and recording.

Energy changes during activity can also be balanced within the same space. For an active window at fixed configuration, denote the bare energy by H0H_0 and specify a self-adjoint generator HonH_{\mathrm{on}} on the full space that preserves the protected code, with actual activity generator K𝒏/tHK_{\mathbf n}/t_H within the code. Let D=Hon−H0D=H_{\mathrm{on}}-H_0, without assuming that H0H_0 preserves the same code subspace. Taking positive work to mean energy supplied to the system by control, rectangular switching gives

ρ′=e−itHHonρeitHHon,Won=Tr⁡(Dρ),Woff=−Tr⁡(Dρ′),Won+Woff=Tr⁡[H0(ρ′−ρ)]. \begin{gathered} \rho'=e^{-it_HH_{\mathrm{on}}}\rho e^{it_HH_{\mathrm{on}}},\qquad W_{\mathrm{on}}=\operatorname{Tr}(D\rho),\quad W_{\mathrm{off}}=-\operatorname{Tr}(D\rho'),\\ \boxed{W_{\mathrm{on}}+W_{\mathrm{off}} =\operatorname{Tr}[H_0(\rho'-\rho)].} \end{gathered} (4.22)

Total energy is conserved within the active window, namely Tr⁡[Hon(ρ′−ρ)]=0\operatorname{Tr}[H_{\mathrm{on}}(\rho'-\rho)]=0; substituting Hon=H0+DH_{\mathrm{on}}=H_0+D gives the identity. Finite switching uses the actual time-ordered propagator and includes ∫Tr⁡(ρtḢt)dt\int\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_t\dot H_t)dt; protection throughout switching must still be checked against the generators used. The original thermal exchange continues to balance the total bare energies of system, copy, and bath, including the energy carried away by exit outputs. Control work, thermal exchange, and exit thus have separate, explicit accounts.

Spatial background differences change carrier momentum through the same maintenance action; within the controlled weak-field, low-speed window, they appear as a potential-energy gradient and give a leading acceleration independent of test mass. Thermal processing determines continued survival and complete timing; greater equilibrium occupation alone does not establish directed motion.

4.5 Strength Calibration

Absolute strength compares two outputs of the same process: the mass phase accumulated by the source itself and the position-dependent phase acquired by the test carrier through the altered background. Their relation is determined jointly by source writing, spatial arrival and return, and local maintenance. Only after converting both phases into mass and potential energy using their total elapsed durations, and obtaining impulse from the same motion process, can actual force be compared with source and test masses. Common background calibration constrains the activity ratios at source and test endpoints, while the actual operation sequence determines the time needed to complete those activities. The spatial kernel and clock must therefore be obtained within the same outgoing-and-return process.

4.5.1 Actual Field Strength

The amplitude of a metric force is determined jointly by how much bias the source writes, how the background transports and replenishes it, and how the carrier responds. Equation (4.20) already combines these actions in one kernel. For a localized single source at ss, let 𝒢=L−1\mathcal G=L^{-1} and take source-site refreshing probability 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1. Let js=ε(bs−ξs)j_s=\varepsilon(b_s-\xi_s) denote the net bias written per round. From the refreshing and transport relations in Eq. (4.6), stationarity gives

cLξ+=jses,ξ=ξ+−jses,ξ+=jsc𝒢⋅s,ξs=(𝒢ssc−1)js,[1−ε+ε𝒢ssc]js=εbs. \begin{gathered} cL\xi^+=j_se_s,\qquad \xi=\xi^+-j_se_s,\qquad \xi^+=\frac{j_s}{c}\mathcal G_{\cdot s},\\ \xi_s=\left(\frac{\mathcal G_{ss}}c-1\right)j_s,\qquad \left[1-\varepsilon+\frac{\varepsilon\mathcal G_{ss}}c\right]j_s =\varepsilon b_s. \end{gathered} (4.23)

Here ese_s is the unit column vector at the source position. The final equation substitutes the bias propagated back to the source into the same writing rule. Solving for jsj_s and using ξi=ξi+\xi_i=\xi_i^+ at i≠si\ne s gives

ξ*,i=ε𝒢isc(1−ε)+ε𝒢ssbs,i≠s. \xi_{*,i}= \frac{\varepsilon\mathcal G_{is}}{c(1-\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\mathcal G_{ss}}\,b_s, \qquad i\ne s. (4.24)

This denominator results from joint balance between source and background: the source writes bias each round, while propagation returns part of it to the source, reducing the difference still available to be written next round. Eliminating the unknown source-site value makes the same return kernel determine net writing and the distant field profile. A weak source only linearizes the writing relation; return feedback remains. Reading this profile as strength in three-dimensional space additionally requires the corresponding actual adjacency and spatial window.

The three-dimensional field profile depends on actual spatial propagation. If positions are realized as an equal-spacing three-dimensional nearest-neighbor grid with equal exchange weights in all six directions, its operator has smooth long-wavelength limit −ℓx2∇2-\ell_x^2\nabla^2. Fourier transformation directly gives the Green kernel of the infinite unit lattice:

𝒢(𝒋)=∫[−π,π]3ei𝒒⋅𝒋2∑a=13(1−cos⁡qa)d3q(2π)3=14π|𝒋|+O(|𝒋|−2). \mathcal G(\mathbf j)=\int_{[-\pi,\pi]^3} \frac{e^{i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf j}}{2\sum_{a=1}^3(1-\cos q_a)} \frac{d^3q}{(2\pi)^3} =\frac1{4\pi|\mathbf j|}+O(|\mathbf j|^{-2}). (4.25)

The denominator near the origin is |𝒒|2+O(|𝒒|4)|\mathbf q|^2+O(|\mathbf q|^4); isolating this low-wave-number part gives the leading term. In a finite box, every missing neighboring edge is connected to unbiased supply, and its kernel tends to this kernel as the boundary recedes. Restoring r=ℓx|𝒋|r=\ell_x|\mathbf j|, the response in the far region outside the source therefore has shape 1/r1/r. This uses three-dimensional adjacency and its spatial calibration; the principal unit-position ring alone does not yield this conclusion.

On the same three-dimensional positions, if test-carrier motion also satisfies the potential-readout conditions of Eqs. (4.18)–(4.19), substituting the far-region kernel into Eq. (4.20) gives the leading radial action

Vt(r)=−Gdynmsmtr,Ft,r=−Gdynmsmtr2,Gdyn=θτεℓx4πaHh02[c(1−ε)+ε𝒢ss]. \boxed{\begin{gathered} V_t(r)=-G_{\mathrm{dyn}}\frac{m_sm_t}{r},\qquad F_{t,r}=-G_{\mathrm{dyn}}\frac{m_sm_t}{r^2},\\ G_{\mathrm{dyn}}=\frac{\theta\tau\varepsilon\ell_x} {4\pi a_Hh_0^2[c(1-\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\mathcal G_{ss}]}. \end{gathered}} (4.26)

Here GdynG_{\mathrm{dyn}} is the leading strength of the present source, transport, and passive-response process. Until the three-dimensional spatial conditions are adopted, the original position ring continues to use the finite kernel of Eq. (4.20), without radial substitution. This establishes both the spatial conditions for field shape and the operational origin of strength; conversion to common physical units further requires the background scale.

4.5.2 Background Scale

The common scale comes from the squared background spectral response. Fix odd prime pp and depth KK, let d=pKd=p^K and M=d−1M=d-1, take spectral function h(n)=log⁡nh(n)=\log n on nonzero integer representatives, and denote spectral-address projections by PnP_n. The increment between adjacent spectral addresses is Δn=log⁡(1+1/n)\Delta_n=\log(1+1/n). Assigning the squared gradient of every spectral edge to both endpoints gives

BK=∑n=1M−1Δn2(Pn+Pn+1),BKP0=0,Tr⁡BK=CM*=2∑n=1M−1log⁡2(1+1/n). \begin{gathered} B_K=\sum_{n=1}^{M-1}\Delta_n^2(P_n+P_{n+1}),\qquad B_KP_0=0,\\ \boxed{\operatorname{Tr}B_K=C_M^* =2\sum_{n=1}^{M-1}\log^2(1+1/n).} \end{gathered} (4.27)

Every edge appears twice, directly giving the trace. Since Δn<1/n\Delta_n<1/n, the total tends to a finite value C*C^* as the spectral cutoff increases, with 0<C*−CM*<2/(M−1)0<C^*-C_M^*<2/(M-1). Spectral addresses, edges, and physical resource positions are counted separately here.

Here h(n)h(n) measures spectral response, whereas the matter-induced potential Φi\Phi_i is determined by the actual background distribution. They are connected through common frequency calibration, without setting Φi\Phi_i equal to the logarithm of a position label. A normalized state gives relative response shares; unnormalized participation weights record the total response.

For a normalized state ρ\rho supplied by the cycle, the mean squared spectral gradient is

Qmet(ρ)=Tr⁡(ρBK),Qmet(I/d)=CM*d,Qmet(I≠0/M)=CM*M. Q_{\mathrm{met}}(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho B_K),\qquad Q_{\mathrm{met}}(I/d)=\frac{C_M^*}{d},\qquad Q_{\mathrm{met}}(I_{\ne0}/M)=\frac{C_M^*}{M}. (4.28)

The finite total squared gradient is distributed among all participating positions in an equal-weight state, so its mean decreases as the number of positions grows. The normalized trace already performs one average and is not divided again by the mode count. This quantity gives the squared response of the specified state; it does not alone determine the actual field amplitude.

Using common background matching, let positive operator Γ\Gamma record unnormalized response weights and let P𝒮P_{\mathcal S} select the participation range. Take W=Tr⁡(P𝒮ΓP𝒮)>1W=\operatorname{Tr}(P_{\mathcal S}\Gamma P_{\mathcal S})>1 and common coefficient log⁡W\log W. Then

E(W)2Cbg=E02Wlog⁡2W,E(W)=E0WCbglog⁡W. \boxed{E(W)^2C_{\mathrm{bg}}=E_0^2W\log^2W,\qquad E(W)=E_0\sqrt{\frac W{C_{\mathrm{bg}}}}\log W.} (4.29)

The quantity CbgC_{\mathrm{bg}} uses the background squared response actually selected: C*C^* for the full spectrum and CM*C_M^* for a finite open chain. The physical energy unit is supplied by E0E_0. This equation retains the physical identification through squared-response matching; a normalized state alone is insufficient to recover WW.

Define the inverse square of the common metric energy scale as the strength scale:

GE(W)=1E(W)2=CbgE02Wlog⁡2W. \boxed{G_E(W)=\frac1{E(W)^2} =\frac{C_{\mathrm{bg}}}{E_0^2W\log^2W}.} (4.30)

When every orthogonal mode has unit response weight and the entire space participates, W=d=pKW=d=p^K. If Cbg=CM*C_{\mathrm{bg}}=C_M^* is also used, E02GE(d)=Qmet(I/d)/log⁡2dE_0^2G_E(d)=Q_{\mathrm{met}}(I/d)/\log^2d. Here 1/d1/d comes from the specified state average, whereas the squared logarithm comes from common energy-scale matching; they play different roles.

This distinction directly affects strength when structural weights change. Retain the positive factor ℒp\mathcal L_p of Chapter 3. If the metric process uses effective participation weight Wmet=dℒp>1W_{\mathrm{met}}=d\mathcal L_p>1, then with the same background and units,

GE(dℒp)GE(d)=1ℒp[log⁡dlog⁡(dℒp)]2. \boxed{\frac{G_E(d\mathcal L_p)}{G_E(d)} =\frac1{\mathcal L_p} \left[\frac{\log d}{\log(d\mathcal L_p)}\right]^2.} (4.31)

The same weight enters both participation and its logarithm, so multiplying only by 1/ℒp1/\mathcal L_p omits part of the contribution. For example, with Γ=ℒpI\Gamma=\mathcal L_pI, the normalized state remains I/dI/d and its QmetQ_{\mathrm{met}} is unchanged, while absolute participation and energy scale change. The Loewy-layer structure supplies the algebraic hierarchy used; assigning metric participation weights this way remains an explicitly adopted physical correspondence.

4.5.3 Strength Matching

Compare this spectral scale with the actual strength in Eq. (4.26). Here take a finite open-chain background Cbg=CM*C_{\mathrm{bg}}=C_M^* and metric-end scale GE=GE(Wm)G_E=G_E(W_m). Write rv=Wvlog⁡Wvr_v=\sqrt{W_v}\log W_v and rm=Wmlog⁡Wmr_m=\sqrt{W_m}\log W_m, where Wv,WmW_v,W_m are the prescribed participation weights at the maintenance and metric endpoints, respectively.

Let aB=∫background active windowg(t)dta_B=\int_{\text{background active window}}g(t)\,dt denote accumulated background activity and g(t)g(t) the common bare drive strength. When maintenance and background share the same active window, aH=rvaBa_H=r_va_B. At the common weak-accumulation level, the squared background phase from the same actual readout is Cph=CM*h02+O(aB2)C_{\mathrm{ph}}=C_M^*h_0^2+O(a_B^2), and the period is calibrated by τ=aBCph/E0\tau=a_B\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{ph}}}/E_0. Hence mf=vspecfm_f=v_{\mathrm{spec}}f and vspec=E0rv/CM*v_{\mathrm{spec}}=E_0r_v/\sqrt{C_M^*}. Further adopting event scale ℓx=1/vspec\ell_x=1/v_{\mathrm{spec}} and substituting into the actual strength gives its ratio to the spectral scale:

GdynGE=θεrm24πh0rv2[c(1−ε)+ε𝒢ss],h0=12. \frac{G_{\mathrm{dyn}}}{G_E} =\frac{\theta\varepsilon r_m^2} {4\pi h_0r_v^2[c(1-\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\mathcal G_{ss}]}, \qquad h_0=\frac12. (4.32)

This compares their common leading order, with source and test masses using the same background clock. It shows how actual source readout, transport, and return enter strength; a common period and common units do not remove these ratios. Adopting Gdyn=GEG_{\mathrm{dyn}}=G_E as a physical calibration requires the selected process to satisfy this correspondence, rather than assigning the same field strength to every allowed exchange.

4.5.4 Static Response at a Common Vertex

Denote the source and test angles in this section by zs=aBrsz_s=a_Br_s and zt=aBrtz_t=a_Br_t. Under the normalization a=rvaBa=r_va_B below, fs=rs/rvf_s=r_s/r_v and ft=rt/rvf_t=r_t/r_v are dimensionless phase coefficients; when produced through the complete common spectral port of S6, rs=r(Ws)r_s=r(W_s) and rt=r(Wt)r_t=r(W_t). Other families must use their own actual phase coefficients; the dimensionful eigenvalue λi\lambda_i of 4.1 cannot be substituted directly here.

When the same vertex supplies both maintenance phase and source readout, field strength and spectral scale can be compared within common preparation, readout, and timing. Take a static process with common refreshing at source and test endpoints, conservative transport outside the source, and unbiased supply at the boundary. Test-end refreshing is retained in the coherent return, giving a different return kernel from the passive test of Eq. (4.11); strength must be calculated independently rather than transferred from Eq. (4.32).

Take contact points s,ts,t, common refreshing probability ε\varepsilon, and probability cc for each exchange edge and supply branch. A fresh resource unit remains coherent until the common-vertex action and coherent readout are complete. The two contact refreshes are mutually exclusive, 0<2ε<10<2\varepsilon<1, and transport retains at least one-half idle probability, namely c|ℰ|≤1/2c|\mathcal E|\le1/2, where ℰ\mathcal E includes supply branches. The bias of the fresh resource unit at the source is bs=sin⁡(afs)/2b_s=\sin(af_s)/2, where a=rvaBa=r_va_B and aBa_B is the effective accumulation at the common background endpoint; after connecting the common capacity of S6, it is calculated from aB=∫gcol(t)/Λdta_B=\int g_{\mathrm{col}}(t)/\Lambda\,dt. At the test endpoint, take the coherence slope at the origin of its own accumulation, where bt=0b_t=0, while retaining unbiased refreshing.

Let PSP_S project onto the two contact points, and set α=c(1−ε)/ε\alpha=c(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon. Stationarity still gives ξ+=(I−εPS)ξ+εPSb\xi^+=(I-\varepsilon P_S)\xi+\varepsilon P_Sb and ξ=(I−cL)ξ+\xi=(I-cL)\xi^+. Outside the source, Lξ+=0L\xi^+=0; substituting at the contacts into the latter equation eliminates ξ\xi and gives (αL+PS)ξ+=PSb(\alpha L+P_S)\xi^+=P_Sb. Write ξ+=𝒢⋅S𝑱\xi^+=\mathcal G_{\cdot S}\mathbf J and denote u=𝒢ssu=\mathcal G_{ss}, v=𝒢ttv=\mathcal G_{tt}, and w=𝒢stw=\mathcal G_{st}. Solving over the whole space reduces to

(α+uwwα+v)(JsJt)=(bs0),Δ=(α+u)(α+v)−w2>0. \begin{pmatrix}\alpha+u&w\\w&\alpha+v\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}J_s\\J_t\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}b_s\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Delta=(\alpha+u)(\alpha+v)-w^2>0. (4.33)

Here 𝑱\mathbf J is the net bias written per round at a contact divided by cc, namely 𝒋=c𝑱\mathbf j=c\mathbf J; it is not a probability. Positive definiteness of the matrix follows from 𝒢>0\mathcal G>0 and α>0\alpha>0. Direct inversion gives Js=(α+v)bs/ΔJ_s=(\alpha+v)b_s/\Delta and Jt=−wbs/ΔJ_t=-wb_s/\Delta, hence ξt+=wJs+vJt=αwbs/Δ\xi_t^+=wJ_s+vJ_t=\alpha wb_s/\Delta. Define the cross-response and its far-region coefficient by

Kts=αw(α+u)(α+v)−w2,F=α(α+u)(α+v),ξt+=Ktsbs. K_{ts}=\frac{\alpha w}{(\alpha+u)(\alpha+v)-w^2},\qquad F=\frac{\alpha}{(\alpha+u)(\alpha+v)},\qquad \xi_t^+=K_{ts}b_s. (4.34)

The test phase must also be read using this instrument. Branches in which the test endpoint is not selected use the response of the old resource unit 1−nt1-n_t; when it is selected, the fresh resource unit gives the unbiased mean 1/21/2 during the coherent process. The normalized slope of the actual coherence root at the origin of test accumulation is therefore

Ht|s=(1−ε)(12−ξt)+ε2=12−ξt+,Φt=Ht|s−1/21/2=−2ξt+=−Ktssin⁡(afs). \begin{gathered} H_{t|s}=(1-\varepsilon)\left(\frac12-\xi_t\right) +\frac{\varepsilon}{2} =\frac12-\xi_t^+,\\ \boxed{\Phi_t=\frac{H_{t|s}-1/2}{1/2} =-2\xi_t^+=-K_{ts}\sin(af_s).} \end{gathered} (4.35)

This uses ξt+=(1−ε)ξt\xi_t^+=(1-\varepsilon)\xi_t when bt=0b_t=0. Test-end refreshing thus enters both the stationary kernel and phase readout; removing that update changes the result. At zero source, the same reading gives source mass ms=afs/(2τ)m_s=af_s/(2\tau). For a weak source, in the three-dimensional far region and the range w2≪(α+u)(α+v)w^2\ll(\alpha+u)(\alpha+v), substitute w≃ℓx/(4πr)w\simeq\ell_x/(4\pi r) and read the actual leading coefficient G(0)=τℓxF/(2π)G^{(0)}=\tau\ell_xF/(2\pi) from test energy shift mtΦtm_t\Phi_t.

For this active two-contact process, thermal survival and replenishment of a positive source can be composed in their complete temporal order. Each round performs source activity, scalar thermal survival, and end-of-round replenishment; the thermal window acts as the identity on resources, test carrier, and their correlations, while complete preparation of a vacant site produces the same positive-source carrier before the next round. Let f=QMf=Q_M be the actual per-round replenishment probability including every readiness step, qTq_T the survival probability of the thermal process transported to the positive-source code subspace, and πj\pi_j the probability of presence before activity in round j+1j+1. Taking (1−f)qT<1(1-f)q_T<1, roundwise counting gives

πj+1=f+(1−f)qTπj,π*=f1−(1−f)qT,Ms=π*Es,Es=zs2τ. \boxed{\begin{gathered} \pi_{j+1}=f+(1-f)q_T\pi_j,\qquad \pi_* =\frac{f}{1-(1-f)q_T},\\ M_s=\pi_*E_s,\qquad E_s=\frac{z_s}{2\tau}. \end{gathered}} (4.36)

Here EsE_s is the individual phase mass verified at the same port, and MsM_s is the mean counting mass of individuals actually present. If additional input loading before formation has not been included, ff must be replaced by the total acceptance probability summed over all accepted histories. The complete joint instrument for source absence and presence and proof for correlated inputs are given in Supplementary Proof S9.4.

Source occupation multiplies both the stationary background response and counting mass, so this common factor cancels in strength per unit mass for a weak source and weak test. Thermal exit still determines individual lifetime, and replenishment still has an actual cost; neither disappears from the complete process. Starting from a vacant site also gives an establishment delay, and finite-angle response must be calculated using the complete instrument.

With persistent replenishment, the stationary weak-test potential is Φ∞=−π*Ktssin⁡zs\Phi_\infty=-\pi_*K_{ts}\sin z_s, where zs=afsz_s=af_s. Substituting Ms=π*EsM_s=\pi_*E_s above and the same reading Es=zs/(2τ)E_s=z_s/(2\tau) gives Φ∞=−2τKtsMssinc⁡zs\Phi_\infty=-2\tau K_{ts}M_s\operatorname{sinc}z_s. Thus, after normalization by actual counting mass, the weak-source leading coefficient remains τℓxF/(2π)\tau\ell_xF/(2\pi). Changing the replenishment schedule changes the complete cycle period, so the old clock cannot continue to be used after this cancellation. Complete finite-source and field-establishment results are given in 4.5.6.

The same test resource unit also connects source writing to background calibration. Let Ht|s=1/2−π*KtsbsH_{t|s}=1/2-\pi_*K_{ts}b_s be the available share after contact. The actual gradient exchange has short-time squared response Cex=CM*Ht|sC_{\mathrm{ex}}=C_M^*H_{t|s}, while the squared weak-angle phase rate is Cph=CM*Ht|s2C_{\mathrm{ph}}=C_M^*H_{t|s}^2. Their baselines are CM*/2C_M^*/2 and CM*/4C_M^*/4 respectively, but their first-order changes at the unbiased reference point are both −CM*π*Ktsbs-C_M^*\pi_*K_{ts}b_s. The source-induced availability deficit therefore enters both exchange response and maintenance phase; the complete signal and proof of this connection are given in Supplementary Proof S9.5.

4.5.5 Complete Timing and Strength

Matter formation, positive-source loading, and thermal replenishment all take actual time. Actual strength therefore depends jointly on the source-to-test return response and the total elapsed duration of a round. We now recalibrate the background within the same gated operating procedure; the bare coefficient for the ungated half-gap in 2.5.3 cannot be additionally applied here.

The same instrument also performs background calibration. Let ℛ\mathcal R be the full-configuration transport matrix and 𝖤b\mathsf E_b unbiased refreshing at contact bb. Retaining the actual coherence between positive and negative test eigenbranches, the zero-source matrix is

Tt(z)=ℛ[(1−2ε)Dt(z)+ε∑b=s,t𝖤bDt(z)𝖤b],Dt(z)=diag⁡e−2iz(1−nt),z=aft. \begin{gathered} T_t(z)=\mathcal R\left[(1-2\varepsilon)D_t(z) +\varepsilon\sum_{b=s,t}\mathsf E_bD_t(z)\mathsf E_b\right],\\ D_t(z)=\operatorname{diag}e^{-2iz(1-n_t)},\qquad z=af_t. \end{gathered} (4.37)

Full-configuration reversal 𝒥\mathcal J commutes with transport and unbiased refreshing and sends 1−nt1-n_t to ntn_t, hence 𝒥Tt(z)¯𝒥=e2izTt(z)\mathcal J\overline{T_t(z)}\mathcal J=e^{2iz}T_t(z). The unique simple root continued from the origin satisfies eizλt(z)∈ℝe^{iz}\lambda_t(z)\in\mathbb R; on a connected branch where it is nonzero and visible and its centered root is positive, arg⁡λt=−z\arg\lambda_t=-z, with normalized frequency −arg⁡λt/(2z)=1/2-\arg\lambda_t/(2z)=1/2. Applying the same reading to every background-gradient branch gives Cph=CM*/4C_{\mathrm{ph}}=C_M^*/4.

Write C=CM*C=C_M^* and Ω=2E0/C\Omega=2E_0/\sqrt C; the common background reading gives aB=Ωτa_B=\Omega\tau. In a serial schedule with common bare rate gcolg_{\mathrm{col}}, AMA_M sums the actual dimensionless cost of inactive steps, including inversion of the formation reference, positive-source loading, thermal transport, replenishment, transport, and completion of failure branches; twt_w is waiting time that does not scale with the bare rate. The active-window cost is ΛaB\Lambda a_B, so

τ=ΛaB+AMgcol+tw,ρclk=gcolΩ,δ=Ωtw,aB=AM+ρclkδρclk−Λ,ρclk>Λ. \boxed{\begin{gathered} \tau=\frac{\Lambda a_B+A_M}{g_{\mathrm{col}}}+t_w,\qquad \rho_{\mathrm{clk}}=\frac{g_{\mathrm{col}}}\Omega,\quad\delta=\Omega t_w,\\ a_B=\frac{A_M+\rho_{\mathrm{clk}}\delta}{\rho_{\mathrm{clk}}-\Lambda}, \qquad \rho_{\mathrm{clk}}>\Lambda. \end{gathered}} (4.38)

This uses a serial procedure in which AMA_M is independent of the accumulation being solved for; if costs depend on that accumulation, retain the implicit relation in the first line. Idle steps also occupy a complete execution window, and the resulting schedule uses the common phase branch of 4.5.6.

Let Fret=FF_{\mathrm{ret}}=F denote the far-region coefficient of Eq. (4.34), and set rm=Wmetlog⁡Wmetr_m=\sqrt{W_{\mathrm{met}}}\log W_{\mathrm{met}} and rv=Wvlog⁡Wvr_v=\sqrt{W_v}\log W_v. With the same three-dimensional spatial correspondence, a stationary weak source and weak test, and a controlled far region, substituting ℓx=2/(Ωrv)\ell_x=2/(\Omega r_v) into the actual response gives

Gresponse(0)=τℓx2πFret,Emet=E0rmC,ℭ0:=Gresponse(0)Emet2=κ0AM+ρclkδρclk−Λ,κ0=rm2Fret4πrv. \boxed{\begin{gathered} G_{\mathrm{response}}^{(0)}=\frac{\tau\ell_x}{2\pi}F_{\mathrm{ret}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{met}}=\frac{E_0r_m}{\sqrt C},\\ \mathfrak C_0:=G_{\mathrm{response}}^{(0)}E_{\mathrm{met}}^2 =\kappa_0\frac{A_M+\rho_{\mathrm{clk}}\delta}{\rho_{\mathrm{clk}}-\Lambda}, \qquad \kappa_0=\frac{r_m^2F_{\mathrm{ret}}}{4\pi r_v}. \end{gathered}} (4.39)

The return coefficient comes from actual contact and propagation, and accumulated action comes from the complete schedule. Once this process is specified, the above equation determines its leading strength. Stationary occupation has canceled through the same counting mass, while preparation and replenishment costs remain in AMA_M; see Supplementary Proofs S9.5–S9.6.

The condition for equality between actual response and the inverse spectral square is therefore

Gresponse(0)=Emet−2⇔ρclk−Λ=κ0(AM+ρclkδ). \boxed{G_{\mathrm{response}}^{(0)}=E_{\mathrm{met}}^{-2} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \rho_{\mathrm{clk}}-\Lambda=\kappa_0(A_M+\rho_{\mathrm{clk}}\delta).} (4.40)

This paper adopts one physical calibration, identifying leading response strength with the inverse square of the spectral energy scale; Eq. (4.40) constrains actual driving, accumulation, and the complete-cycle timing under that calibration. It does not follow from the common background clock alone. For dynamically controlled actions that can be scaled together, the required action and schedule are given in Supplementary Proof S9.6; for an independently fixed process, Eq. (4.39) directly gives strength. Subsequent evaluations use this same calibration, with finite-source and propagation corrections calculated from the complete outputs below.

4.5.6 Finite Response

Finite source angle, propagation buildup, and test readout all come from the same complete process. Let 𝕋(zt;bs)\mathbb T(z_t;b_s) retain the source-presence flag, all resource configurations, and test coherence, and let v0v_0 be the specified joint input. Composing two-contact activity, thermal exit, and end-of-round replenishment in order gives the finite signal and source-induced phase:

CN(zt;bs)=𝟏𝖳𝕋(zt;bs)Nv0,φN=Arg⁡unfoldCN(zt;bs)CN(zt;0),ΦN=−φNNzt,bs=sin⁡zs2. \begin{gathered} C_N(z_t;b_s)=\boldsymbol1^{\mathsf T}\mathbb T(z_t;b_s)^Nv_0,\\ \varphi_N=\operatorname{Arg}_{\mathrm{unfold}} \frac{C_N(z_t;b_s)}{C_N(z_t;0)},\qquad \Phi_N=-\frac{\varphi_N}{Nz_t},\quad b_s=\frac{\sin z_s}{2}. \end{gathered} (4.41)

The potential reading requires established common baseline masses for source and test, nonzero signals, and a phase unwrapped along the actual continuous branch. At finite test angle, ΦN\Phi_N generally depends on the test port; only the weak-test limit gives a common response. The complete operator and proof are given in Supplementary Proofs S9.4 and S9.7.

Starting with an unbiased resource preparation, write 𝖠=(I−εPS)(I−cL)\mathsf A=(I-\varepsilon P_S)(I-cL). The finite buildup kernel of the original active process is

KN=εN∑l=0N−1(N−l)(𝖠l)ts,KN↗Kts. K_N=\frac{\varepsilon}{N}\sum_{l=0}^{N-1}(N-l)(\mathsf A^l)_{ts}, \qquad K_N\nearrow K_{ts}. (4.42)

A sufficiently long kernel response does not mean infinite individual survival, nor guarantee that rereading mass over the same long window preserves the original phase identification.

A common phase reading also requires signals to remain nonzero and visible throughout the observation window. Supplementary Proof S9.7 gives a sufficient finite-window bound; a specific process uses KNK_N to assess field buildup and CNC_N to assess phase and visibility.

In the stationary weak-test reading, let η=w2/[(α+u)(α+v)]<1\eta=w^2/[(\alpha+u)(\alpha+v)]<1. Retaining the source sine and finite return gives the potential in the three-dimensional bulk:

Φ∞(r)=−Gresponse(0)Msrsinc⁡zs1−η,sinc⁡zs=sin⁡zszs. \boxed{\Phi_\infty(r)=-\frac{G_{\mathrm{response}}^{(0)}M_s}{r} \frac{\operatorname{sinc}z_s}{1-\eta},\qquad \operatorname{sinc}z_s=\frac{\sin z_s}{z_s}.} (4.43)

Use continuous extension at zero source angle and account separately for lattice and boundary errors. Actual force requires a positional difference or derivative of this potential. If source mass, source angle, period, and contact parameters do not vary with test position, u,vu,v are approximately constant in the bulk, and the spatial approximation w≃ℓx/(4πr)w\simeq\ell_x/(4\pi r) also controls derivatives, the leading radial force is

ℱr=−Gresponse(0)Msmtr2sinc⁡zs1+η(1−η)2. \boxed{\mathcal F_r=-\frac{G_{\mathrm{response}}^{(0)}M_sm_t}{r^2} \operatorname{sinc}z_s\frac{1+\eta}{(1-\eta)^2}.} (4.44)

Return corrections to potential and force therefore differ. Finite buildup, finite test angle, and general geometry are calculated in Supplementary Proof S9.7; these corrections describe actual outputs beyond the leading calibration, and their magnitudes are compared separately with experimental uncertainties.

4.5.7 Calibration and Strength of the Common Round Trip

The round trip of the same resource packet uses the occupation preparation of 4.1, with source-end matching effect EE determining both matter phase and packet occupation. Unlike refreshing that removes the old resource unit, this process retains the same packet and its transport records and reverses their order on return; without remote readout, the packet can be restored while holding along the path still leaves a phase. We calculate visits, reception, impulse, and clock consecutively for this process.

For the same resource packet returning along its original path, actual paths give a finite visit kernel. Let R=I−cL be the mean transport matrix of the actual edge-swap and idle-step selection rule, where L is the Laplacian of the undirected position graph used. Freeze and read after every complete edge swap; after m outgoing steps, return in reverse order using the same record. The position sequence is x₁,…,xmx_m,xm−1x_{m−1},…,x₀, with each endpoint read once and intermediate positions twice. The mean visit counts for unit source column ex0e_{x_0} are

u(m)=(I+R)∑j=0m−1Rjex0,𝟏𝖳u(m)=2m. \boxed{u^{(m)}=(I+R)\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}R^je_{x_0},\qquad \mathbf1^{\mathsf T}u^{(m)}=2m.} (4.45)

This visit kernel and the refreshing stationary kernel of 4.2 describe their respective processes. A single terminal readout reads only Rmex0R^me_{x_0}; accumulated readout along the path produces the geometric sum above. On a finite connected graph with idle steps, its nonuniform part has an exact Green decomposition and finite remainder; see Supplementary Proof S10.2. The original position ring’s L⁺ gives a periodic quadratic profile; neither the configuration space of 6.2 nor the calibration graph of the gradient spectrum automatically becomes a three-dimensional position graph.

During these frozen windows, the same resource packet controls the common final segment of the receiving matter. Let KtK_t be the joint action of the target’s complete matter and original background gradient, and OBO_B the incoming resource packet’s occupation projection; local swap-in, holding, and return implement Kt(I−OB)K_t(I−O_B). The target code preserves its pattern exactly, but finite reception generally entangles it with the packet. For resource-packet occupation probability qs=se/2q_s=se/2 of a fixed source branch, time integral b of the target holding envelope in each window, and time integral hth_t of the additional ungated holding envelope, the actual coherence for spectral difference Δκ between two values of KtK_t at the same position x is

𝒞m,x=e−i(ht+2mb)Δκ[1−qs+qs𝔼ηeibΔκNx(η)]. \mathcal C_{m,x}=e^{-i(h_t+2mb)\Delta\kappa} \left[1-q_s+q_s\,\mathbb E_\eta e^{ib\Delta\kappa N_x(\eta)}\right]. (4.46)

Here NxN_x is the visit count of the same outgoing-and-return history, and 𝔼η\mathbb E_\eta sums actual exchange-selection records. This is not a channel power for independent fresh resource packets, and mean visits cannot be placed inside the exponential in advance. Within the accumulated weak-readout regime, the complete output gives

ΔHt(1)=Ht(0)Φm(X),Ht(0)=ht+2mbτKt,Φm(x)=−qsbht+2mbux(m). \boxed{\Delta H_t^{(1)}=H_t^{(0)}\Phi_m(X),\quad H_t^{(0)}=\frac{h_t+2mb}{\tau}K_t,\quad \Phi_m(x)=-\frac{q_sb}{h_t+2mb}u_x^{(m)}.} (4.47)

The same Φm\Phi_m multiplies the target’s entire zero-field action, so matter phase and original background gradient acquire the same leading relative change. This explicitly connects the common background to a universal response: for the adopted common coupling structure, different stable states read local changes through their complete maintenance action. At finite angles, the complete output also gives visibility changes, gradient occupation probabilities, and source residuals; these and phase follow from the same history formula, as shown in Supplementary Proof S10.1.

This round trip can be calculated directly for a target in a position superposition. Initially the target is independent of source and network, with internal network correlations retained; target displacement is paused during frozen readout. The leading impulse of the complete position-controlled action is

Δ⟨Π⟩(1)=−iqsb⟨Kt[u(m)(X),Π]⟩. \boxed{\Delta\langle\Pi\rangle^{(1)} =-iq_sb\langle K_t[u^{(m)}(X),\Pi]\rangle.} (4.48)

This is a momentum difference of the complete output, not a total derivative obtained by moving the target and recomputing stationarity. It reduces to a potential gradient only in the original long-wavelength, slowly varying window; when the original gradient input has zero mean, the leading mean force on a fixed matter branch is −Mt∇Φm−M_t∇Φ_m. Further identifying this phase mass with inertial mass requires checking the complete zero-field process formed by this round trip and actual motion, without borrowing free curvature from another schedule. A fully reflection-symmetric isolated source may change its surrounding background while having zero net self-impulse; its background response need not vanish.

The common round trip also constrains accumulation at source and target through the same background scale. Place both endpoints themselves in the same zero-blockage reference r0=sr_0=\sqrt s, with common original gradient coefficient cBc_B and complete period τ; also take an unoccupied baseline for the target’s incoming resource packet. The calibrated gradient coefficient V₀ requires

V0=2r0cBtHτ=2r0cBht+2mbτ. V_0=2r_0c_B\frac{t_H}{\tau} =2r_0c_B\frac{h_t+2mb}{\tau}. (4.49)

Preparing only the incoming resource packet in the unoccupied state does not remove blockage of the target itself. Under this chapter’s connection in which all target maintenance is resource-gated, run the actual pause/compensation procedure outside reception windows, namely ht=0h_t=0; repeating the same equal-window module along the path gives 2mb=tH2mb=t_H. Unequal windows generally fix only total time integral of the reception envelope, while the actual envelope remains determined by the controls used.

Source holding and target readout use constant unit normalized envelopes and are performed serially; outgoing and return transport, resource-packet swapping, and thermal processing have total fixed positive cost CmC_m. The complete period is τ=2tH+Cm\tau=2t_H+C_m. Common calibration fixes holding ratio α=V0/(2r0cB)=tH/τ\alpha=V_0/(2r_0c_B)=t_H/\tau, giving the unique positive solution tH=αCm/(1−2α)t_H=\alpha C_m/(1-2\alpha) and b=tH/(2m)b=t_H/(2m) when 0<α<1/20<\alpha<1/2. Initial loading is timed as startup, while operations executed each round enter CmC_m; the duration of each operation in the specified sequence and nonunit envelopes are given in Supplementary Proof S10.3.

Substitution into actual reception gives Φm(x)=−qsux(m)/(2m)Φ_m(x)=−q_su_x^{(m)}/(2m). Take 0<e<10<e<1 and rs=s(1−e)r_s=\sqrt{s(1-e)}, and read the source phase already accumulated before reception as Ms=rsgMetH/(2τ)M_s=r_sg_Met_H/(2\tau) using the same τ. The finite first-order potential difference between two nonsource positions satisfies

Φm(x)−Φm(y)Ms=−sr0cBmrsgMV0(ux(m)−uy(m)). \boxed{\frac{\Phi_m(x)-\Phi_m(y)}{M_s} =-\frac{s r_0c_B}{m r_sg_MV_0} \bigl(u_x^{(m)}-u_y^{(m)}\bigr).} (4.50)

The common factor from accumulated holding cancels from this complete first-order ratio. With a controlled finite Green tail, weak matching rs→r0r_s\to r_0, and gB=gMg_B=g_M, the coefficient of the Green difference at nonsource positions is 𝒜Green(0)=2sq0/(mcΛV0)\mathcal A_{\mathrm{Green}}^{(0)}=2sq_0/(mc\Lambda V_0). In a window where the actual three-dimensional position graph gives Lxs+≃ℓx/(4πr)L^+_{xs}\simeq\ell_x/(4\pi r), the corresponding leading strength is G(0)=𝒜Green(0)ℓx/(4π)G^{(0)}=\mathcal A_{\mathrm{Green}}^{(0)}\ell_x/(4\pi). It uses this process’s exchange-selection rule, cycle length, complete-cycle timing, and source phase mass. The inertial reading in the same procedure, its correspondence with the spectral scale, and source residuals left by finite readout are given in Supplementary Proof S10. The physical calibration of 4.5.5 must be established separately for this procedure.

Metric force thus develops along one physical chain: matter matching changes background availability; actual exchange propagates that change; and local complete maintenance produces phase gradients and impulses. The common carrier fixes ratios between responses, while the return kernel and complete-cycle timing determine actual strength; this paper adopts the physical calibration to the inverse spectral square for the process used.

Chapter 5. State Space and p-Channels

The preceding chapters retained odd prime pp as a parameter while discussing stable patterns, address point-pair groupings, and exchange channels. Evaluating specific matter requires choosing one channel and relating directions, representations, and actual branches. This chapter determines which structural conditions select p=7p=7 and which definite objects this choice supplies for subsequent mass and coupling calculations.

For a fixed odd prime pp, the state spaces and constructions at all finite depths KK are collectively called a pp-channel. The parameter pp determines the arithmetic structure of the species layer, while KK determines address-resolution depth; exchanges, phases, and preparations of the actual cycle must still be specified. Channel selection therefore first constrains structure, with physical identities subsequently tested on the corresponding carriers and actions.

5.1 Structure of p-Channels

The directional decomposition of Chapter 2 and CRT channels of Chapter 3 supply the structural quantities needed to compare different pp. The species-layer unit group is cyclic of order p−1p-1; after excluding the trivial character, its direction-label count and number of negation-pair groups are respectively

#(Ĝp,1 ∖ {1}) = p − 2,
m = #(Gp,1/{±1}) = (p − 1)/2
.(5.1)

Both counts are independent of depth KK. A deeper unit shell has (p−1)pK−1(p-1)p^{K-1} addresses, with each species point-pair group lifting to pK−1p^{K-1} deeper point pairs; the complete direction space, including higher-conductor directions and directions on other shells, has dimension pK−K−1p^K-K-1.

Choose a generator of the unit group and label characters by ℓ\ell. Conjugation, negation parity, and order satisfy

χℓ = χ−ℓ, 　χℓ(−1) = (−1)ℓ,
ord χℓ = (p − 1)/gcd(ℓ,p − 1).
(5.2)

There is exactly one nontrivial self-conjugate direction χm\chi_m, while the others form (p−3)/2(p-3)/2 pairs; the negation parity of χm\chi_m is (−1)m(-1)^m. The symmetric whole-group formation of 2.3.2 uses a faithful nonreal character of quotient group Gp,1/{±1}G_{p,1}/\{\pm1\}, whose order is mm. Thus

m≥3⇔p≥7(pis an odd prime).m\ge3 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\ge7 \qquad(p\ \text{is an odd prime}).(5.3)

This excludes smaller channels but still permits larger odd primes. Further decomposing p−1=∏inip-1=\prod_i n_i into pairwise coprime prime powers gives the complete species space and factor-preserving group of Chapter 3:

ℋsp ≃ ⊗i=1rℂnᵢ,
𝒢fact ≃ [U(1) × ∏i=1rSU(ni)]/ℤp−1,
𝔤fact ≃ 𝔲(1) ⊕ ⊕i=1r𝔰𝔲(ni).
(5.4)

The number of structural factors is 1+ω(p−1)1+\omega(p-1) and the real Lie-algebra dimension is 1+∑i(ni2−1)1+\sum_i(n_i^2-1). The decomposition uses whole prime powers; for example, factor 4 corresponds to SU(4).

Channels can therefore be compared as follows. The label count includes only nontrivial species characters. The group-before-central-quotient column lists U(1) and SU factors before taking the central quotient, without identifying the factor-preserving group in advance with the symmetry group of a fixed cycle.
