For example, p=7, 11, and 13 all have three structural factors, but their SU-factor dimensions differ; having three factors alone does not select a unique channel. The point-pair group count and nontrivial-label count each determine p and satisfy p−2=2m−1, so they are not independent arithmetic information. If associated with different observables, their independence comes from the separate grounds for the two physical correspondences.

Comparing channels also requires distinguishing different action types within the same label set. Following 3.2, labels with exactly one nonzero CRT coordinate describe single-factor steps, while labels with several nonzero coordinates have composite support. Choosing zero or nonzero for each coordinate decomposes the complete label count over nonempty supports:

p−2=∏i=1rni−1=∑⌀≠S⊆{1,…,r}∏i∈S(ni−1),#{single-factor nontrivial labels}=∑i=1r(ni−1).p-2=\prod_{i=1}^{r}n_i-1 =\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}} \ \prod_{i\in S}(n_i-1), \qquad \#\{\text{single-factor nontrivial labels}\}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}(n_i-1).(5.5)

This identity follows by expanding ∏ᵢ[1+(nᵢ−1)]. For p=7, factors 2 and 3 give 1+2=3 single-factor nontrivial labels and 1×2=2 two-factor labels, totaling 5. The latter two have order 6, while single-factor labels have order 2 or 3. A classification of single-factor steps therefore applies only to the corresponding label set and cannot be extended unchecked to all elementary directions.

For every odd prime, nonzero negation pairs give two-dimensional complex observation units; the positive-cone and unit conditions used in 4.2 give signature (1,3), as proved in §§5.1–5.2 of Ref. 2. The scaling-invariant direction over the entire space is always ℂb, and logarithmic position readings have the same structure; see §5.5 of that paper. These shared structures permit comparison of different p-channels but neither select p nor exhaust collective-matter identities.

Channels differ in their species-layer point-pair grouping, nontrivial phase directions, conjugation and negation structures, and composition of coprime factors. We now relate these features to the matter structure adopted.

5.2 Channel Selection and Physical Correspondence

We first give the structural conditions selecting p=7, then explain the species, complete matter representations, and interaction correspondences within that channel.

5.2.1 Selection Conditions for Single-Factor Channels

Adopt the single-factor step rule of 3.2. Write p−1 as a product of pairwise coprime prime powers nᵢ, and let ℒ contain all labels in the full character group with exactly one nonzero CRT coordinate. The complete single-factor label set is required here. Among possible relations for a repeated nontrivial label χ in this set, two are particularly simple: its square equals the trivial label, or its square equals its conjugate. Denoting these by A and B respectively,

A：χ² = 1　⇔　ord χ = 2,
B：χ² = χ　⇔　ord χ = 3.
(5.6)

The first equivalence follows directly from nontriviality of χ; the second uses χ̄=χ⁻¹ to rewrite the relation as χ³=1 and then excludes the trivial label. If every label in ℒ is required to belong to A or B, every nontrivial character in each factor must have order two or three. Every cyclic factor has a character of order exactly nᵢ, forcing nᵢ to be 2 or 3. Conversely, if the factors are only 2 or 3, all their nontrivial labels satisfy the corresponding relations. Hence

[∀χ∈ℒ,A or B]⇔[ni∈{2,3} for all i]⇔p−1∣6⇔p∈{3,7}.\bigl[\forall\chi\in\mathcal L,\ \mathrm A\text{ or }\mathrm B\bigr] \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \bigl[n_i\in\{2,3\}\text{ for all }i\bigr] \ \Longleftrightarrow\ p-1\mid6 \ \Longleftrightarrow\ p\in\{3,7\}.(5.7)

This uses the fact that p is an odd prime, so p−1 is even, and no factor repeats in the coprime prime-power decomposition. A-class labels exist in every odd-prime channel because its unit-group order is even. B-class labels exist exactly when 3 divides p−1. Requiring both A and B therefore excludes p=3 and gives

ℒ is the complete set of single-factor nontrivial labels,[A,B exhaust ℒ and both types occur]⇔p=7.\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathcal L\text{ is the complete set of single-factor nontrivial labels},\\ \bigl[\mathrm A,\mathrm B\text{ exhaust }\mathcal L\text{ and both types occur}\bigr] \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p=7. \end{gathered}}(5.8)

This gives the complete arithmetic content of the selection conditions. It expresses a requirement on elementary steps: the square of every single-factor label falls into one of the two relations, with both relations present. Finite reduction and the cycle axioms alone do not enforce this requirement; if only some labels of a larger channel are opened, the proof also does not select a unique p. Subsequent evaluations adopt it as a channel-selection condition.

Label multiplication must also connect to actual processes. For example, the excursion operator of 2.4.2 satisfies Jχ2Jχ1|z⟩=−χ1(−1)δχ2,χ¯1|z⟩J_{χ_{2}}J_{χ_{1}}\vert z\rangle =-χ_{1}(-1)δ_{χ_{2},\overline{χ}_{1}}\vert z\rangle at the zero-element endpoint. Although an order-three χ has χ²=χ̄ at the label level, JχJχ|z⟩J_{χ}J_{χ}\vert z\rangle at that endpoint vanishes. The square relations therefore classify labels only; nonzero amplitude of actual compositions and return to the original pattern still depend on vertices and endpoints.

Correspondence with physical generations provides another check. The known classification of elementary fermions contains three generations (see the PDG electroweak review) 15. If all m whole groups of 2.3.2 are identified with all generation branches, with each group corresponding to an actually maintainable branch, m=3 gives (p−1)/2=3 and also selects p=7. Thus the two classes of label relations and the identification of all generation branches are compatible at p=7. If a larger channel forms only three visible branches, the three-generation count no longer determines p by itself.

5.2.2 Matter Species

At p=7, use 3 as a generator of the unit group modulo 7 and write characters as χℓχ_{ℓ}. Their CRT coordinates and orders are

χℓ(3a) = e2πiℓa/6, 　ℓ ↔ (ℓ mod 2, ℓ mod 3),
ord χℓ = 6/gcd(ℓ,6).
(5.9)

The five nontrivial labels comprise one real direction and two complex-conjugate pairs. Table 5-2 fixes the matter names used in subsequent evaluations: species labels record phase structure, whereas color, orientation, and charge belong to the complete matter representation; formation and maintenance processes give the mass branches. This section lists the representation relations needed for that correspondence; masses and couplings are calculated in later chapters.

The three sets of mass formulas use specified preparations and endpoints. The quark and neutrino branches of Chapter 8 obtain nonzero responses through real-direction connections, complete spectral paths with odd and even visits, and indirect-chain endpoints. Their masses are therefore calculated from the respective complete processes.

5.2.3 Channel Structure of Forces

Matter correspondences must use the same representations as interactions. The CRT decomposition at p=7 gives factors of dimensions two and three; following 3.2, the factor-preserving action is

ℋsp ≃ ℂ² ⊗ ℂ³,
𝒢fact ≃ [U(1) × SU(2) × SU(3)]/ℤ₆.
(5.13)

The nonzero steps of the two- and three-dimensional factors are χ3\chi_3 and χ2,χ4\chi_2,\chi_4 respectively; together with diagonal actions, they give 3 and 8 traceless self-adjoint directions, supplying the structural origins of weak and color interactions.

The complete matter representation must also accommodate color-singlet leptons. The natural action I2⊗SU(3)I_2\otimes SU(3) on species space gives

ℋsp│SU(3) ≃ 3 ⊕ 3, 　(ℋsp)SU(3) = {0}.
(5.14)

The central element e2πi/3I3e^{2\pi i/3}I_3 multiplies the entire space by a nontrivial phase, so no nonzero vector is fixed by every color action. This natural representation therefore cannot directly serve as a complete matter representation containing both leptons and quarks.

The charge generator must likewise be determined in the complete representation 15. The generator of the central U(1)U(1) takes the same value on all six directions. If charge is required to commute with every color action in the natural color representation above, irreducibility gives, block by block,

[Q, I₂ ⊗ U] = 0　(for all U ∈ SU(3))
⇒　Q = Q₂ ⊗ I₃.
(5.15)

Self-adjoint Q2Q_2 can give at most two charge values, each at least triply degenerate. Thus the lepton, quark, and antiparticle names used in Table 5-2 require a corresponding complete matter representation, whose descent through the central quotient must be checked. Negation parity, real or complex species, and step labels play their respective roles in subsequent endpoint selection; weak symmetry breaking and color-singlet formation are determined by their actual actions.

Charge, color, spin, and chirality describe different structures of action on the same matter state. Charge and color are carried by the complete internal representation; in the propagation realization with simultaneous coupling along three directions, spin and chirality are determined by the same propagation matrices. The four types of action admit a compatible joint representation, in which the mass action connects left- and right-chiral components. The operator construction, propagation relations, and conditional selection mechanism of weak contact are given in Supplementary Proofs S15, “Joint representation of quantum attributes”.

Collective exchange and metric response retain the process definitions of the preceding chapters. Nuclear interaction uses the collective exchange and response combination of 3.5, with the trivial unit-shell direction e₀ and full-space constant direction b serving their respective endpoints. The metric process uses coefficient GEG_E obtained in 4.5 for the chosen participation range and energy scale; its connection to gravitational coupling continues to be tested through that section’s mass source, spatial calibration, and actual return response.

Under the stated single-factor selection conditions, the channel is fixed as p=7p=7. Its three species-layer point-pair groups and the matter correspondences in Table 5-2 supply the objects for subsequent evaluation: Chapter 6 establishes the common energy scale, and Chapters 7 and 8 calculate couplings and masses, respectively.

Chapter 6. Energy Scales

Different processes have widely separated scales, yet must be compared using the same background and energy unit. In the p=7p=7-channel selected in Chapter 5, electroweak processes use the remaining participation of the unit shell, metric processes use the weighted full space, and nucleon processes use a collective spectral preparation. All three face the same question: which components actually participate, and how are their squared responses matched to the same background?

Adopt the matching relation E(W)=E0W/C*log⁡WE(W)=E_0\sqrt{W/C^*}\log W of 2.5, retaining the common physical energy calibration E0E_0 and the full logarithmic-spectrum background constant C*C^*. Each section calculates a different WW and then gives the energy scale, comparison quantities, and conditions of applicability.

This chapter retains the coherent return and background matching of Chapter 2, using r(W)=Wlog⁡Wr(W)=\sqrt W\log W as the dimensionless response coefficient of the common port. For rest-frame branches, common switching histories, and inactive segments that act as the identity or are compensated, complete timing gives νW=g‾effr(W)\nu_W=\bar g_{\mathrm{eff}}r(W), where g‾eff=T−1∫0Tgeff(t)dt\bar g_{\mathrm{eff}}=T^{-1}\int_0^Tg_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)\,dt includes actual capacity and active and paused durations. Vacuum squared-response matching fixes g‾eff=E0/Cbg\bar g_{\mathrm{eff}}=E_0/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{bg}}}, hence νW=E(W)\nu_W=E(W). Section 6.2 constructs the metric port from actual return, and 9.3.2 supplies the collective spectral port; their preparation and action conditions remain attached to this ungated interface. The resource-gated process of Chapter 4 performs a new common calibration using the complete phase of 4.5.5, with the same spectral energy scale but without applying both bare-drive normalizations together.

6.1 Electroweak Scale

Here the electroweak scale supplies the common energy scale for elementary-state mass readings. It depends on unit addresses distinguishable by the process and the weight on those addresses still participating in the common background response. The calculation must determine resolution depth, bare participation, and effective participation after exchange in sequence, then substitute into the same energy-scale formula.

6.1.1 Resolution Depth of the Electroweak Process

Let k denote the resolution depth used by this process, retaining K for the complete construction depth, with K≥k. For every odd prime p, the unit group at depth k has a Teichmüller decomposition, and the filtration of its principal-unit part is

(ℤ/pkℤ)× ≃ μp−1 × U₁, 　Uj = 1 + pjℤ/pkℤ,
Uk = {1}, 　Uj/Uj+1 ≃ (𝔽p, +)　（1 ≤ j < k）.
(6.1)

The map 1+pʲa↦a mod p gives the final isomorphism: multiplication of two principal units corresponds modulo pʲ⁺¹ to addition of a, and its kernel is exactly the next layer. There are therefore k−1 p-valued layer directions, with pᵏ⁻¹ principal units in total. For a Teichmüller unit ξ, use the power action u↦uξu↦u^{ξ} on principal units, whose action on each layer satisfies

(1 + pja)ξ ≡ 1 + pjξa　mod pj+1.
(6.2)

In this power action, ξ is a finite-precision representative of the corresponding p-adic unit. Since 2j≥j+1, quadratic and higher terms of the binomial expansion vanish in this quotient layer. All layers therefore have the same 𝔽ₚ-linear action, but these finite-field layers do not yet constitute a complex color carrier or automatically give a continuous unitary symmetry mixing the layers.

Adopt the following depth-matching condition: identify the three component labels of the actual color carrier one-to-one with the principal-unit layer labels used, with one component carried by each layer, all three components included, and no extra layer. This correspondence and its actual representation must still be realized as in 5.2. Given this prescription, k−1=3, so the process uses k=4. This choice restricts electroweak participation, while the complete state space may have any K≥4.

At resolution depth k, deeper addresses in the same residue class modulo pᵏ are combined with equal amplitude and phase. Representing this preparation in a deeper K-layer state space, define for every unit address a

|a;k⟩ = p−(K−k)/2∑x≡a (mod pᵏ)|x⟩,
Pk = ∑a∈(ℤ/pᵏℤ)×|a;k⟩⟨a;k|,
rank Pk = φ(pk) = (p − 1)pk−1.
(6.3)

Each sum contains pᴷ⁻ᵏ orthogonal point basis states, and its prefactor normalizes the vector; distinct a have disjoint supports and are therefore orthogonal. The projection PkP_{k} selects one coherent direction in each address fiber, excluding other phase arrangements within the fiber. With this participation range and one unit weight per mode, bare participation is

NEW(0) = Tr P₄ = φ(7⁴) = 6 × 7³ = 2058.(6.4)

Four-layer resolution and equal-amplitude lifting form the participation scheme selected here, and 2058 is its orthogonal-mode count. Equal amplitudes refer to each address fiber internally and do not prescribe equal-amplitude matching of the weak endpoint over all labels. The complete K-layer unit shell contains 6×7ᴷ⁻¹ points; a process participating in all these independent directions uses that count instead. Section 5.2 fixes p, and this section’s depth and lifting scheme further fix the participation range of the electroweak process.

6.1.2 Effective Participation

Weak exchange releases and replenishes some participating modes. The same process forms an occupied preparation and leaves a remainder available for continued background response. In the independent-label preparation of 3.3, χ₃ is a real character of order two, its kernel has 3 elements, and there are 3 species-layer point-pair groups. Combining two orientation alternatives carried by distinct preparations or environments into one class gives c₃=2. The bare matching class has label count

NW = |ker χ₃| m c₃ = 3 × 3 × 2 = 18.
(6.5)

Three independent registers carry these 18 labels. This section uses a role embedding in the same participation space P4P_4 compatible with joint energy and group charge: initial occupation projection PBP_B has rank 18, and release projection Pr≤PBP_r\le P_B rank 3; two replenishment projections P2,P3P_2,P_3 have ranks 1 and 2, are mutually orthogonal, and are orthogonal to PBP_B. All 21 roles lie within P4P_4. This embedding, unit occupation, and 3/1/2 routing belong to the selected participation scheme.

Let wℓ=|Rℓ|2∈[0,1]w_\ell=|R_\ell|^2\in[0,1]. Each role accesses its corresponding fixed spectral probe χ1,χ2,χ3\chi_1,\chi_2,\chi_3, using the complete success and failure outputs of the unit-capacity spectral instrument. A success record controls only an occupation-bit flip, without moving the address: the three release roles leave occupation upon spectral acceptance and remain occupied upon failure; the one and two replenishment roles load upon their respective spectral acceptance and remain empty upon failure. The other 15 roles remain occupied throughout, and all original spectral-failure records are retained. With an orthogonal address reference retained for the uniform address preparation, the occupied output is proportional to

BW=PB−w1Pr+w2P2+w3P3,0≤BW≤P4. \boxed{B_W=P_B-w_1P_r+w_2P_2+w_3P_3,\qquad 0\le B_W\le P_4.} (6.6)

The block occupation weights are respectively 1, 1−w11-w_1, w2w_2, and w3w_3, so positivity and the upper bound hold blockwise, with total occupation Nocc=Tr⁡BW=18−3w1+w2+2w3N_{\mathrm{occ}}=\operatorname{Tr}B_W=18-3w_1+w_2+2w_3. Let Z0Z_0 be the common normalization of the complete address preparation. The unnormalized reduced address outputs for occupation and the remainder within the participation space are BW/Z0B_W/Z_0 and (P4−BW)/Z0(P_4-B_W)/Z_0 respectively; complete spectral records remain in the respective branches, and reference-background addresses are also retained. Total and matching weights thus come from the same actual output.

Fix normalized matching endpoint v∈Ran⁡PBv\in\operatorname{Ran}P_B, unchanged by replenishment modes. After loading, read the weak response with independent or refreshed spectral auxiliaries, and let η=⟨v|Pr|v⟩\eta=\langle v|P_r|v\rangle. Equation (3.38) directly gives

hW=⟨v|BW|v⟩=1−w1η,NWeff=Nocc1−w1η,αW=w3(1−w1η)Nocc. \begin{aligned} h_W&=\langle v|B_W|v\rangle=1-w_1\eta,\\ N_W^{\mathrm{eff}}&=\frac{N_{\mathrm{occ}}}{1-w_1\eta},\qquad \alpha_W=\frac{w_3(1-w_1\eta)}{N_{\mathrm{occ}}}. \end{aligned} (6.7)

The effective denominator requires hW>0h_W>0; the response vanishes when hW=0h_W=0. When w1>0w_1>0, the effective matching denominator equals the occupation trace if and only if Prv=0P_rv=0. One specific coupling structure uses orientation reversal modulo 2 and places the three color-release roles in the intermediate block of a self-loop: Pr=Iu⊗|j0⟩⟨j0|⊗|−o0⟩⟨−o0|P_r=I_u\otimes|j_0\rangle\langle j_0|\otimes|-o_0\rangle\langle-o_0|. Endpoint v=ξ⊗|o0⟩v=\xi\otimes|o_0\rangle is therefore orthogonal to the release space, while ξ\xi may be arbitrarily superposed over kernel and point-pair-group labels. Definite orientation is a sufficient realization of matching preservation here; the general criterion remains Prv=0P_rv=0, with orientation reversal and release location specified by the adopted actual coupling structure.

In this matching-preserving process, release reduces total occupation without weakening endpoint weight, giving

NWeff=Nocc=18−3w1+w2+2w3,wℓ=|L(12,χℓ)ζ(12)|2. \boxed{N_W^{\mathrm{eff}}=N_{\mathrm{occ}}=18-3w_1+w_2+2w_3,}\qquad w_\ell=\left|\frac{L(\tfrac12,\chi_\ell)}{\zeta(\tfrac12)}\right|^2. (6.8)

Equation (6.8) is a finite result under the complete spectral control above, independent of a first-order truncation. Changing the matching endpoint or release location requires returning to Eq. (6.7) and calculating matching weight as well. For example, equal-amplitude matching over all 18 labels gives η=1/6\eta=1/6, so the same denominator cannot be retained. Using the χℓ(3a)=exp⁡(2πiℓa/6)χ_{ℓ}(3^{a})=\exp (2πiℓa/6) convention of 5.2, direct evaluation gives

w₁ = 0.344759924154…, 　w₂ = 0.047561935882…,

The unoccupied branch of the same preparation supplies the background response. Since 0≤BW≤P40\le B_W\le P_4 has been constructed, the remaining participation operator and total weight are

Γvac = P₄ − BW ≥ 0,

All other outputs and rejection flags are retained. = 2039.753821900881….

A noninteger value represents partial occupation of modes. 6.1.3 Evaluation of the Electroweak Scale

Sum the squared bidirectional logarithmic intervals of the complete background using Eq. (2.72), then apply squared-response matching from Eq. (2.74) to obtain the common energy scale:

C* = 2∑n=1∞log²(1 + 1/n) = 1.954378366537873…,
E(W) = E₀√(W/C*) log W　（W > 1）.
(6.13)

This section retains common response coefficient log⁡W\log W and the full logarithmic-spectrum background reference; if finite background CJ*C_J^* is used, the denominator must be changed accordingly, and the two normalizations cannot be mixed within one numerical comparison. Substitute the WvacW_{\mathrm{vac}} obtained here and denote the resulting candidate electroweak scale by vEWv_{\mathrm{EW}}. This gives

vEW/E₀ = √(Wvac/C*) log Wvac
= 246.191373933421…
.(6.14)

Without occupation subtraction, E(2058)/E₀=247.579034659055…; subtracting only the Born-level label count 18 gives E(2040)/E₀=246.210128943076…; including the finite correction above gives electroweak scale E(Wvac)/E0=246.191373933421…E(W_{\mathrm{vac}})/E_{0}=246.191373933421\ldots. All three steps use the same background squared-response constant and energy calibration, isolating the contributions of participation subtraction and finite correction.

With physical calibration E0=1GeVE_0=1\ \mathrm{GeV}, one obtains vEW≃246.1914GeVv_{\mathrm{EW}}\simeq246.1914\ \mathrm{GeV}. This calibration connects dimensionless response to actual time and energy. Chapter 2 gives the common-background relation factgp0/Λ=vEWf_{\mathrm{act}}gp_0/\Lambda=v_{\mathrm{EW}}, with complete timing as in 2.4.6; below we abbreviate v=vEWv=v_{\mathrm{EW}}.

For an independent numerical comparison, the PDG electroweak review gives Fermi constant GF=1.1663785(6)×10−5GeV−2G_{F}=1.1663785(6)×10^{-5} \mathrm{GeV}^{-2}. Its conventional Fermi-scale definition vF=(2GF)−1/2v_{F}=(\sqrt{2}G_{F})^{-1/2} gives vF≈246.21967GeVv_{F}≈246.21967 \mathrm{GeV} (see §10.3.2) 15. With E₀=1 GeV and the above prescription, the difference is

vEW − vF ≃ −0.02830 GeV,
(vEW − vF)/vF ≃ −1.1493 × 10−4 = −0.01149%.
(6.15)

The quantity GFG_{F} defines only the external comparison; E₀ and correction coefficients are specified under the preceding conditions. The bare count 18 gives a relative deviation of approximately −0.00388%; the finite correction lowers the result and does not improve this comparison. No theoretical error bound has yet been established for the participation identification and correction prescription, so numerical proximity does not mean attainment of the experimental precision of GFG_{F} or completion of the weak-interaction correspondence.

Sensitivity of the energy scale to participation follows from its derivative. Fix E₀, C*, and bare participation, and increase estimated occupation by a small amount δNWδN_{W}. Then

δvEW/vEW
= −[1/2 + 1/log Wvac] δNW/Wvac + O((δNW/Wvac)²).
(6.16)

The current values give δvEW≃−0.07619δNWGeV\delta v_{\mathrm{EW}}\simeq-0.07619\,\delta N_W\ \mathrm{GeV}. Changes in participation can thus be converted directly into changes in energy scale; physical estimation error and numerical convergence accuracy are calculated separately. Subsequent masses and couplings share this scale.

6.2 Planck Scale

Participation in metric action covers the entire state space. Unlike the preceding section, which resolves one set of unit-shell modes, this includes all valuation shells and the zero element, weighted by actual responses of the metric process. The common energy-scale formula established in 4.5 calculates the scale associated with this full-space participation; identifying it as the Planck scale additionally retains the physical correspondences for mass sources, spatial readings, and gravitational coupling.

6.2.1 Full-Space Participation and Construction Depth

First fix odd prime pp and finite depth KK. If every orthogonal mode carries one unit of weight in the same response units, both participation projection and weight operator are the identity. Using this chapter’s intrinsic metric constant C* for the full logarithmic spectrum gives bare participation and energy scale

Wmet(0) = Tr Iℋ = pK,
Mmet(0)(p,K) = E₀√(pK/C*) K log p.
(6.17)

Here MmetM_{\mathrm{met}} denotes the metric scale in energy units; it may be read as mass in natural units ℏ=c=1. Although the zero element is absent from the nonzero-address open chain of 4.5, it retains one unit of weight in this full-space participation range. The support of the gradient background and the range of participating modes are specified separately; the open-chain edge count cannot replace pᴷ.

The augmentation ideal of the affine group algebra supplies a configuration space whose dimension must be separately related to address depth. Let Gaff=Aff⁡(𝔽p)G_{\mathrm{aff}}=\operatorname{Aff}(𝔽_{p}), with p(p−1) elements x↦ax+b, a≠0. The augmentation map on the group algebra sums the coefficients of a formal linear combination; its kernel IaugI_{\mathrm{aug}} satisfies

A = 𝔽p[Gaff], 　ε(∑gagg) = ∑gag,
Iaug = ker ε, 　r := dim𝔽ₚIaug = p(p − 1) − 1.
(6.18)

The augmentation map sends every group element to 1, and rank–nullity gives rr. The vectors g−1g-1 after excluding the identity element form a basis, giving prp^r configurations. The comparison using a common source below supplies their actual formation and complete encoding. This paper takes this configuration code as the participating object in the metric process and carries it in the smallest p-adic register capable of distinguishing every configuration: capacity pK≥prp^K\ge p^r gives minimum K=rK=r, which is 41 at p=7p=7. This depth belongs to the configuration code used and does not bound the maximum depth of the entire background.

These configurations can be established explicitly by comparing outgoing and return transport of the same source. Take the translation and scaling generators of the original affine transport, with one p-valued program coordinate in the source for each group element. Comparing two transports of the same source reads coordinate differences; all edge differences remove only the common constant coordinate. The actually distinguishable settings and their dual are therefore

Q=𝔽pGaff/𝔽p𝒋,Q*≃Iaug,NC=|Q|=pp(p−1)−1. \boxed{Q=\mathbb F_p^{G_{\mathrm{aff}}}/\mathbb F_p\mathbf j, \qquad Q^*\simeq I_{\mathrm{aug}},\qquad N_C=|Q|=p^{p(p-1)-1}.} (6.19)

Under the specified coherent uniform source preparation, write comparison outcomes into fresh probe records that no longer couple back, forming edge-difference modes round by round. Connectivity of the graph generated by the two transports ensures that after finitely many rounds every direction in the Fourier basis labeled by IaugI_{\mathrm{aug}} has nonzero occupation probability; continued updating approaches uniformity. Complete encoding uses the distinguishable configuration outputs below. Proofs concerning the multicoordinate source, probe preparation, and destination of records are given in Supplementary Proofs S6.4.1–S6.4.2.

Configuration counts must become event shares through actual matching. A complete edge-difference query encodes different quotient classes as orthogonal outputs; the receiver decodes inversely according to its own setting and detects the ready output, giving

Peq=∑q∈Q|q,q⟩⟨q,q|,pmatch=Tr⁡(ρSRPeq),ρSR=ρS⊗ρR,⟨q|ρS|q⟩=NC−1⇒pmatch=NC−1. \begin{gathered} P_{\mathrm{eq}}=\sum_{q\in Q}|q,q\rangle\langle q,q|,\qquad p_{\mathrm{match}}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{SR}P_{\mathrm{eq}}),\\ \rho_{SR}=\rho_S\otimes\rho_R,\quad \langle q|\rho_S|q\rangle=N_C^{-1} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_{\mathrm{match}}=N_C^{-1}. \end{gathered} (6.20)

Independent uniform preparation gives a one-shot configuration-matching share; correlated inputs use the full matching trace in the first line. The distinction between a finite echo and complete encoding, and the corresponding convergence, are given in Supplementary Proof S6.4.3.

6.2.2 Layer Structure and Participation-Weight Corrections

Full-space participation uses the projective cover P0P_0 and layer weights constructed in 3.5.4. Its radical filtration has p layers: the first and last are trivial characters, and each nontrivial character occurs once in between. At p=7, the labels used in this chapter give S₀, S₁, S₂, S₃, S₄, S₅, S₀ from top to bottom. Here P0P_0 has dimension 7; it and the preceding 41-dimensional comparison space IaugI_{\mathrm{aug}} serve layer counting and configuration comparison, respectively. The node prescription below connects layer labels to complex spectral responses.

Now assign weights by the node prescription of 3.5: use the corresponding positive factor when a CRT coordinate is zero and one when nonzero, then multiply over every nontrivial layer. For p−1=2×3, specify node factors t₂=1/√2 and t₃=3/|ζ(1/2)|. The five layer weights are

(𝒯₁, 𝒯₂, 𝒯₃, 𝒯₄, 𝒯₅)
= (1, 1/√2, 3/|ζ(1/2)|, 1/√2, 1).
(6.21)

Labels 2 and 4 have zero mod-2 coordinate, while label 3 has zero mod-3 coordinate, so t₂ occurs twice and t₃ once. Their product is

ℒ₇ = ∏j=15𝒯j = 3/(2|ζ(1/2)|) = 1.027147854134904784….(6.22)

The layer structure specifies where these nodes occur. For their product to become an actual participation weight, one must also determine input, return, and reference readout within the same process. Here we use return from a common source: the signal retains one coherent endpoint of the binary node, while the reference retains one point of the ternary orbit, with common normalized preparation, actual input coefficient, and spectral-background control.

Specifically, write Z=|ζ(1/2)|Z=|\zeta(1/2)|, with input-address dimension dd. Common isometric preparation CC and retained projections Qs,QrQ_s,Q_r relative to an internal group reference satisfy C†QsC=Id/2C^\dagger Q_sC=I_d/2 and C†QrC=Id/3C^\dagger Q_rC=I_d/3. 𝒮s=Fs†Bs−1Fs=|γ|22cBZId,𝒮r=Fr†Br−1Fr=crefId,cref=|γ|23cB,𝒮scref=32ZId=ℒ7Id. \begin{aligned} \mathcal S_s&=F_s^\dagger B_s^{-1}F_s =\frac{|\gamma|^2}{2c_BZ}I_d,\\ \mathcal S_r&=F_r^\dagger B_r^{-1}F_r=c_{\mathrm{ref}}I_d, \qquad c_{\mathrm{ref}}=\frac{|\gamma|^2}{3c_B},\\ \frac{\mathcal S_s}{c_{\mathrm{ref}}}&=\frac{3}{2Z}I_d=\mathcal L_7I_d . \end{aligned} (6.23)

Using the same single-point reference response as the common participation unit and deploying the same procedure at all d=7Kd=7^K addresses gives

Γmet = ℒ₇ Iℋ, 　Wmet = Tr Γmet = 7Kℒ₇,

Here Γmet\Gamma_{\mathrm{met}} is an unnormalized weight operator in fixed response units and need not be bounded by the identity. The vacuum remainder column and metric return column use the same capacity, drive history, and background action, and one squared-response matching fixes effective strength. Supplementary Proof S6.3 proves this connection and includes the total preparation and control duration. The actual force process after gating is recalibrated once as in 4.5.5; here we retain the common spectral scale. Taking full background Cbg=C*C_{\mathrm{bg}}=C^*, obtain the metric energy scale from Eq. (2.80), then take its inverse square according to Eq. (4.30):

Mmet(K) = E₀√(7Kℒ₇/C*) (K log 7 + log ℒ₇),
GE(K) = C*/[E₀² 7Kℒ₇ (K log 7 + log ℒ₇)²]
= 1/Mmet(K)²
.(6.26)

The layer correction enters both the square root and logarithm. Relative to the bare value at the same K, the exact ratio of energy scales is

Mmet(K)/Mmet(0)(7,K)
= √ℒ₇ [1 + log ℒ₇/(K log 7)].
(6.27)

Now adopt the minimum depth K=41 for the above configurations and calculate with unrounded C* and ℒ₇. The bare mode count and effective weight are

7⁴¹ = 4.456764032636… × 10³⁴,
Wmet = 7⁴¹ℒ₇ = 4.577755612508… × 10³⁴.
(6.28)

These give, respectively,

Mmet(0)(7,41)/E₀ = 1.204792171318… × 10¹⁹,
Mmet(41)/E₀ = 1.221446368809… × 10¹⁹,
E₀²GE(41) = 6.702721805350… × 10⁻³⁹.
(6.29)

With the same physical calibration E₀=1 GeV as in the preceding section, the corrected scale is approximately 1.2214464×10¹⁹ GeV, and GEG_{E} approximately 6.70272×10⁻³⁹ GeV⁻². The layer correction increases the energy scale by about 1.3823%. Replacing the full background with the nonzero open-chain background at the same depth, the bound of 4.5 gives 0<C*−C7K−1*<2/(7K−2)0<C^*-C_{7^K-1}^*<2/(7^K-2), below 4.49×10⁻³⁵ at K=41. This truncation difference is far smaller than the numerical deviation below.

The comparison uses the nonreduced Planck scale, defined in ℏ=c=1 units by MP=GN−1/2M_{P}=G_{N}^{-1/2}; the reduced scale is MP/8πM_{P}/\sqrt{8π}, and the two cannot be interchanged. CODATA 2022 gives Planck-mass energy equivalent 1.220890(14)×10¹⁹ GeV, using gravitational constant GN=6.67430(15)×10−11m3kg−1s−2G_{N}=6.67430(15)×10^{-11} \mathrm{m}^{3}\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2} (see page 1 of the constants table) 18. Calculating the comparison center with this GNG_{N} and exact unit conversions gives, under the conditions of this section,

(Mmet(0) − MP)/MP ≃ −1.3185%,
(Mmet − MP)/MP ≃ +0.04556%,
(GE − GN)/GN ≃ −0.09106%　（ℏ = c = 1）.
(6.30)

The final quantity first converts GNG_{N} to the same natural units; the equivalent SI reading is GE≈6.66822×10−11m3kg−1s−2G_{E}≈6.66822×10^{-11} \mathrm{m}^{3}\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}. Conversion uses GSI=ℏc5/EJ2G_{\mathrm{SI}}=ℏc^{5}/E_{J}^{2}, where EJE_{J} is the metric energy scale in joules. Experimental constants serve as external comparisons; ℒ₇ is determined by the reference procedure above, and E₀ retains the physical calibration. Since MPM_{P} is defined by GNG_{N}, comparing the energy scale and gravitational constant gives two forms of the same test, not independent observational constraints.

The layer correction improves the central-value comparison, but the deviation still exceeds the experimental relative uncertainty of GNG_{N}, and no combined theoretical error bound has yet been established for layer weights, depth, and the common energy scale. Section 4.5.5 derives the leading field strength of the active process from positive-source preparation, actual return, and complete timing, and states the calibration condition equating it with the inverse spectral square here. When participation changes, both the square root and logarithm must be updated.

Relative to the electroweak scale, the common E₀ and C* cancel, giving a hierarchy relation independent of the absolute unit:

Mmet(41)/vEW
= √(7⁴¹ℒ₇/Wvac) log(7⁴¹ℒ₇)/log Wvac
= 4.961369479745… × 10¹⁶.
(6.31)

This hierarchy mainly comes from the enormous difference between the two participation ranges: electroweak evaluation uses effective weights on four-layer unit addresses, whereas metric evaluation in this example uses full-space weights at 41 layers. The factor ℒ₇ supplies only a finite correction. Holding the layer factor fixed while increasing depth by one gives exactly

Mmet(K + 1)/Mmet(K)
= √7 [1 + log 7/(K log 7 + log ℒ₇)],
Mmet(42)/Mmet(41) = 2.710260172825….
(6.32)

A one-layer depth change is much larger than the layer-weight correction here, showing the dominant role of participation range in the energy-scale hierarchy. The next scale concerns the full-space constant-function pattern bb, whose collective participation is determined by spectral preparation.

6.3 Nucleon Scale

The nucleon scale is established using the collective-pattern mass reading of 2.5. The spectral weight of collective participation determines its energy scale, while internal color structure restricts allowed representations. We first find the number of fundamental color representations in the minimal color singlet, then adopt the corresponding spectral preparation, and finally substitute the sum of positive weights into the common energy-scale formula.

6.3.1 Minimal Color Singlet

Suppose the actual color carrier has been realized as Vc=ℂdcV_c=\mathbb C^{d_c} (dc≥2d_c\ge2) according to 5.2, with color acting in the fundamental representation of SU(dc)SU(d_c). Consider the tensor product Vc⊗nV_c^{\otimes n} of n such representations and require the color part of the collective state to be invariant under every color action. Here n counts fundamental-color-representation tensor factors; their interpretation as a particular internal projection of the collective state still requires actual formation and readout. Tensor notation alone does not establish a bound state of several independent particles.

The counting condition for a color singlet follows directly. Central element exp⁡(2πi/dc)I\exp (2πi/d_{c})I acts on n tensor factors as exp⁡(2πin/dc)\exp (2πin/d_{c}), so a nonzero invariant vector requires dcd_{c} to divide n. Conversely, the fully antisymmetric tensor in dcd_{c} fundamental representations is multiplied by det g=1 under g; taking products of these tensors in groups gives an invariant vector in every n=dcrn=d_{c} r. Hence

(Vc⊗n)SU(dc) ≠ {0}　⇔　dc ∣ n, 　n ≥ 1.
(6.33)

At the minimum n=dcn=d_{c}, this invariant subspace is exactly one-dimensional. Diagonal color transformations require every color label to occur once, so an invariant tensor can contain only permutations of all labels. Applying an SU(2) mixing of any two colors further requires the coefficient to change sign when those labels are exchanged. All coefficients are thus fixed by one coefficient, yielding the fully antisymmetric tensor. With unit normalization,

|εdc⟩ = (dc!)−1/2 ∑σ∈Sdcsgn(σ)|σ(1), …, σ(dc)⟩,
g⊗dc|εdc⟩ = |εdc⟩　（g ∈ SU(dc)）.
(6.34)

In the candidate matter correspondence at p=7, dc=3d_{c}=3, so the minimal nonempty color singlet has n=3 and color part εabcε^{abc}. This does not require three distinct species labels; color indices are carried separately from species, spatial, and spin indices. Identifying specific matter additionally requires specifying the remaining parts and checking statistics and maintenance conditions for the complete state.

This minimality applies only to tensor products of the same fundamental color representation. If conjugate representations are included, Vc⊗V¯cV_{c}⊗\overline{V}_{c} already contains a singlet corresponding to the identity matrix, a different internal representation class. For the three-dimensional fundamental representation alone, allowed n are 3, 6, 9, …; n=4 and 5 fail the necessary color-singlet condition above. If higher excitations use those integers as labels, the degrees of freedom being counted must be specified separately.

6.3.2 Nucleon Spectral Preparation

Color structure fixes the minimal internal representation but has not yet fixed collective participation weight. Following 2.5, use the logarithmic spectrum indexed by positive integers Hlog|j⟩=log⁡j|j⟩H_{\mathrm{log}}\vert j\rangle =\log j\vert j\rangle as the evaluation reference, fixing the energy zero at j=1. Denote spectral cutoff by L, separately from address depth K. The corresponding positive weights, normalized shares, and infinite sum are

ZL(β) = ∑j=1Lj−β, 　wj,L(β) = j−β/ZL(β),
ZL(β) → ζ(β)　（β > 1, L → ∞）.
(6.35)

The complete logarithmic spectrum indexed by positive integers and its ζ partition function for β>1 are standard structures in BC quantum statistics 19. Here β is the dimensionless parameter of this spectral preparation. The shell generator HKH_{K} has its own shell energies and degeneracies, so the two partition sums cannot be equated merely by using the same temperature-parameter name. The full-space constant-function pattern b satisfies Tjb=bT_{j}b=b for every multiplicative pullback; consequently the unnormalized response ∑jj−βTj\sum _{j} j^{-β}T_{j} gives ZL(β)Z_{L}(β) on b. Only upon adopting the participation correspondence of 2.5 do we take WB=ZL(β)W_{B}=Z_{L}(β) and, for the infinite spectral reference, WB=ζ(β)W_{B}=ζ(β). The trivial unit-shell direction excludes multiples of p and has a response different from this full integer sum.

Averaging over these normalized spectral shares and differentiating ZLZ_{L} directly gives the mean and variance of logarithmic energy:

⟨Hlog⟩β,L = −∂βlog ZL,
VL(β) := Varβ,L(Hlog) = ∂β²log ZL.
(6.36)

The first expression sums weighted log j, and another derivative gives ⟨Hlog2⟩−⟨Hlog⟩2\langle H_{\mathrm{log}}^{2}\rangle -\langle H_{\mathrm{log}}\rangle ^{2}. For β>1, logarithmic moments of every order converge locally uniformly, so the infinite sum can be differentiated in the same way. If E0HlogE_{0}H_{\mathrm{log}} is taken as physical energy, its variance has an additional factor E₀²; below we use dimensionless V. The Laurent expansion of ζ near β=1 gives

V(β) = ∂β²log ζ(β)
= 1/(β − 1)² − 2γ₁ − γ² + O(β − 1)　（β → 1⁺）.
(6.37)

Here γ is Euler’s constant and γ₁ is defined by ζ(1+u)=1/u+γ−γ₁u+O(u²). Expanding log ζ as −log u+γu+(−γ₁−γ²/2)u²+O(u³) and differentiating twice gives the formula. For fixed finite L, ZLZ_{L} is finite at β=1 and has no such pole.

The collective spectral preparation adopts this parameter condition: for collective evaluation with n fundamental-color-representation factors, choose β by setting the leading term of the infinite-spectrum variance equal to n. This connects the number of fundamental color factors to spectral preparation and is an evaluation rule independent of the color-singlet condition. On the β>1 side, it gives

1/(β − 1)² = n　⇒　β(n) = 1 + 1/√n,
βB = 1 + 1/√3
.(6.38)

This equation follows neither from Gibbs shares nor from the color-singlet requirement alone, and it is not equivalent to the exact condition V(β)=n. Here βB−1≈0.5774β_{B}-1≈0.5774, outside a limit arbitrarily close to the pole. We therefore use it as the prescribed leading-term rule and separately examine its difference from the exact variance.

6.3.3 Nucleon Scale and Approximation Range

For the minimal nonempty color singlet made solely of fundamental color representations, n=3, with the above β prescription and complete spectral participation, the unrounded parameter and total weight are

βB = 1.577350269189…, 　WB = ζ(βB) = 2.349636114511….
(6.39)

Continue using the same intrinsic metric constant C* and common energy calibration E₀, substitute into the collective energy-scale formula of 2.5, and denote the resulting candidate nucleon scale by MBM_{B}:

MB/E₀ = √[ζ(1 + 1/√3)/C*] log ζ(1 + 1/√3)
= 0.936669312626…
.(6.40)

With E₀=1 GeV, this gives MB≈936.6693MeVM_{B}≈936.6693 \mathrm{MeV}, the overall scale of collective participation. Sections 9.1 and 9.3 give collective-pattern formation, complete return, and calibration using a common source, making the rest-frame phase of the specified carrier satisfy −τBMB-τ_{B}M_{B}; τBτ_{B} counts the actual total elapsed duration. This conditional realization connects the spectral evaluation here to mass while retaining its port, protection, and calibration assumptions.

Using proton mass for this comparison, CODATA 2022 gives mass energy equivalent mpc2=938.27208943(29)MeVm_{p} c^{2}=938.27208943(29) \mathrm{MeV} (see page 3 of the constants table) 18. Under the above conditions, the difference is

MB − mp ≃ −1.60278 MeV,
(MB − mp)/mp ≃ −0.17082%　（c = 1）.
(6.41)

This number is determined by spectral-preparation parameter βBβ_{B}, participation weight, background, and physical calibration E₀, with proton mass serving as an independent comparison. Splitting between nucleon species and other internal readings depend on the corresponding matter structures. Numerical precision and the accuracy of the participation and β prescriptions must be evaluated separately.

At the same β_B, the exact variance is V(β_B)=2.860214657918…, approximately 4.6595% below 3. This confirms that the prescription used is the leading-term one; the deviation cannot directly serve as a mass error bar. Comparisons with alternative prescriptions and finite spectral cutoffs are given in Supplementary Proof S11.

Within the allowed family containing only fundamental color representations and retaining the above β prescription and common calibration, the energy scale increases with factor count n, so n=3 gives the lowest scale. Subsequent stability is determined by the actual return and exit processes of Chapter 9.

Electroweak, metric, and nucleon scales thus share the same background-matching function. Their differences come respectively from remaining unit-shell weight, full-space participation with node weights, and collective spectral preparation, rather than separate energy units for each class. Their participation ranges, spectral preparations, and physical correspondences determine applicability; subsequent couplings and masses are calculated using these scales.

Chapter 7. Force Coupling Constants

Exchange between stable states depends both on their respective spectral responses and on the share of the input preparation that can enter the common endpoint. When the background and environment participate, intermediate processes also modify the matching share at the endpoint. The coupling strength must therefore be read from the relationship among the spectral response, the actual preparation, and the complete output.

Chapter 3 established the operator relations among these quantities. This chapter adopts the p=7p=7 channel and physical identifications of Chapter 5 and evaluates them using the common energy scale of Chapter 6. The spectral response is denoted by RℓR_\ell, and the response ratio obtained through endpoint matching by αi\alpha_i. Converting the latter into an event probability or a record rate per unit time still requires the normalization of the actual instrument and the elapsed duration of the cycle.

7.1 Vertex Spectral Response

The same stable state can participate in exchange through different endpoints. Its spectral response describes the propagation coefficient in the selected direction; endpoint selection and the preparation share determine how much of it enters the actual process. We first determine this common spectral factor RℓR_\ell. In this chapter, the spectral parameter s*s_* retained in Chapter 3 is set to s0=1/2s_0=1/2 following Supplementary Proof S5.1.

7.1.1 Spectral Weights

When a spectral weight enters a coherent amplitude, the square root of the probability weight is used. Taking the logarithmic spectrum Hlog|n⟩=log⁡n|n⟩H_{\mathrm{log}}|n\rangle=\log n|n\rangle as a reference, the normalized thermal preparation at a given β\beta, within a finite cutoff LL, and its standard purification are

ρβ,L = ZL(β)−1∑n=1Ln−β|n⟩⟨n|,
|Ωβ,L⟩ = ZL(β)−1/2∑n=1Ln−β/2|n⟩ ⊗ |n⟩.
(7.1)

Taking the partial trace over the second factor recovers ρβ,L\rho_{\beta,L}. Thus the probability weight n−βn^{-\beta} corresponds to the unnormalized amplitude modulus n−β/2n^{-\beta/2}. This relation fixes the modulus; the relative phases also depend on the auxiliary preparation and actual paths. Here β\beta belongs to the logarithmic-spectrum preparation and is defined separately from the thermal parameter of the shell generator HKH_K.

This chapter adopts the exponent s0=1/2s_0=1/2 corresponding to the critical parameter β=1\beta=1. This vertex spectral prescription is used together with the relative phases, reference, and actual exchange. The preparation at finite LL remains normalizable, whereas the partition sum over the infinite logarithmic spectrum diverges at this parameter.

Accordingly, this chapter retains the following vertex spectral prescription and denotes its squared response by wℓw_{ℓ}:

s₀ = 1/2, 　Rℓ = L(s₀, χℓ)/ζ(s₀), 　wℓ = |Rℓ|²
.(7.2)

Here ζ(s0)\zeta(s_0) is the common analytic spectral reference: ζ(1/2)<0\zeta(1/2)<0, which differs from the partition sum of a finite positive thermal preparation. Equation (7.2) gives the directional response to be realized. The actual success block must still be constructed using a complete spectral instrument, with all other outputs retained.

Fix the generator 3, label the six characters by χℓ(3a)=exp⁡(2πiℓa/6)χ_{ℓ}(3^{a})=\exp (2πiℓa/6), and extend them by zero on multiples of 7. 7.2 Born-Level Couplings

Once the spectral instrument supplies the directional response, the strength of exchange still depends on matching the preparation to the endpoint. An equal-weight input is distributed over several independent labels, whereas the selected endpoint accepts only one normalized direction, producing a matching share. Section 3.3 expressed this share as a trace in label space; here we calculate its denominator for p=7p=7. Born level means that corrections from virtual processes have not yet been included.

A force’s transfer label and its participating direction are used separately. For an endpoint transition from ℓ to ℓ′, the channel character is χℓ′−ℓχ_{ℓ′-ℓ}, expressing the species difference that the environment must balance. The vertex spectral factor RℓR_{ℓ} instead uses the response of the participating stable state. Under the candidate physical identifications in Section 5.2, color channels transfer along the modulo-3 coordinate and weak channels along the modulo-2 coordinate; electromagnetic relative phases are implemented separately through the actual charges and reference. Spectral evaluations use χ₁/χ₅, χ₂/χ₄, and χ₃ as the representative responses for color, electromagnetic, and weak vertices, respectively.

The correspondence between these representative responses and physical interactions follows Section 5.2: the color, weak, and charge readings of matter must be implemented jointly by the complete representation, exchange vertices, and readout. The overall U(1)U(1) of the species layer gives a common phase within a fixed sector; the charges of different stable states use their respective charge representations. The following counts are made under this correspondence.

For the species-layer unit group G=𝔽₇×, take m=3 opposite-point-pair groups. Let dℓ=ord⁡χℓd_{ℓ}=\operatorname{ord} χ_{ℓ}. The preimage of a phase class is a coset of ker⁡χℓ\ker χ_{ℓ}, giving 6/dℓ6/d_{ℓ} relative group actions. There are m alternatives for the point-pair group; if χℓχ_{ℓ} is self-conjugate, the classification also includes two orientation alternatives. The factor 2 for the weak direction corresponds to two orientations carried by different preparations or environmental alternatives. For example, take Mi=κiRℓi|fi⟩⟨vi|M_i=\kappa_iR_{\ell_i}|f_i\rangle\langle v_i| and complete the remaining outputs when κi2wℓi≤1\kappa_i^2w_{\ell_i}\le1. The Born preparation then gives pi(0)=κi2αi(0)p_i^{(0)}=\kappa_i^2\alpha_i^{(0)}. When several outcome types share one round, the contraction condition applies to the total effect. The spectral response, matching share, and instrument calibration thus jointly determine the actual events.

Here αi(0)\alpha_i^{(0)} is the Born response under the label preparation. The representative electromagnetic direction gives precisely αEM(0)=w2/6=wsp\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}^{(0)}=w_2/6=w_{\mathrm{sp}}, equal to the single-address reading at formation. The two arise from label matching and address projection, respectively, and each retains its own complete channels and records. The persistent port of Section 3.1.2 can feed this value into the exchange angle and then read the exchange probability through its squared sine. Virtual processes use the Born value here as input; the corrected response is denoted by αi\alpha_i.

7.3 Virtual-Process Corrections

An intermediate process can preserve the vertex spectral response while changing the preparation reaching the endpoint and its matching share. Following Section 3.4, let the unnormalized positive preparation be Γi≥0\Gamma_i\ge0 and the matching weight at the endpoint be hi=⟨vi|Γi|vi⟩>0h_i=\langle v_i|\Gamma_i|v_i\rangle>0. The effective denominator is then Nieff=Tr⁡Γi/hiN_i^{\mathrm{eff}}=\operatorname{Tr}\Gamma_i/h_i. It compares the total preparation weight with the accepted weight, so the following corrections act on the matching share without requiring a change to RℓiR_{\ell_i}.

7.3.1 Effective-Denominator Corrections

The three representative characters for p=7 satisfy χ₁²=χ₂, χ₂²=χ₄=χ̄₂, and χ₃²=χ₀. If the composition of two actions carrying the same charge is nonzero, its composite charge is χ². Thus the color and electromagnetic representatives are Type I, and the weak representative is Type II. The trivial character here only states that the composite charge is zero; by itself, it selects neither a particular background state nor a neutral return path.

For Type I, take the connected background contribution to be V0=w3V_0=w_3 and the total contribution of the two endpoint enhancements to be 2wℓ2w_\ell. If the connected contribution arises from the variance of an actual background operator BB, this correspondence requires the background preparation to satisfy ⟨B†B⟩−|⟨B⟩|2=w3\langle B^\dagger B\rangle-|\langle B\rangle|^2=w_3. This defines the connected quantity. Merely naming R0−w3R_0-w_3 the disconnected part and subtracting it does not determine that variance.

In the first-order expansion of Eq. (3.41), these rules correspond to γi−Nigi=V0−2wℓiγ_{i}-N_{i} g_{i}=V_{0}-2w_{ℓ_{i}}. Using this shift to form the finitely corrected denominator according to Eq. (3.42) then gives

Nseff = 3 + w₃ − 2w₁ = 2.926928119541…,
NEMeff = 6 + w₃ − 2w₂ = 6.521324096085….
(7.12)

The shift for the color direction is approximately −0.07307, increasing the matching share; that for the electromagnetic direction is approximately +0.52132, decreasing the matching share. These signs follow from comparing the specific response values and are not predetermined by the Type I label.

For the Type II weak direction, specify three color contributions that reduce the denominator, together with one electromagnetic contribution and two self-conjugate weak contributions that increase it. One contribution w₁ or w₂ here uses the weight of the selected representative direction, or equivalently the normalized average of the conjugate pair. Actually summing two orthogonal conjugate outputs with equal responses would give 2w rather than w. The actual routing, orthogonality, and weights of these three terms must satisfy the conditions in Section 3.4. Character multiplication determines the allowed charge destinations, while the coefficients −3, +1, and +2 belong to this routing prescription. Substitution of these coefficients and the same set of w into Eq. (3.44) gives

NWeff = 18 − 3w₁ + w₂ + 2w₃
= 18.246178099119…
.(7.13)

The complete occupation process in Section 6.1.2 already realizes this finite denominator. For the positive occupation output in Eq. (6.6), when the released subspace is orthogonal to the matching direction, the weight subtracted by release does not diminish the endpoint matching weight. Equation (6.7) then gives Eq. (7.13). The weak coupling and background remainder are determined by the same output. If the actual endpoint overlaps the released subspace, the matching weight and background remainder must still be calculated separately from that same output.

7.3.2 Higher-Order Electromagnetic Corrections

An intermediate electromagnetic excursion passes through the conjugate direction and returns to the original port. When the returning part reenters the same intermediate action, it produces a nested response. Whether the contributions combine coherently depends on whether the complete final state retains an excursion record; the distinction between two orientation labels alone cannot decide this. We give a coherent static realization that retains all spectral auxiliaries and uses explicit port connections. Its insertion order and the actual termination-round count described in Section 3.4.3 are calculated separately.

Denote the Born inputs by e=αEM(0)=w2/6e=\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}^{(0)}=w_2/6 and u=αW(0)=w3/18u=\alpha_W^{(0)}=w_3/18. Distribute the first-order net shift equally among the six electromagnetic labels. At second order, assign weights along the routing of two weak returns and one conjugate return of fixed orientation, obtaining

x=3u−2e=w3−2w26,y=e(2u+e),r=yx,x=0.086887349348…,r=0.006972132346…. \begin{gathered} x=3u-2e=\frac{w_3-2w_2}{6},\qquad y=e(2u+e),\qquad r=\frac yx,\\ x=0.086887349348\ldots,\qquad r=0.006972132346\ldots . \end{gathered} (7.14)

These multiplicities are retained as routing conditions. xx is the net response shift, and yy is the second-order weight; neither directly defines a continuation or termination probability. To place them in the same persistent action, use two independent electromagnetic spectral auxiliary units and one weak spectral auxiliary unit. All purification auxiliaries are coherently accessible and are prepared only once, before the entire intermediate process begins. Denote the complete spectral action of each unit by UiU_i and its acceptance projection by Πi\Pi_i. The acceptance projection checks both spectral success and rank-one matching in label space, with the equal-weight label preparation of Section 7.2. The ready-state expectations of the pulled-back projections Qi=Ui†ΠiUiQ_i=U_i^\dagger\Pi_iU_i are therefore e,e,ue,e,u, respectively. The actual intermediate action neither reads these flags nor discards the other spectral outputs.

Let the common ready state be ss and the preparation code projection be Pc=Icarrier⊗|s⟩⟨s|P_c=I_{\mathrm{carrier}}\otimes|s\rangle\langle s|. Following the simultaneous equal-strength arms of Chapter 2, apply reflection averaging to the joint operator:

A0=3QW−2QEa,A1=2QEaQW+QEaQEb,Sc=2Pc−I,Φc(A)=12(A+ScASc),X̂=Φc(A0),Ŷ=Φc(A1),X̂Pc=xPc,ŶPc=yPc. \begin{aligned} A_0&=3Q_W-2Q_{E_a},\qquad A_1=2Q_{E_a}Q_W+Q_{E_a}Q_{E_b},\\ S_c&=2P_c-I,\qquad \Phi_c(A)=\tfrac12(A+S_cAS_c),\\ \widehat X&=\Phi_c(A_0),\quad \widehat Y=\Phi_c(A_1),\qquad \widehat X P_c=xP_c,\quad \widehat YP_c=yP_c. \end{aligned} (7.15)

Projections on different spectral auxiliary units commute. Independent preparation gives ⟨A0⟩s=x\langle A_0\rangle_s=x and ⟨A1⟩s=y\langle A_1\rangle_s=y. Moreover, because Φc(A)=PcAPc+(I−Pc)A(I−Pc)\Phi_c(A)=P_cAP_c+(I-P_c)A(I-P_c), the code subspace decouples from its complement. The expression above therefore preserves the same preparation for every insertion order and depth, while the output space outside the code remains fully retained.

Between a neutral, equal-energy external port aa and virtual port bb, use the same X̂\widehat X as the round-trip vertex and take the virtual-port self-term to be −X̂−Ŷ-\widehat X-\widehat Y. The complete self-adjoint generator and its restriction to the code are

HJ/g=(|a⟩⟨b|+|b⟩⟨a|)⊗X̂−|b⟩⟨b|⊗(X̂+Ŷ),HJ/g|code=(0xx−(x+y)),g>0. \begin{aligned} H_J/g&=(|a\rangle\langle b|+|b\rangle\langle a|)\otimes\widehat X -|b\rangle\langle b|\otimes(\widehat X+\widehat Y),\\ \left.H_J/g\right|_{\mathrm{code}} &=\begin{pmatrix}0&x\\x&-(x+y)\end{pmatrix},\qquad g>0. \end{aligned} (7.16)

The matrix within the code omits the identity factor on the spectator carrier. The same-vertex connection, virtual-port self-term, and controllable preparation code are conditions on the action in this realization. Fix the amplitude of the driven external port at aa. The zero-frequency virtual-port equation is 0=xa−(x+y)b0=xa-(x+y)b, and the returned contribution is xbxb. Eliminating the virtual port gives

D(0)=x2x+y=x1+r,D(0)=∑n=0∞x(−r)n(|r|<1). \boxed{D(0)=\frac{x^2}{x+y}=\frac{x}{1+r},\qquad D(0)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x(-r)^n\quad(|r|<1).} (7.17)

At nonzero frequency ν=ω/g\nu=\omega/g, the same elimination gives D(ν)=x2/(ν+x+y)D(\nu)=x^2/(\nu+x+y), with static window |ν|≪x+y|\nu|\ll x+y. This is a driven response, with physical self-energy gDgD. Undriven unitary evolution can still oscillate; waiting a long time does not automatically produce a zero-frequency static state. These results make the all-order coefficients consequences of this joint generator.

Under the effective-path interpretation of Section 3.4.4, identify the returned contribution with the denominator shift for six labels. Then δNn=6x(−r)n\delta N_n=6x(-r)^n, and the original denominator is

NEMfull = 6 + ∑j=0∞δNj = 6 + (w₃ − 2w₂)/(1 + r)
= 6.517714521921…
.(7.18)

The shift from the first J+1J+1 terms is 6x[1−(−r)J+1]/(1+r)6x[1-(-r)^{J+1}]/(1+r), and the remainder tends to zero when |r|<1|r|<1. Equation (7.18) has the same all-order structure as the static response. Reading this response as an actual coupling additionally requires the same positive preparation to satisfy Tr⁡Γ/h=6+6D\operatorname{Tr}\Gamma/h=6+6D. Recorded termination histories still contribute nonnegative probabilities according to Eq. (3.47); the alternating insertion terms are not treated as round-by-round event probabilities.

For the color and weak directions, take Nsfull=NseffN_s^{\mathrm{full}}=N_s^{\mathrm{eff}} and NWfull=NWeffN_W^{\mathrm{full}}=N_W^{\mathrm{eff}}. The weak denominator is supplied by the complete occupation process above, while the color direction retains the stated finite-correction prescription. More general round-trip actions must be evaluated from their respective complete outputs. Electromagnetic resummation acts only on the virtual-process shift and leaves the Born-level denominator 6 unchanged.

7.3.3 Corrected Preparations

Coupling normalization compares the total and matching weights of the same output. For the weak process, the complete spectral control in Section 6.1.2 already gives BWB_W. When matching is preserved, using BW/Tr⁡BWB_W/\operatorname{Tr}B_W yields Eq. (7.13). The electromagnetic process uses the six-label projection PP, a rank-two projection Rd≤PR_d\le P onto two excluded modes, and a background mode PbP_b orthogonal to them. K+=P−w2Rd+Pb,L+=w2Rd,K−=P,L−=Pb,K±†K±+L±†L±=Ipool. \begin{aligned} K_+&=\sqrt{P-w_2R_d}+P_b,&L_+&=\sqrt{w_2R_d},\\ K_-&=P,&L_-&=P_b,\\ K_\pm^\dagger K_\pm+L_\pm^\dagger L_\pm&=I_{\mathrm{pool}}.&& \end{aligned} (7.19)

Negative corrections appear only in the difference between two positive preparations.

To give a fully normalized conditional realization, take the squared amplitudes of two terminal transfers to correspond to x,yx,y and use a common interaction strength. This is an additional physical identification at the terminal stage. Introduce a neutral, equal-energy three-state record |0⟩,|+⟩,|−⟩|0\rangle,|+\rangle,|-\rangle independent of the virtual port, and on the invariant preparation code above use

CR=x|+⟩⟨0|+y|−⟩⟨0|,HR=igR(CR−CR†),θ=gRtRx+y,sR=sin⁡2θ>0,p+=sRxx+y,p−=sRyx+y,p0=1−sR. \begin{gathered} C_R=\sqrt{x}|+\rangle\langle0|+\sqrt{y}|-\rangle\langle0|, \qquad H_R=i g_R(C_R-C_R^\dagger),\\ \theta=g_Rt_R\sqrt{x+y},\quad s_R=\sin^2\theta>0,\qquad p_+=\frac{s_Rx}{x+y},\quad p_-=\frac{s_Ry}{x+y},\quad p_0=1-s_R. \end{gathered} (7.20)

Starting from record state |0⟩|0\rangle, HRH_R couples only to the bright direction (x|+⟩+y|−⟩)/x+y(\sqrt{x}|+\rangle+\sqrt{y}|-\rangle)/\sqrt{x+y}. The matrix exponential directly gives the three probabilities above. The record is generated at the boundary after the entire virtual process. ++ and −- control the two filtering paths, respectively, while 0 produces no delivery. Combining the retained outcomes of the two orthogonal records, the actual unnormalized output is

Γkeep=sR6+w3(P+xx+yBEM),Tr⁡Γkeep⟨vm|Γkeep|vm⟩=6+6x2x+y=NEMfull. \boxed{\begin{aligned} \Gamma_{\mathrm{keep}} &=\frac{s_R}{6+w_3}\left(P+\frac{x}{x+y}B_{\mathrm{EM}}\right),\\ \frac{\operatorname{Tr}\Gamma_{\mathrm{keep}}} {\langle v_m|\Gamma_{\mathrm{keep}}|v_m\rangle} &=6+\frac{6x^2}{x+y}=N_{\mathrm{EM}}^{\mathrm{full}}. \end{aligned}} (7.21)

The expression in parentheses equals [x(P+BEM)+yP]/(x+y)[x(P+B_{\mathrm{EM}})+yP]/(x+y) and is therefore positive. The matching weight is sR/(6+w3)s_R/(6+w_3), and the total weight is 6+6x2/(x+y)6+6x^2/(x+y) times that matching weight. Thus the same output supplies the preparation, matching, and αEM=w2/NEMfull\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}=w_2/N_{\mathrm{EM}}^{\mathrm{full}} together. The probabilities of all retained outcomes, excluded outcomes, and record 0 sum to 1. When a common survival factor preserves this complete output, it cancels in the conditional ratio. The actual count rate still includes the total elapsed duration of preparation, action, failure, and readout.

The complete filtering process above also permits finite repetition: each round uses the same instrument, history records remain orthogonal and never recouple, and the continuation process does not access the independently prepared auxiliary system before filtering. Only the first terminal outcome triggers filtering, while every other exit and cutoff outcome is retained. Denote the two terminal effects by E+,E−E_+,E_-. The local condition for preserving the same delivery ratio for every input is

yE+=xE−,NL=6+6x2x+y. \boxed{yE_+=xE_-,\qquad N_L=6+\frac{6x^2}{x+y}.} (7.22)

The common continuation process may change the internal state; the relation between the two effects ensures preservation of the ratio. See Supplementary Proof S8 for the proof. The three-state terminal stage in this section actually realizes this relation. It does not read the virtual port and yields the same output even after HJH_J is removed. Thus identifying this Born normalization with the static return of the preceding section still requires the original virtual process to generate the terminal effects used here. This physical identification is retained explicitly at this point.

The color direction continues to retain the finite prescription in Eq. (7.12). Once the three responses are connected to the fixed instrument of Section 7.2, their conditional event shares are all pi=κi2αip_i=\kappa_i^2\alpha_i, with the spectral vertices and calibration conditions retained.

7.4 Numerical Values of the Elementary Resonance Forces

The three elementary resonance forces share the same spectral point and background reference; their differences arise from the participating directions and endpoint matching. The weak denominator uses the matching-preserving occupation output of Section 6.1.2. The electromagnetic denominator uses the conditional realization under the static response and terminal identification described in Section 7.3. The color direction retains the finite-correction prescription. Taking traces with unrounded spectral values under the same spectral vertices gives

αs = w₁/(3 + w₃ − 2w₁),
αEM = w₂/[6 + (w₃ − 2w₂)/(1 + r)],
αW = w₃/(18 − 3w₁ + w₂ + 2w₃)
.(7.23)

The usual reference value for the color coupling has an energy scale and a renormalization scheme. External numerical values are used only for comparison and do not enter the spectral weights, label counts, or virtual-process corrections. The common structure of the three results is a directional response multiplied by a matching share. Precise comparison with experimental quantities additionally depends on the scale, scheme, and normalization corresponding to the actual process.

7.6 The Metric Force Constant

The metric force is transmitted through the background. Equation (4.26) obtains the actual leading-order strength from source writing, background transport, and the passive carrier’s maintenance response. Equation (6.26), following the common-source return, common amplitude, and single background calibration of Section 6.2, gives the metric energy scale from WK=7Kℒ7W_K=7^K\mathcal L_7. Taking the inverse square of the energy scale according to Eq. (4.30), and retaining the complete background C*C^* used for the numerical values in this section, we have in units of ℏ=c=1\hbar=c=1

GE(K) := Mmet(K)−2 = C*/[E₀²WK(log WK)²],
WK = 7Kℒ₇
.(7.29)

GEG_E has units of inverse energy squared. At mass scale mm, the dimensionless gravitational strength is GEm2G_Em^2. This section retains the single physical calibration of Section 4.5.5, using the inverse square of the spectral energy scale as the leading Newtonian strength of the process under consideration. Each realization uses its own return kernel and complete-cycle timing; finite-source and propagation corrections are calculated as in Section 4.5.6.

Taking the conditional parameters K=41 and E₀=1 GeV, with the complete background and node weights of Section 6.2, gives

GE = 6.702721805351 × 10−39 GeV−2,
Mmet = 1.221446368810 × 1019 GeV.
(7.30)

Compared in the same units with the CODATA 2022 Newton constant, the relative difference is approximately −0.0910582% (CODATA 2022 table of constants) 18. The difference is calculated from the SI value of G using exact unit conversion and still exceeds the cited measurement uncertainty. A small relative difference alone therefore does not establish agreement within experimental precision. The Planck energy scale and GEG_{E} are related by an inverse square by definition, so their proximity provides only the same single comparison.

Retaining general K also allows the dependence of this result to be checked directly. The coupling ratio between adjacent depths is

GE(K + 1)/GE(K)
= (1/7)[log WK/(log WK + log 7)]², 　GE ∝ E₀−2.
(7.31)

The construction depth K and energy calibration E₀ determine this dependence of the metric force constant. Within their respective required participating spaces, the three elementary couplings follow from species-layer spectral ratios and label denominators, and nuclear exchange from affine-channel weights. None of these formulas uses K=41. The metric depth can therefore be tested as a separate physical input while the other couplings continue to be evaluated from their respective processes.

Elementary resonance-force couplings are jointly determined by directional spectral responses and endpoint matching shares. Collective exchange additionally sums distinguishable outputs, while metric action connects the background participation energy scale to the actual field strength. These quantities enter the same dynamical description through their respective preparations, exchanges, and readouts. Chapter 8 continues to use the relevant spectral responses in the mass processes of each family, distinguishing Born-level from corrected inputs according to the actual mode of coupling.

Chapter 8. Elementary-State Mass Spectrum

Why do elementary states in the same background exhibit both mass hierarchies within families and scale differences between families? Formation first leaves a coherent pattern, after which excitations flow out, exchange, and return along their respective paths. Branches that persist yield frequencies read against the same phase reference. The common background supplies the energy calibration; paths and nodes determine the coefficients of actual exchange, while projections of the pattern onto the different endpoint groups distinguish some branches within a family. Mass differences arise from combining these actions in the same persistent process.

This chapter adopts the physical identifications for p=7p=7 in Chapter 5, the background energy scale vv in Chapter 6, and the spectral responses in Chapter 7. The complete preparations, persistent actions, and calibration using a common source constructed in Chapter 2 connect each family’s path response to its mass reading. We determine the paths, nodes, records, and return mechanisms of the respective families below. Finite-link truncation and feedback tails are given with each realization.

8.1 Phases and Generational Factors

The even conjugate directions χ₂ and χ₄ form a common part of several formation paths. The modulus of the same complex spectral value enters the path scale, while its phase changes the pattern formed by their superposition with the background. Three endpoint groups assign different intensities to this pattern, providing one source of mass relations across generations. Phase modification during formation and frequency shifts during maintenance act on the pattern and cycle reading, respectively, and must be calculated against the same phase reference.

8.1.1 Spectral Phase

Fix the generator 3 and character convention χ2(3a)=e2πia/3\chi_2(3^a)=e^{2\pi ia/3} of Section 7.1, and write L2=L(1/2,χ2)L_2=L(1/2,\chi_2). χ2\chi_2 is an even primitive character, with conjugate χ4\chi_4. This phase can also be related to finite Gauss and Jacobi sums. We use the standard definitions and product relations over finite fields 23. Extending the characters by zero at the zero element, define

8.1.3 Cycle Frequency Shifts

Formation modification determines the pattern produced, while maintenance causes that pattern to accumulate phase persistently. Under the persistent repair of Section 2.3.7, the spectral round trip conjugates the entire feedback process, driving the source toward the same Φδ\Phi_\delta. The formation angle does not accumulate from round to round. Insertions during maintenance change the phase accumulated by each branch per round and thereby enter the frequency reading.

By Eq. (2.64), eigenvalues of the actual persistent generator give masses after complete time accounting. Once the pattern enters the persistent action, path spectral responses and node overlaps determine the family coefficient AfA_f, generational factors Genf,j\mathrm{Gen}_{f,j} distinguish branches in the same family, and the common background supplies the energy scale vv. If different paths are used within one physical family, their AfA_f must be calculated separately.

Following the complete time accounting and negative-argument convention of Eq. (2.60)–Eq. The superscript (0)(0) excludes only the maintenance frequency shift; the source already includes formation modification. Dividing the actual accumulated phase by the complete cycle period, calibration using a common source gives

Mf,j=Bf,j−κf,jτf,j′,Bf,j=tHμf,j(0)=τf,j′vAfGenf,j. M_{f,j}=\frac{B_{f,j}-\kappa_{f,j}}{\tau^{\prime}_{f,j}},\qquad B_{f,j}=t_H\mu_{f,j}^{(0)}=\tau^{\prime}_{f,j}vA_f\,\mathrm{Gen}_{f,j}. (8.12)

(2.59), independent modification auxiliaries give the joint correlation term CX,A=0C_{X,A}=0. Under the same spectral normalization a=αeffa=\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}, the generator acquires a proportional correction, so κf,j=Bf,jαeff\kappa_{f,j}=B_{f,j}\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}. Writing the common frequency-shift factor as F:=1−αeffF:=1-\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}, charged branches that use this maintenance insertion and satisfy the factorization and path conditions above have

Mf,j = vAf Genf,j(1−αeff)
1−αeff = 0.992109289737287….
(8.13)

For branches with the same path coefficient, common period, and relative frequency shift, the overall factor cancels from mass ratios. If the branch identification is Genf,j=𝜚j\mathrm{Gen}_{f,j}=\varrho_j, then

Mf,j/Mf,0 = Genf,j/Genf,0 = ϱj,

Formation modification enters the mass baseline through the source pattern, while maintenance insertions change its persistent phase rate. Each family’s masses then follow from its paths, nodes, and branch actions. Formation and thermal-survival shares govern formation convergence and the survival envelope, respectively; active intervals, waiting, and inverse operations are timed together as in Section 2.4.6.

8.2 Charged Leptons

Charged-lepton formation selects the even conjugate directions χ₂ and χ₄. They are in phase under negation but have different phases across the three observation units of the species layer. The same family therefore has both a common formation scale and three distinct group readings. Under the physical identifications of Chapter 5, χ₂ is the representative and χ₄ supplies the conjugate orientation. Under the branch identification of Section 8.1, groups 0, 1, and 2 correspond to τ, μ, and e, respectively.

8.2.1 Conjugate Lepton Paths

Use the double excursion of Section 2.4.2: connect from the zero element to the χ₂ direction, pass through its spectral response, and return; then connect to χ₄ and return again. The intermediate zero element serves only as a connection and inserts no additional spectral response. Since the spectral point used is real, L₄=L̄₂. The two excursions preserve the specified conjugate connection, with spectral product L₂L₄. Applying a closed-path intensity readout to this complete component gives

a₂₄ = L₂L₄ = |L₂|²,
Sℓ = |a₂₄|² = |L₂|⁴ = 0.0102885039752424….
(8.15)

The closed-path readout takes the squared modulus of the complete spectral product of both excursions, yielding the lepton path’s spectral intensity. Through the node exchange and same-group matching of Sections 2.4.1–2.4.4, this intensity enters the generator; calibration using a common source in Section 2.5.3 then cancels the common capacity. Re L₂, read by directional diagonal averaging, is a different response.

In this chapter set β=π/8\beta=\pi/8. For the node preparation nβn_\beta of Section 2.4.3, the two-way exchange has compression coefficient ηN=2cos⁡βsin⁡β=1/2\eta_N=2\cos\beta\sin\beta=1/\sqrt2. The three group readings were already normalized together in Section 8.1; the node coefficient is supplied separately by this exchange and counted once. Combining it with the closed-path spectral quantity in the persistent action gives the family coefficient and generational factors:

Aℓ=|L2|42,Genℓ,j=𝜚j,(j=0,1,2). A_\ell=\frac{|L_2|^4}{\sqrt2},\qquad \mathrm{Gen}_{\ell,j}=\varrho_j,\qquad (j=0,1,2). (8.16)

The node exchange compression coefficient 1/21/\sqrt2 enters AℓA_\ell, and the relative intensity 𝜚j\varrho_j after same-group matching enters the generational factor; each is counted once. The phase per round enters τ′v\tau'v according to Eq. (8.12), where τ′\tau' is the complete cycle period. Node and generational factors must be recalculated if the endpoints or the source’s relative background amplitude change.

8.2.2 Masses of Three Generations

The three branches use a common period and the frequency-shift factor FF of Section 8.1. Multiplying their respective 𝜚j\varrho_j by the common path factor, node factor, and background energy scale gives the three absolute masses. Using 𝜚0=1\varrho_0=1, write them as

mτ = v|L₂|⁴√2F, 　F = 1−αeff,
mμ = mτϱ₁, 　me = mτϱ₂
.(8.17)

With the E₀=1 GeV calibration of Section 6.1, calculation using unrounded v, L₂, and the three group readings gives

mτ = 1776.926974… MeV,
mμ = 105.6553711… MeV,
me = 0.5110122512… MeV.
(8.18)

The τ reading sets the reference scale for this preparation. The μ and e masses differ through the intensities of the same coherent pattern at the other two endpoint groups. Group 2 in particular is near cancellation, so a small phase change can substantially change its relative intensity. The significant digits of the electron mass are therefore limited not only by numerical precision but also by the accuracy of the formation phase and relative background amplitude. Comparisons with experiment and the common spectral-shape relation are collected in Section 8.6.

8.3 Down-Type Quarks

The common down-type process connects the even conjugate round trip to the real-direction response. The source pattern left by formation determines whether the return continues, and a continued visit changes color retrieval. The link direction further distinguishes persistent responses within one group. We derive the mass matrix from this complete return and identify its b, s, and d modules using the matter correspondence of Chapter 5.

8.3.1 Propagation Paths of Down-Type Quarks

Character multiplication gives χ2χ3=χ5\chi_2\chi_3=\chi_5. The return makes one node visit in the source reference group. The remaining groups continue after the first visit succeeds, using the same two-port node without resetting it between visits. For the node success action 𝖠=FNK3+FN†K3†\mathsf A=F_NK_3+F_N^\dagger K_3^\dagger, the original normal spectral kernel gives 𝖠2=INK3†K3\mathsf A^2=I_NK_3^\dagger K_3. Complete output columns are given in Supplementary Proof S16.3.
