8.4 Up-Type Quarks

The representative up-type quark direction χ1\chi_1 has CRT coordinates (1,1)(1,1) and satisfies χ4χ3=χ1\chi_4\chi_3=\chi_1. Its path contains a closed combination of even, real, and odd directions. The three branches share its spectral and node coefficients: cc uses the reference readout, tt accumulates closed returns, and uu takes a single weak-channel delivery after a flip.

8.4.1 Spectral Factor of the Closed Path

The even and odd directions each make one conjugate double excursion, joined by a visit to the real direction. Contributions with the same net group action are first combined coherently, and one complete-path acceptance effect is then read at the common capacity: each conjugate pair leaves a fourth spectral power, and the real direction leaves L32L_3^2. The entrance uses the binary node of Section 8.2, counting its exchange compression once. Both CRT coordinates at the endpoint are nonzero; no background reference or terminal color sum is added. Denote the common path coefficient of the entire up-type family by AuA_u, where the subscript uu here denotes the up-type family. Then

χ₂χ₃χ₁ = χ₀,
Su = |L₂|⁴L₃²|L₁|⁴, 　Au = Su/√2.
(8.26)

Chapter 9. Baryons, Quarks, and Color Confinement

Baryon formation requires internal color components to enter a whole pattern together and to continue maintaining that whole after exchange. Nucleons have both a common collective scale and distinguishable charge, species, and spin readings. To place these properties in one state, we must specify what the full-space mode carries, what the internal representation carries, and how the cycle preserves both simultaneously.

Retaining the p=7p=7 identification of Chapter 5, the complete nucleon object consists of the common mode bb and internal color, species, and spin states. Cross-shell coherence specifies the whole pattern, the internal representation distinguishes proton from neutron, and the actual return determines both phase and survival. We use this object to calculate the common scale, internal mass difference, and exchange response, then test whether a colored component can become an independent output.

9.1 Collective Baryon Structure

A nucleon’s integrity is first expressed by its participating components jointly producing one maintainable pattern. The full-space vector b of Chapter 2 provides a candidate form of such collective participation. It is invariant under all multiplicative pullbacks and gives every address the same amplitude. These addresses label modes in state space; position in observational spacetime is still determined by the corresponding readout. Participation of every address does not directly specify the nucleon’s spatial size.

9.1.1 The Full-Space Collective Pattern

First retain an arbitrary finite depth K≥1. Write d=pKd=p^{K}, with normalized shell-average states eje_{j} and shares hj=|Sj|/dh_{j}=\vert S_{j}\vert /d. The common pattern and its shell expansion are

b = 1√d∑x∈XK|x⟩ = ∑j=0K√hj ej,
hj = |Sj|/d, 　∑jhj = 1.
(9.1)

For the multiplicative pullback (Tnf)(x)=f(nx)(T_{n} f)(x)=f(nx), a constant function clearly satisfies Tnb=bT_{n} b=b. Conversely, if f is fixed by every TnT_{n}, then in particular Tpf=fT_{p} f=f. Repeating K times gives f(x)=f(pKx)=f(0)f(x)=f(p^{K}x)=f(0). Thus the common fixed space is exactly one-dimensional:

⋂n≥1 ker(Tn−I) = span{b}
.(9.2)

Invariance under all multiplications includes cross-shell scaling, and TpT_{p} alone already determines the unique direction above. Invariance under the unit group alone permits different constant values on different shells; the fixed space remains 𝒞=span⁡{e0,…,eK}𝒞=\operatorname{span}\{e_{0},\ldots ,e_{K}\}, of dimension K+1. The unit-shell average state e₀ belongs to 𝒞 but differs from b. Cross-shell action links the independent shell constants, leaving the same full-space pattern.

TnT_{n} describes the arithmetic response structure here. When p divides n, it is generally not unitary. The common fixed-point property of all TnT_{n} determines the arithmetic structure of b. Formation and maintenance of this pattern in the actual cycle still require examination of the joint action of formation exchange, coherent retrieval, and background restoration, as well as establishment of the required coherence between shells.

In b, all shell phases are aligned to the same reference. Writing the mode density operator as ρ, the matrix element between shells j and ℓ can be tested through two self-adjoint observables:

Ajℓ = |ej⟩⟨eℓ|＋|eℓ⟩⟨ej|,
Bjℓ = i(|ej⟩⟨eℓ|−|eℓ⟩⟨ej|), 　j<ℓ.
(9.3)

Their expectations are 2ℜ⟨ej|ρ|eℓ⟩2\Re \langle e_{j}\vert ρ\vert e_{ℓ}\rangle and 2ℑ⟨ej|ρ|eℓ⟩2\Im \langle e_{j}\vert ρ\vert e_{ℓ}\rangle, respectively. For b, the former is 2hjhℓ2\sqrt{h_{j}h_{ℓ}} and the latter zero; for the shell-dephased background σhshσ_{h}^{\mathrm{sh}}, both vanish. The shell shares are identical, but the cross-shell response still distinguishes these preparations. Actually making this distinction requires a joint readout realizing these operators and retention of the phase reference used.

9.1.2 Internal Degrees of Freedom of Collective States

The common pattern b occupies only one ray. A single pure-state ray cannot distinguish proton from neutron; their difference must be represented by internal states and the corresponding observables. The color part may share one singlet, while the remaining species, spin, and associated spatial parts must be organized according to the complete representation.

To clarify this organization, distinguish the mode factor ℋKℋ_{K} from the internal factor ℋintℋ_{\mathrm{int}} in the specified joint carrier, and denote the normalized joint state by ΩBΩ_{B}. This tensor decomposition differs from the direct-sum decomposition into shell-average and direction spaces. It is a condition of the physical identification, requiring the existing color, species, and other degrees of freedom to be implemented in actual carriers and actions. The fixed-vector property of b does not itself construct this decomposition. If the reduced mode state equals PbP_{b} exactly, the complete state must have

TrintΩB = Pb　⇔　ΩB = Pb⊗σB,
σB ≥ 0, 　Tr σB = 1
.(9.4)

Let Qb=(I−Pb)⊗IQ_{b}=(I-P_{b})⊗I. By positivity, Tr⁡(QbΩB)=‖QbΩB1/2‖HS2=0\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{b}Ω_{B})=\Vert Q_{b}Ω_{B}^{1/2}\Vert ^{2}_{\mathrm{HS}}=0 forces ΩBΩ_{B} to be supported on span⁡{b}⊗ℋint\operatorname{span}\{b\}⊗ℋ_{\mathrm{int}}, so the normalized state must be Pb⊗σBP_{b}⊗σ_{B}. The converse follows by taking the partial trace.

The internal state may be entangled or mixed. If the mode and internal factors are nontrivially entangled, the mode marginal is no longer PbP_{b} and must be calculated from the complete joint state.

In this representation, the expectation of a mode observable O is determined by the common pattern, whereas that of an internal observable E is determined by the internal preparation:

Tr[ΩB(O⊗I)] = ⟨b|O|b⟩,
Tr[ΩB(I⊗E)] = Tr(σBE).
(9.5)

Different internal states σAσ_{A} and σCσ_{C} can produce different internal responses while preserving the same mode readings. Proton and neutron labels must therefore be accompanied by concrete internal states and distinguishable readouts. Error-free distinction in a single measurement requires orthogonal supports, and the actual instrument must give definite and different outcomes on those supports. For necessity and sufficiency over the complete measurement class, see Supplementary Proof S4.1. The one-dimensionality of the common pattern does not determine the number of particle species.

In the candidate nucleon identification, this division of roles allows a common collective scale to coexist with an internal mass difference: overall participation uses the same mode structure, while internal responses vary with species and exchange paths. A common mode does not require the complete generator to act only on the mode factor, and therefore does not require two internal states to have identical cycle phases. Specific charge and color readings can be calculated only after the corresponding internal representations have been fixed.

9.1.3 Cross-Shell Coherence

Following the common-final-state criterion of Section 2.5.4, formation must preserve the relative phases of the shells within one collective pattern. For a normalized joint component,

|Ψ⟩ = ∑j=0K|ej⟩⊗|ξj⟩, 　∑j‖ξj‖² = 1,
ρmode = ∑j,ℓ⟨ξℓ|ξj⟩|ej⟩⟨eℓ|.
(9.6)

Actually producing PbP_b requires precisely

ρmode = Pb　⇔　ξj = √hj ξ,
0≤j≤K, 　‖ξ‖ = 1
.(9.7)

Then Ψ=b⊗ξ\Psi=b\otimes\xi, while the internal factor and remaining environment may still be correlated. If formation has several outcomes, the total formation share sums mutually exclusive outcomes satisfying this criterion. Orthogonal records of different shells yield only mixed restoration, as explained in Section 2.5.4.

This common final state has a finite energy-conserving realization. Take an isospectral reference copy of the shell-average space, set HRejR=EjejRH_Re_j^R=E_je_j^R, and prepare bR=∑jhjejRb_R=\sum_j\sqrt{h_j}e_j^R. Swap the two shell-average spaces while bypassing the direction space:

UR(ej⊗ekR)=ek⊗ejR,[UR,HK+HR]=0,UR(c⊗bR)=b⊗cR. U_R(e_j\otimes e_k^R)=e_k\otimes e_j^R,\qquad [U_R,H_K+H_R]=0,\qquad U_R(c\otimes b_R)=b\otimes c_R. (9.8)

The joint energy before and after the swap is Ej+EkE_j+E_k. Both reference and shell-average states carry trivial group charge, so group charge is also balanced. Retaining color, flavor, spin, and spectator correlations in the internal factor, and tracing out the reference, gives

(ℛ⊗Id)(ρ𝒞,int)=Pb⊗Tr⁡𝒞ρ𝒞,int. \boxed{(\mathcal R\otimes\mathrm{Id})(\rho_{\mathcal C,\mathrm{int}})=P_b\otimes\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal C}\rho_{\mathcal C,\mathrm{int}}.} (9.9)

This swap works for any input supported on the shell-average space, including its entanglement with the internal factor: the original mode information enters the reference output, the internal marginal is preserved, and the cross-shell coherence of bRb_R is transferred completely to the collective pattern. Thus with a coherent reference bRb_R, collective formation already has a finite energy-conserving realization. A mixed reference with the same occupations instead produces the corresponding mixed state.

After formation, the reference is generally cRc_R and must actually be prepared anew, or the swap must stop; it cannot immediately be reused unchanged. If both ends already contain bb and bRb_R, the swap returns both ends together. A bare HKH_K free segment still changes relative shell phases, so the persistent action must next be connected to the same pattern. The internal representation and readout are carried by the same internal state below.

9.2 Baryon Quantum Numbers

The collective pattern supplies the common mode structure, while the internal color singlet determines which color components can form a whole invariant under changes of color reference. Nucleons must also have definite flavor and spin readings. Writing these parts as one candidate state allows their transformation properties to be checked directly, without inferring internal structure from a name.

9.2.1 The Three-Color Singlet

Use the color carrier Vc=ℂ3V_{c}=ℂ^{3} specified in Sections 5.2 and 6.3, with the fundamental SU(3) representation U as the color action. The species-space action I₂⊗U of Section 5.2.3 and U and U⊗U⊗U here are representations of the same abstract group on different carriers. The complete matter representation must still embed color-singlet, three-dimensional, and conjugate carriers into the established construction compatibly with species labels, physical charges, and exchange vertices. In the specified three copies of the fundamental representation, the normalized singlet is

|ε₃⟩ = 1√6∑a,b,c=13εabc|a,b,c⟩,
U⊗3|ε₃⟩ = det(U)|ε₃⟩ = |ε₃⟩.
(9.10)

The completely antisymmetric tensor uses each distinct label once among the three color indices. It spans the top exterior power of the fundamental representation, on which the action is the determinant representation and hence trivial under the special unitary group 27. Section 6.3 proved that the SU(3)-invariant subspace of three fundamental representations is precisely this ray. One or two fundamental representations have no singlet, and allowed nonzero numbers of copies are positive multiples of 3. This result is restricted to the representation used and does not exclude a two-factor singlet formed from a fundamental and a conjugate representation.

Neutrality of the cyclic grading is a weaker condition. Averaging only over the cyclic subgroup of order three tests whether the gradings sum to zero. For example, gradings 1 and 2 sum to zero but still cannot form an SU(3) singlet in Vc⊗VcV_{c}⊗V_{c}. A full color singlet must be tested against all color actions. Antisymmetry of the three copies follows from this invariant representation, without yet invoking Fermi statistics.

The three tensor positions here label the three factors of the internal representation. The color singlet determines only the color part; flavor, spin, and spatial parts must be organized separately. Having one of each color does not require three distinct flavor labels, so it is compatible with both uud and udd but does not by itself select these combinations.

9.2.2 Flavor and Spin Structure

Quark flavor names and fractional charges follow the usual quark-model conventions 28. We now give an explicit carrier for the internal nucleon readings. Take the internal flavor space span⁡{u,d}\operatorname{span}\{u,d\} spanned by u and d, with charges 2/3 and −1/3 as adopted in Section 5.2. Independently take the two-dimensional SU(2) representation for spin, with basis ↑, ↓ and ℏ=1. The spin representation and fermionic exchange rule here are conditions of the physical identification; they do not follow from the binary CRT label alone.

On the three tensor positions, two normalized vectors with total spin projection +1/2 can be chosen as

ηρ = |↑↓↑⟩−|↓↑↑⟩√2,
ηλ = 2|↑↑↓⟩−|↑↓↑⟩−|↓↑↑⟩√6.
(9.11)

These vectors are orthogonal and both satisfy Szη=η/2S_{z}η=η/2 and S+η=0S_{+}η=0. Using S2=S−S++Sz(Sz+1)S^{2}=S_{-}S_{+}+S_{z}(S_{z}+1) gives S²η=3η/4, so they indeed belong to spin-1/2 representations. Use the same permutation forms for the two flavor combinations:

φp,ρ = |udu⟩−|duu⟩√2,
φp,λ = 2|uud⟩−|udu⟩−|duu⟩√6,
φn,a = φp,a│u↔d, 　a=ρ,λ.
(9.12)

Every flavor component of the proton candidate contains two u and one d; the neutron candidate has the reverse composition. Here ρ and λ label only two permutation vectors and are unrelated to the thermal density operator or the flip parameter of Chapter 8. Let

ΦN,↑ = φN,ρ⊗ηρ＋φN,λ⊗ηλ√2, 　N=p,n.
(9.13)

When two flavor positions and their corresponding spin positions are exchanged together, both sets of ρ and λ vectors transform by the same real orthogonal matrix, leaving the inner-product combination above invariant. This uses the two-dimensional representation of the permutation group on three positions and its invariant tensor-product pairing 29. Specifically, exchanging the first two positions gives diag(−1,1), and exchanging the last two gives the matrix below; together they generate every permutation of the three positions:

D₂₃ = 1/2√3/2√3/2−1/2, 　D₂₃TD₂₃ = I₂,
PπΦN,↑ = ΦN,↑, 　π∈S₃.
(9.14)

Provided the common mode b transforms trivially under permutations of these three internal positions and the remaining spatial part is symmetric, normalized candidate states can be written as follows, omitting the additional symmetric spatial factor:

|BN,↑⟩ = b⊗|ε₃⟩⊗ΦN,↑, 　N=p,n
.(9.15)

Under simultaneous permutation of the three internal positions, the color part acquires the permutation sign while the flavor–spin part remains invariant. The complete internal state is therefore antisymmetric and satisfies the specified fermionic exchange rule. If the spatial part has another permutation type, the flavor–spin part must change accordingly. This construction proves the existence of compatible candidate states in the given representations. Their actual preparation and cycle maintenance must still be checked as in Sections 9.1 and 9.3.

9.2.3 Charge Structure

Write the charge operator on flavor space as q=diag(2/3,−1/3). The total charge of the three internal readings is the sum of its actions at the three positions. Since every candidate vector has fixed numbers of u and d,

Q = q⊗I⊗I＋I⊗q⊗I＋I⊗I⊗q,
QΦp,↑ = Φp,↑, 　QΦn,↑ = 0
.(9.16)

Q acts as the identity on spin, color, and the common mode. An overall color singlet can therefore simultaneously have nonzero charge; the two conditions act on different representations. The relation of flavor labels u and d to the directions χ₁ and χ₅ of Chapter 8 still uses the physical identifications of Section 5.2. Character labels alone do not automatically produce this additive charge operator.

The reduced color state at any one position is I₃/3. This follows by tracing the ε tensor term by term: each color appears in exactly two nonzero permutations, and off-diagonal terms vanish. For the globally pure color-singlet preparation here, the reduced mixed state reflects internal correlations. A local reading obtained by an internal projection does not mean that the corresponding component has separated from the whole and become an independently maintainable output.

9.3 Total Mass and Maintenance

Collective nucleon participation and internal actions jointly enter persistent evolution. Relative to the same background reference, collective participation supplies a reference frequency shared by both nucleons, while internal actions give their branches different phases. Return and exit shares determine survival of the original excitation. Mass and survival are read from the phase and return share of the same complete cycle, respectively.

9.3.1 Collective Mass Scale

Using the complete logarithmic spectrum, prescription based on the leading term of the variance, and common-background matching of Section 6.3, the lowest singlet of three fundamental color representations uses βB=1+1/3β_{B}=1+1/\sqrt{3}. By Eq. (6.40), its participation and common energy scale are

WB = ζ(βB), 　E₀ = 1 GeV,
MB = E₀√(WB/C*) log WB
= 936.669312626… MeV.
(9.17)

This value inherits the spectral preparation and approximation conditions of Section 6.3. βBβ_{B} uses the prescription that the leading term of the variance equals 3; an exact variance condition would give a different value. Finite address depth, the cutoff on the positive-integer labels, and the full ζ sum have separate definitions and do not automatically coincide because the same collective pattern is used.

Mass reads the phase slope of the returning branch relative to the common reference. As in Eq. (2.60)–Eq. (2.61), the physical duration τBτ_{B} of one round includes all processing and waiting. φNφ_{N} is the single-branch phase relative to the calibrated zero, unwrapped continuously along the evolution. If the total beat phase between two symmetric orientation branches is read, it must first be halved. Writing the common scale and internal frequency shifts within this candidate subspace gives

mN = −φN/τB,
φN = −τB(MB＋δN), 　N=p,n.
(9.18)

δNδ_{N} contains the internal response relative to the common reference. Actual mass readout must retain coherence with an internal clock or another branch; a pure-state projection alone does not display a common phase. The collective-mass identification here requires MBM_{B} to become the actual persistent frequency of pattern b. Color invariance and a constant pattern determine only state structure; frequency also depends on the action maintaining it.

Under this identification, uud and udd specify internal charge and flavor content, while the common collective energy scale is supplied by the participation weights of Section 6.3. Comparing component masses, interaction energy, and total mass requires a decomposition of the same generator and its expectation values. Binding properties likewise require an explicit description of components and interactions.

9.3.2 Maintenance Frequency and Collective Mass

The outward and return parts of the spectral path must both generate phase and preserve the common mode b and its internal color state. Maintenance must therefore cover the complete mode, port, and internal carrier, so that participation weights enter actual exchange matrix elements. The frequencies generated by these matrix elements are then compared with the background response in the same process.

Let Jbψ=b⊗ψJ_b\psi=b\otimes\psi, where ψ\psi includes all ports and internal degrees of freedom; identity actions on internal factors are omitted. Following Eq. (2.39)–Eq. Equation (9.20) preserves pattern bb throughout the outward and return paths, while the ports and internal states evolve under XBX_B. Simultaneous protection covering every port promotes the compressed matrix elements to a complete intertwining relation. The specified port coherence, common coefficient log⁡ZL\log Z_L, and path amplitudes wn\sqrt{w_n} jointly give the dimensionless eigenvalue rBr_B on the bright subspace. Nonunitary pullbacks are realized here as matrix elements of a self-adjoint action; required energy compensation or control work is included as in Section 4.4.3.

Couple gÂBg\widehat A_B to the existing self-adjoint unitary orientation operator QQ and prepare the positive bright branch. Target displacement leaves the mode bb, path ports, and color singlet as spectators, and the velocity orientation anticommutes with QQ. The shared motion port therefore gives grBQ+2ωZDxgr_BQ+2\omega ZD_x on the complete carrier. The dispersion during a constant active segment is E±(k)=±g2rB2+4ω2sin⁡2(kℓx)E_\pm(k)=\pm\sqrt{g^2r_B^2+4\omega^2\sin^2(k\ell_x)}, and the rest mass reads the half-gap grBgr_B between the two orientation branches. The negative bright and dark branches remain part of the complete space; selecting a positive bright preparation does not exclude the other states.

Thermal processing uses isospectral temporary storage as in Section 4.4.3. The entire mode, path ports, and internally correlated state must be stored, not just bb. Let 𝒞B\mathcal C_B be the space to be stored, aRa_R the copy’s entrance state, and gauxg_{\mathrm{aux}} the processing-auxiliary preparation. On success, the inverse swap returns the original carrier, and every outcome satisfies

Kη(ψ𝒞B,int⊗aR⊗gaux)=rηψ𝒞B,int⊗aR⊗gaux. \boxed{K_\eta(\psi_{\mathcal C_B,\mathrm{int}}\otimes a_R\otimes g_{\mathrm{aux}}) =\sqrt{r_\eta}\,\psi_{\mathcal C_B,\mathrm{int}}\otimes a_R\otimes g_{\mathrm{aux}}.} (9.21)

Successful copies and auxiliaries proved to be reversible can be reused; thermal outputs and history records remain retained. On failure, the stored state exits together with the output and is not reused as a new preparation. Active evolution, storage, thermal processing, the inverse swap, and free-phase compensation all count toward elapsed time. Processing segments accumulate no additional phase, or that phase is compensated by actual control.

(2.77), this section calibrates the vacuum endpoint with the actual background frequency νref,h=g‾hrvac\nu_{{\mathrm{ref}},h}=\bar g_hr_{\mathrm{vac}}. For a positive drive,

∑nΩn,h2E02=Wvaclog⁡2Wvac⇒g‾h=E0Cbg,mB,h=E0ZLCbglog⁡ZL. \begin{gathered} \frac{\sum_n\Omega_{n,h}^2}{E_0^2} =W_{\mathrm{vac}}\log^2W_{\mathrm{vac}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar g_h=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{bg}}}},\\ \boxed{m_{B,h}=E_0\sqrt{\frac{Z_L}{C_{\mathrm{bg}}}}\log Z_L.} \end{gathered} (9.23)

(9.23) to the common nucleon energy scale in Eq. (9.17). Finite-truncation differences remain treated as in Section 6.3. This connection places the common mode’s participation weights, actual maintenance phase, and common nucleon mass within one process.

9.3.3 Stability Conditions

Complete thermal return ensures conditional evolution of the selected carrier; absolute stability additionally requires examination of every exit outcome. Under the general criteria of Chapter 2 and Section 11.5, after fixing the environmental preparation, a candidate BB should satisfy RrB=crBR_rB=c_rB, DsB=0D_sB=0, and ∑r|cr|2=1\sum_r|c_r|^2=1. If only collinear return and sB=∑r|cr|2<1s_B=\sum_r|c_r|^2<1 hold, the continuous-survival share under independent cycles with the same preparation is sBms_B^m. State-dependent or memory-dependent exits require composition of the actual survival subchannels. The common frequency in this section does not by itself determine nucleon lifetimes.

A vanishing diagonal response of the common pattern does not mean it cannot exchange with directional excitations. For example, take a nontrivial-direction vertex whose endpoint is the terminal shell, with normalized unit-shell vector ψχψ_{χ}. Then

Vχ = |eK⟩⟨ψχ̄|−χ(−1)|ψχ⟩⟨eK|,
⟨b|Vχ|b⟩ = 0, 　Vχb = −χ(−1)p−K/2ψχ ≠ 0.
(9.24)

The first expression is the mode-side vertex; a conserving complete exchange must also include environmental charge. Character orthogonality makes the diagonal element vanish, but the zero-element share gives a nonzero component leaving the original pattern. Protecting the candidate state requires these components to cancel in the actual action, be excluded conditionally by the selected channel, or restore the original pattern through subsequent retrieval.

The collective energy scale of Section 6.3 increases with the allowed number of fundamental color factors in a singlet, showing only that three fundamental representations are lowest within that family. Complete final states may involve other internal representations, different particle numbers, or environmental outputs. Only excluding every actual exit channel allowed by joint conservation and energy conditions can make sBs_{B} exactly one. The “lowest three-color singlet” alone cannot prove absolute proton stability; nor can the sign of the mass difference alone determine the lifetime of an allowed neutron-to-proton conversion.

Both nucleons can therefore share the lowest collective scale while having different internal frequency shifts and return shares. The mass difference and maintenance duration test the phase and exit parts of the complete cycle, respectively, and must be calculated on the same internal states.

9.4 The Neutron–Proton Mass Difference

The proton and neutron candidates use the same b and color singlet, with their difference residing in the flavor–spin part. Subtracting the common baseline from both masses isolates the internal phase and electromagnetic response. Under the stated evaluation identification, these terms have opposite signs and produce a mass difference far smaller than the common nucleon energy scale.

9.4.1 Nucleon Spectral Phase

Retain the generator 3 and χ₁, χ₅ conventions of Section 7.1, but evaluate at the nucleon spectral point βBβ_{B} rather than the elementary-state point 1/2. Termwise conjugation and absolute convergence of βB>1β_{B}>1 give L(βB,χ5)=L¯(βB,χ1)L(β_{B},χ_{5})=\overline{L}(β_{B},χ_{1}). Denote the present principal argument by θ. Numerically,

L(βB,χ₁) = 0.869968720699…＋0.298172012211…i,
θ = arg L(βB,χ₁) = 0.330191432349…,
tan θ = 0.342738773379….
(9.25)

The present spectral value lies in the right half-plane, and the conjugate direction has principal phase −θ. Conjugacy here means complex conjugation of spectral data, not a particle–antiparticle identification. Specify multiplication of component spectral responses along the complete coherent connection. Every uud permutation contains two L₁ and one L₅, and every udd permutation the reverse. The permutation superposition of Section 9.2 therefore leaves this total phase unchanged:

ap = L₁²L₅ = |L₁|²L₁, 　an = L₁L₅² = āp,
Θp = +θ, 　Θn = −θ, 　Lk := L(βB,χk).
(9.26)

The two responses have equal moduli and real parts. Nucleon splitting therefore reads the conjugation-odd part relative to the same reference; below, their opposite phases are used for the mass identification.

9.4.2 Nucleon Mass Corrections

Adopt the phase–mass prescription δN(L)=−(MB2/v)tan⁡ΘN\delta_N^{(L)}=-(M_B^2/v)\tan\Theta_N, with vv taken from the electroweak energy scale. This function, sign, and scale constitute the physical identification used in this section; the conjugate spectra determine phase antisymmetry. Substitution gives

δp(L) = −(MB²/v)tan θ, 　δn(L) = +(MB²/v)tan θ,
Δm(L) = 2MB² tan θ/v
.(9.27)

For the electromagnetic term, independently adopt a self-energy-difference prescription equally divided among six paths: the charged branch gains αEMMB/6α_{\mathrm{EM}} M_{B}/6 relative to the neutral branch. αEMα_{\mathrm{EM}} uses the complete response of Section 7.4, and the factor 6 is the independently specified number of equally weighted paths. Thus

δp(EM)−δn(EM) = αEMMB/6,
Δm(EM) = −αEMMB/6
.(9.28)

This term specifies the electromagnetic difference; denote the common shift by δ0\delta_0. The independent equal division among six paths and the matching denominator of αEM=w2/NEMfull\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}=w_2/N_{\mathrm{EM}}^{\mathrm{full}} jointly give the total denominator 6NEMfull6N_{\mathrm{EM}}^{\mathrm{full}}.

Both terms use the same energy reference and compatible effective generators. When free mass readout preserves charge, off-diagonal elements between the proton and neutron branches vanish. Writing all undetermined common shifts as δ₀ gives

mp = MB＋δ₀−(MB²/v)tan θ＋αEMMB/6,
mn = MB＋δ₀＋(MB²/v)tan θ.
(9.29)

The common term cancels exactly when the branches are subtracted. Additivity here comes from the adopted charge-preserving generator. Nucleon frequency shifts do not acquire an additional factor from the charged elementary-state frequency shift of Section 8.1.

9.5 Resonance Between Nucleons

When two nucleons interact, exchange acts between their complete states. The common collective structure supplies the scope of participation, while internal representations determine how vertices connect initial and final states. The emission–propagation–absorption process of Chapter 3 continues to apply, with the nuclear-force response using the channels and weights fixed in Section 7.5.

9.5.1 Internucleon Exchange

Label the two nucleons A and B, with inputs consisting of the selected complete states and environmental preparation. If each has the actual two-level port, independent complete preparation, and resonance conditions required by Section 3.1.2, three-stage exchange and retrieval can restore the mediator while retaining each source and its auxiliaries. This conditional realization provides one complete coupling construction. Multimode nucleon exchange must still use its own actual endpoints; sharing the status of stable states does not justify importing a two-level matrix. Denote available exchange modes by μ, ν, emission operators by JμJ_{μ}, absorption operators by AνA_{ν}, and the propagation matrix by GνμG_{νμ}. Under the chosen emission–propagation–absorption decomposition and product-state endpoints, the path amplitude for a specified complete output record g has the form below, with all operators and endpoints taking the corresponding components for that record:

𝒜g = ∑μ,ν⟨N′B|Aν|NB⟩ Gνμ ⟨N′A|Jμ|NA⟩.
(9.31)

The μ, ν paths not distinguished by the complete record are summed within one amplitude; mutually orthogonal final records are then summed at the probability level. If final states still overlap, the record-overlap matrix must be retained. This order places internal vertices, propagation, and actual statistics within one exchange process.

A common mode pattern does not imply automatic resonance of every nucleon transition. Phase matching involves the complete endpoint masses, internal energy-level differences, and exchange environment. Proton–neutron conversion must also balance charge and other actual conserved quantities. Comparing only the common b would omit the internal frequency shifts of Section 9.4. Elastic and inelastic processes require separately selected endpoints and energy conditions.

9.5.2 Nuclear Response and Spatial Interaction

Following Section 7.5, nucleon exchange uses 42 distinguishable complete outputs and the node weights, giving coupling αnuclear=(42/ℒ7)w1\alpha_{\mathrm{nuclear}}=(42/\mathcal L_7)w_1. Actual probabilities are fully normalized as in Section 3.5.3; the πNN comparison retains the vertex and scattering definitions of Section 7.5.

The spatial interaction below remains determined by the endpoint vertices and propagation kernel.

Interaction range, attraction or repulsion, and spin dependence in space are contained in the propagation kernel GνμG_{νμ} and endpoint vertices. A specific spatial interaction requires these operators to be connected to position readout and propagation conditions in observational spacetime. The common cycle specifies the calculation order, and Section 7.5 supplies the strength normalization under the present channel prescription.

9.6 Color Confinement and Independent Outputs

A nucleon’s internal color singlet constrains the joint representation. To determine whether a colored component can become independent matter, one must additionally follow the actual separated output and its subsequent maintenance. This section first gives a process criterion for zero colored output, then distinguishes a global singlet from local colored outputs.

9.6.1 Conditions Excluding Colored Outputs

Fix the output object under discussion and the actual formation or separation instrument. Denote the input-support projection by ΠSΠ_{S}, the output object’s color-singlet projection by ΠsingΠ_{\mathrm{sing}}, and its colored projection by Qcol=I−ΠsingQ_{\mathrm{col}}=I-Π_{\mathrm{sing}}. The colored projection is defined by the full SU(3) representation decomposition; vanishing of one cyclic label cannot replace this definition. Let the selected output process be the completely positive, trace-nonincreasing map 𝒥(ρ)=∑rKrρKr†𝒥(ρ)=\sum _{r} K_{r} ρ K_{r}^{\dagger}.

For any normalized input ψ∈ran⁡ΠSψ∈\operatorname{ran} Π_{S}, the unnormalized output share entering colored representations is a sum of squared norms. This gives the necessary and sufficient criterion:

Tr[Qcol𝒥(Pψ)] = ∑r‖QcolKrψ‖²,
Tr[Qcol𝒥(ρ)] = 0　（∀ρ=ΠSρΠS）
⇔　QcolKrΠS = 0　（∀r）
.(9.32)

The proof uses only nonnegativity of each term. If the colored share vanishes for every input, each KrK_{r} produces no colored output from any vector in the input support. Conversely, substitution gives zero, and mixed inputs follow by linearity. If 𝒥 is a conditional process, its total success probability is Tr 𝒥(ρ), and the conditional colored share must also be divided by that nonzero number. The zero condition itself is unchanged.

Representation theory supplies a sufficient condition: the input support is a color-singlet space, and every actual KrK_{r} intertwines the input and output color representations. Then for every g∈SU(3),

Uout(g)Kr = KrUin(g), 　Uin(g)ΠS = ΠS
⇒　QcolKrΠS = 0.
(9.33)

Because KrψK_{r} ψ remains invariant under every color action, it must lie in the output singlet subspace. One checkable realization is that the complete joint action preserves the color representation, the environmental preparation lies in the trivial color representation, and every environmental output actually coupled to the process also lies in the trivial representation. Only then do the corresponding environmental matrix elements individually become intertwiners.

Intertwining by each KrK_{r} is stronger than covariance of the reduced channel as a whole. If the environment can carry compensating color, the KrK_{r} may mix as a nontrivial representation while the channel remains covariant, without satisfying the termwise condition above. The no-colored-output criterion must hold for the complete actual outcome set before colored outcomes have been filtered out.

9.6.2 Color Separation and Compensation

Preservation of a total color singlet does not suffice to exclude local colored representations. The normalized singlet of a fundamental and conjugate representation provides a direct test:

|Ωc⟩ = 1√3∑a=13|a⟩⊗|ā⟩,
(U⊗Ū)|Ωc⟩ = |Ωc⟩, 　Tr₂PΩc = I₃/3.
(9.34)

The local I₃/3 is invariant as a density operator under color transformations but is supported in the three-dimensional fundamental representation, which has no singlet vector. Thus “group-invariant density operator” and “state supported in the singlet subspace” are different conditions. The same distinction applies to the one-position reduction of a nucleon’s color tensor.

Taking this partial trace does not itself accomplish physical separation. An independent output also requires a definite carrier capable of continued cycle maintenance, together with examination of its interactions and records with the system carrying compensating color. If an actual process satisfies the termwise zero condition of Section 9.6.1, that process produces no colored output. Otherwise its output branches and subsequent survival must be calculated to determine whether an independent stable state results.

Universal confinement must cover every allowed separation process. Algebraic grading and relative suppression in the complete spectrum cannot replace examination of actual outputs and subsequent survival.

The collective baryon pattern, internal flavor–spin representation, mass readout, and exchange process admit a consistent state description. Common participation gives the nucleon energy scale; the adopted internal-phase and electromagnetic prescriptions give the mass difference; complete output records determine nuclear responses and maintenance shares. Absolute stability and universal confinement require coverage of all exit and separation processes, respectively. The next chapter examines exchange-channel excitations and collective oscillations to calculate bosonic states and energy readings.

Chapter 10. Bosons

Exchange between stable states requires actual propagating components, and perturbing a condensate can produce new oscillations. In records, these appear as delivery of energy and charge, or periodic changes relative to the background. Connecting such processes to photons, W and Z bosons, gluons, pions, and the Higgs requires the carrier, transformation properties, and cycle data read as mass to be determined for each excitation.

The mass inputs here come respectively from the condensate share acquired by a channel, the two-layer response of internal nucleon transitions, and the restoring action on radial perturbations. They share the rules for amplitude composition, record summation, and phase timing. Their respective carriers, representations, and actual actions determine the physical identities of the excitations. We first establish how these inputs become cycle readings, then calculate the different masses.

10.1 Channel Excitations and Condensate Oscillations

10.1.1 Channel Excitations

The resonance process of Chapter 3 consists of emission, propagation, and absorption. Part of an initial stable state’s amplitude enters an exchange component, reaches the other endpoint through propagation, and forms an output jointly with the receiving stable state and environment. A channel specifies the charge and phase transformations permitted by this connection; the state actually propagating in that channel is the excitation. A vertex coefficient or group generator does not simultaneously specify its spatial waveform and frequency.

Section 3.1.2 already gave exchange with mediator restoration on the selected complete carrier. That mediator is an auxiliary that temporarily stores logical components within the process. Identifying one of its excitations as an independently propagating boson additionally requires a propagation space, energy, and readout; complete retrieval alone does not supply this identification.

After fixing input, output, and environmental preparation, the relevant exchange component can be written A G J: J produces the exchange component, G propagates it, and A receives it. Joint conservation in the complete process relates what the emitter loses, the exchange component carries, and the receiver gains. Orthogonal final records require probability summation, whereas paths reaching the same undistinguished record require amplitude summation first. The presence and frequency of an excitation must be read from these actual components.

Internucleon exchange involves the common collective mode and internal flavor changes; condensate oscillations involve departures and restoration of the background amplitude. They share earlier parameters with channel propagation, but their participating states, exchange actions, and readout conditions are determined by their respective processes.

10.1.2 Quantum Numbers and Mass

The internal channel carriers of this chapter retain the U(1), SU(2), and SU(3) identifications of Chapter 5. Electric and color charges act on these internal representations, while spin concerns rotations in observational space. These actions must be specified separately. In a vector propagation representation, rotations act on three spatial components; for a scalar amplitude, rotations leave it unchanged. Character order or parity under negation does not replace these rotation representations.

Calling an excitation a boson also adopts symmetric exchange for multiexcitation states. For two identical excitations, the symmetric projection of the exchange operator S12S_{12} is Π+=(I+S12)/2Π_{+}=(I+S_{12})/2, and the selected two-excitation state lies in its image. 10.2.2 Propagation and Two Polarizations

Polarization describes how the propagation amplitude varies relative to spatial directions. For an explicit readout, take a nonzero real propagation vector k∈ℝ³, a complex three-dimensional vector amplitude, and impose k·ε=0. The rotation action distinguishes the two senses of rotation; linear polarizations are their coherent combinations. The transverse constraint, vector representation, and identification between propagation vector and observed displacement are conditions of this realization. Taking χ₁ and χ₅ as internal labels for the two senses makes conjugate pairing compatible with them. Two conjugate characters alone do not conversely imply transversality.

In records, photon detection appears as a change in the receiving endpoint’s energy and state. Zero rest mass allows the corresponding propagation model to have no mass threshold, but the propagation kernel, speed, and spatial range must still follow from the actual phase–displacement relation. The two polarizations obtained here belong to the stated vector-propagation realization.

MZ/MW = √(NW/NZ) = 1.134554387139…
,
sM² = 1−NZ/NW = 0.223128193000….
(10.12)

sv2s_{v}^{2} reads the Born vertex-response ratio, while sM2s_{M}^{2} reads the two corrected masses. They use different process quantities and differ by approximately 0.00834 under the present specifications. Before comparing them with experimental definitions such as effective mixing angles or on-shell mass ratios, their vertices, scales, and schemes must be matched. Similar names do not make their numerical values interchangeable.

As a separate mass-ratio test, using MZ=91.1880GeVM_{Z}=91.1880 \mathrm{GeV} from the PDG 2025 gauge and Higgs boson summary 17 with only the ratio above gives MW=80.3734056593…GeVM_{W}=80.3734056593\ldots \mathrm{GeV}. This calculation already uses an experimental mass as its scale and tests something different from independently calculating both absolute masses from v and C*C^*. Its smaller residual cannot replace the approximately 0.25% deviations of the latter calculation.

The cited W and Z measurements use Breit–Wigner mass definitions with mass-dependent widths. Comparing cycle rest-frame frequencies with such resonance masses still requires matching mass schemes. The detailed PDG W listing 17 states that its summary excludes the CDF 2022 measurement, while the Z listing 17 also distinguishes this mass from the complex-pole definition. The same summary gives MW=80.3692±0.0133GeVM_{W}=80.3692±0.0133 \mathrm{GeV} and MZ=91.1880±0.0020GeVM_{Z}=91.1880±0.0020 \mathrm{GeV}. The present absolute evaluations are higher by 0.25396% and 0.24872%, respectively, exceeding the listed experimental uncertainties. Deviations in the same direction suggest checking the energy scale and mass-share identification together. Numerical convergence supplies no theoretical error bounds on these identifications.

10.4 Gluons

10.4.1 The Eight-Dimensional Color Channel

Color exchange acts on the three-dimensional internal carrier Vc=ℂ3V_{c}=ℂ^{3}. A local color response is represented by an operator in End⁡(Vc)\operatorname{End}(V_{c}). Separating trace and traceless parts gives

End(ℂ³) = ℂI₃ ⊕ sl₃(ℂ),
𝒞₈ := {X=X†：Tr X=0}, 　dimℝ𝒞₈ = 8.
(10.13)

A self-adjoint three-by-three matrix has nine real parameters; imposing one trace condition leaves eight. A concrete basis consists of three pairs of off-diagonal matrices Eab+EbaE_{ab}+E_{ba} and −i(Eab−Eba)-i(E_{ab}-E_{ba}), together with two independent traceless diagonal matrices. Multiplication by i gives the anti-self-adjoint convention for su(3); both conventions describe the same eight-dimensional real representation.

Color transformations act by X↦U X U†. Identifying the internal modes of channel excitations with this adjoint representation yields eight internal color directions. Propagation polarizations are counted separately through the spatial propagation representation. Whether these modes can be prepared in isolation must be tested through actual separation processes and subsequent maintenance conditions.

The trace part commutes with every color action and is a color-blind response. Its decomposition from traceless exchange follows from the representation structure. General traceless directions have nonzero commutators, so composing two color responses can again produce a color response, unlike the vanishing Abelian bracket. Concrete self-interaction strengths and occurrence rates still require actual vertices and records.

10.4.2 Mass Contributions and Independent Outputs

Under the factor identification of Chapter 5, the quadratic character χ₃ lies in the binary factor, while χ₂ and χ₄ are trivial on it. Specify that symmetry breaking acts only on that factor and that the color channel acquires no condensate mass share. Then ϖg=0ϖ_{g}=0 makes the mass contribution in Section 10.1 vanish. Preservation of the color representation alone allows positive mass: on the irreducible adjoint representation, an invariant positive mass-squared operator may be μ²I₈ for any μ²≥0. Thus Mg=0M_{g}=0 depends on the chosen mass mechanism and the absence of additional mass terms.

Gluon modes have a definite role in internal nucleon exchange. The color response of Chapter 7 and internucleon exchange of Chapter 9 already use the corresponding vertices; the adjoint representation here specifies how the excitations carry and transfer color information. Being colored and being readable are different questions, and self-adjoint color operators can contain superpositions of opposite gradings.

For a separated independent gluon output, Section 9.6 tests the complete output and subsequent maintenance on the adjoint carrier. The eight-dimensional color structure, zero mass under the adopted condensate mechanism, and conditions of independent existence each act on a clearly specified object.

10.5 Pions

10.5.1 Pion Quantum Numbers

The nucleon exchange of Chapter 9 can change internal flavor while preserving the common collective pattern. Here one color-singlet, flavor-nontrivial exchange component is identified with the pion. Its carrier includes a fundamental color representation and a conjugate representation, allowing a two-factor color singlet, unlike the three-fundamental-representation structure of a baryon.

Let |ā⟩ carry the conjugate of the fundamental representation. Use the normalized color vector ΩcΩ_{c} and the following flavor and spin components:

|Ωc⟩ = (1/√3)∑a=13|a⟩|ā⟩,
(U⊗Ū)|Ωc⟩ = |Ωc⟩, 　η₀ = (|↑↓⟩−|↓↑⟩)/√2.
(10.14)
φπ⁺ = |ud̄⟩, 　φπ⁻ = |dū⟩,

(10.15)

The antiparticle representation has the opposite charge, so the charges in these expressions add directly. Introducing an antiparticle factor is part of the physical representation identification; arithmetic χ̄ alone is not treated as an already constructed antiparticle. The spin state η₀ is invariant under total SU(2), giving S=0. For relative orbital angular momentum L=0, the total angular momentum is J=0.

Spatial inversion must be specified separately. Adopting intrinsic parities whose product for component and anticomponent is −1 gives negative total parity at L=0. The pion is then read as JP=0−J^{P}=0^{-}, a pseudoscalar. Evenness of a character under negation is not spatial parity and cannot identify the pion with the positive-parity scalar Higgs. The pion quantum numbers listed in the PDG 2025 meson summary 17 correspond to this representation realization.

These vectors provide testable internal carriers. Actual emission and absorption must still connect to nucleon endpoints, joint conservation, and complete propagation. Writing a color singlet does not by itself calculate the transition amplitude or lifetime.

10.6 Condensate Oscillations and the Higgs

10.6.1 Radial Oscillations

Condensate oscillations change the amplitude of the collective background. Let v denote the selected background scale and h a nearby real radial displacement; restoration and phase evolution of h constitute a candidate oscillation. Real h describes an amplitude coordinate and does not require every participating complex restoration mode to be a real character. The actual oscillation frequency must be read from the response or generator near that background.

In the original Higgs model, amplitude fluctuations around a symmetry-breaking background include a massive scalar excitation 31. This chapter selects an electrically neutral amplitude h that is invariant under rotations of observational space and even under spatial inversion, and identifies it with a Higgs candidate of JP=0+J^{P}=0^{+}. The trivial internal representation preserves the corresponding internal labels, while the spatial scalar property is specified by the rotation realization of h. The condensate pattern b, the trivial pole in the logarithmic spectrum, and preparation of a concrete maintainable background retain their separate definitions from Chapters 2 and 9.

This section calculates the actual return frequency of the selected radial process; Section 11.4 discusses this branch’s coverage.

Chapter 11. Spectral Completeness

The preceding chapters gave concrete representations and evaluations for elementary-state species patterns, collective baryon structures, and exchange excitations. Bringing them together raises a further question: have all allowed structures been listed, and does every listed structure correspond to a mode that can actually form and persist? Only after both ranges are established does completeness of the matter and force inventory have a definite meaning.

This chapter tests the inventory at three levels of the same objects: whether species bases and representations cover the stated space, whether actual cycles preserve candidate carriers, and whether unlisted modes can form, persist, and be read. Construction parameters remain an odd prime pp and finite depth KK, with the physical identifications for p=7p=7 following Chapter 5. Completeness of structural classification and exhaustion of the physical spectrum are assessed separately at these levels.

11.1 Elementary States and Generation Structure

11.1.1 Species Layer and Complete Direction Space

Character orthogonality within shells in Section 2.2.1 gives p−1p-1 orthonormal directions in the modulo-p species layer, whose trivial direction is the unit-shell average state e0e_0. Thus

ℋsp = ℂe₀ ⊕ 𝓜sp,

.(11.2)

For p=7p=7, the five nontrivial labels exhaust the species layer ℳsp\mathcal M_{\mathrm{sp}}, while the complete direction space has dimension 7K−K−17^K-K-1. Actual modes in the remaining shells and higher-conductor directions are tested by the return criterion of Section 11.5.

Following Sections 2.2.3 and 5.1, nontrivial species split into one real direction and several complex-conjugate pairs. Writing m=(p−1)/2 gives

p−2 = 1＋2·(p−3)/2,

{χ₃}, {χ₂,χ₄}, {χ₁,χ₅}；

Under the physical identifications of Chapter 5, Chapter 8 lists three mass readings each for neutrinos, charged leptons, up-type quarks, and down-type quarks, twelve in total. Antiparticles, color, and spin enter through the complete representations. Table 11-1 gives the actual mode coverage of this inventory.

11.1.3 Pattern-Preserving Modes

First classify the pattern-preserving modes of the shell-preserving spectral response TT. Suppose it is diagonal in the character basis of the space under consideration, Tfa=RχafaTf_a=R_{\chi_a}f_a. Writing an arbitrary vector as ψ=∑acafa\psi=\sum_ac_af_a gives

Tψ = λψ　⇔　(Rχₐ−λ)ca = 0　（∀a）,
λ ≠ 0.
(11.5)

Comparing coefficients shows that nonzero pattern-preserving states lie precisely in eigenspaces of nonzero eigenvalues. Components with different complex eigenvalues cannot mix within one mode; components with the same eigenvalue may be coherently superposed arbitrarily. Equal moduli with different phases do not suffice to preserve the whole pattern. Although the zero eigenspace belongs to the expansion basis, it does not satisfy the nonzero-return condition used here.

An eigenspace of dimension two or greater contains infinitely many distinct pure-state rays, but each ray does not introduce another particle species. Physical species also depend on symmetry representations, readable distinctions, and complete cycles. For a simple spectrum, each nonzero eigenspace is one character direction; with degeneracy, the proper object of classification is the whole eigenspace.

These eigenspaces exhaust nonzero pattern-preserving modes of the given spectral response TT. The complete return also includes internal-mode mixing and transfer to the background. Its classification uses the common-eigenvector conditions of Section 11.5, applied to the complete joint carrier or, once intertwining holds, to the corresponding logical space.

11.3 Forces and Channel Excitations

11.3.1 Complete Classification of Factor-Preserving Actions

Elementary resonance channels are organized by the single-factor effective actions of Chapter 3. The coverage criterion must apply to the object that actually persists. For the construction in Chapter 2, one may calculate on the complete joint carrier or move to its logical space when the intertwining relation holds. Retained sources, auxiliaries, and permanent records must be consistent with that representation. Fix such a finite carrier, the environmental preparation per round, and the return outcomes under consideration. Denote the return Kraus operators by RaR_a. 12.4 Closing Remarks

This paper connects the persistence of matter with its interactions. Stable states form through exchange with the background and sustain themselves through subsequent propagation and return. Their masses and modes of participation in interactions are studied on these persistently evolving objects. Matter’s structure, mass, and forces thereby acquire a common dynamical description, with mass-spectrum and coupling calculations giving this connection quantitative content. Internal references and records further connect these processes to observational spacetime, allowing matter, the background, and their observable changes to be described within one state space.

This common description rests on three basic relations: excitations are countable, energies of independent systems add, and independent states compose multiplicatively. Combining countable objects corresponds to addition, independent pairing to multiplication, and distributivity expresses compatibility of these two forms of composition. Unique factorization of natural numbers and the logarithmic energy spectrum further connect compositional structure with energy:

n=∏ppap,H=log⁡n=∑paplog⁡p. n=\prod_p p^{a_p},\qquad H=\log n=\sum_p a_p\log p. (12.10)

The Bost–Connes system combines this multiplicative structure with time evolution, while finite pp-adic reduction provides a concrete state space for excitations, propagation, and exchange. Countability, additivity, and multiplicative composition thus run through the combination of excitations and their energy description, supplying a common arithmetic foundation for this paper’s connection of matter, forces, and spacetime.
